Infantino remains under major pressure in his role following a summer full of controversy surrounding the World Cup.

3 Wenger has been told to run against the under-pressure Infantino in the next FIFA presidential election Credit: Getty

His creation of the FIFA Peace Prize, a phone call with Donald Trump regarding Folarin Balogun's red card at the 2026 World Cup and his subsequently exposed plans to sell off stakes in the tournament (FFE) have led to backlash from the world of football.

The Italian went on to scrap FFE, but he isn't planning on resigning, intending to stand again for FIFA's presidency instead.

But that hasn't stopped people from hitting out at him, with UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin the latest to do so again.

In a recent address to the European Football Clubs (EFC) general assembly, Ceferin didn't mention Infantino by name, but largely hinted that things need to change at FIFA.

“An emperor is persuaded that he is wearing magnificent clothes – clothes which, he is told, only the foolish or unfit cannot see," he said. "His court goes along with it. Until a child simply says aloud what everyone can see: the emperor is naked. Perhaps the moral of the story is this: convenient words cannot change uncomfortable realities."

Ceferin added: "Imagine that he creates a Peace Prize for a political leader without his own board having any say in its creation or its recipient.

"Then the same political leader calls, during the biggest competition in world football, to complain about a decision on the pitch, the rules say one thing, the phone rings and the decision changes.

"Well my friends, it's time to say enough."

Could Wenger replace Infantino?

A FIFA council meeting will take place in October, with the next presidential elections scheduled for March 2027.

But will voters say 'enough' as Ceferin called for? And if they do, who could be the person to replace Infantino?

3 UEFA president Ceferin has slammed Infantino and called for change at the top of FIFA Credit: Getty

3 And Wenger has been urged by Jordan to be that change, taking over from Infantino Credit: Getty

talkSPORT's Simon Jordan agreed with Ceferin that a change needs to be made and the cycle of presidents corrupted by power.

"Ceferin has resonance in what he is saying," Jordan said. "We are looking at Infantino's attitude and the fact that he has gotten drunk on his own power and influence.

"This is a system thing. If the system keeps on throwing out people who get into positions of great authority and don't do the things they should be doing as an NFP (not-for-profit organisation), whose sole function in life is to protect the values of the game, how do you get these people repeatedly thrown into these positions that replicate each time the next incarnation comes up?"

Jordan then urged Wenger to run for the position to bring his values and love for the game to the forefront of FIFA.

The legendary Arsenal manager has been FIFA's Chief of Global Football Development since 2019 and has often been lauded for his impact on the sport and new rule suggestions.

"I think he [Infantino] is now [open to reform]," Jordan said. "Stand against him Ceferin, or someone like that. Or Wenger.

What has Wenger said on Infantino? Wenger released a statement denying any involvement in Infantino's controversial FFE plans in a statement last month. He said: "The recent events at FIFA deserve some clarity from my side. "At FIFA, I am the Chief of Global Football Development. "Together with my team, I oversee the data analysis of the game, the FIFA online training centre, the development of youth education through 60 academies across 60 countries where they are most needed, and youth competitions around the world. "In addition, I am a technical adviser to IFAB. "I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports. "The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent FIFA that serves our game with commitment, transparency, and integrity."

"Wenger will be distancing himself, like Wile E. Coyote, from Gianni Infantino in terms of what Infantino has said and done.

"Wenger is all about the purity of football and the value of football to the society that it seeks to serve.

"Someone like Wenger...he's a very intelligent man. Stand against Infantino, create different outcomes if that's what you want."

Sports.title: Man City face lawsuit of at least £400m and future chaos as rivals sharpen knives after verdict
Sports.content:
Man City face lawsuit of at least £400m and future chaos as rivals sharpen knives after verdict

Manchester City have been warned they face 'years and years' of legal cases if their Premier League rivals sue them for damages.

Prior to the verdict in the club's Premier League financial rules case, four top-flight sides pre-reserved their right to sue City for damages.



4 The walls are closing in on City but they still maintain their innocence Credit: Getty

talkSPORT's Ben Jacobs has now detailed how Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur could seek over £100million each, and could even join forces to pursue a mammoth lawsuit against them.

Meanwhile, additional legal challenges from other Premier League clubs past and present could follow along with sides across Europe seeking damages of their own.

talkSPORT previously revealed clubs were considering launching collective legal action in light of the independent commission's ruling.



City have been found guilty of all charges against them, the Premier League announced on Tuesday.

The club are expected to appeal against the decision, having been given a deadline of Friday to respond to the verdict.



City face potential £400m lawsuit

Providing an update on what is set to come next for City, Jacobs explained: "Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal and Spurs have all pre-reserved their rights to sue Manchester City for damages, predominantly for seasons where they missed out on Champions League football or potentially silverware.

"Each could seek over £100million, but you have a wider issue for City if found guilty subject to appeal and that is collective action.



"There’s two routes. One is the clubs could pool together and start their own individual action for compensation, but for one lump payment distributed in different ways.

"Or the simpler legal solution is for the Premier League to take class action for damages and then choose how to distribute it.

"You could say clubs that went down might want compensation. You could say at a very base level, clubs that feel Manchester City should be removed from the league in those seasons bump themselves up a place and that’s a little bit extra prize money.

4 United are one of four Premier League clubs who have pre-reserved their right to sue City for damages Credit: Getty



"You’ll have teams that missed out on European football and silverware. So this is a very complicated legal situation.

"Whereas the City case can hopefully resolve itself before the season is out, the damages if they’re found guilty subject to appeal could lead to years and years and years of legal cases.

"This is why certain clubs like the four I mentioned are already prepared.

"There’s even a chance European clubs look at the situation and they lost out to Manchester City in the Champions League in some of the seasons in question and they decide they’re entitled to something as well."



City's offences took place between 2009 and 2018, a period in which they did not finish lower than fifth in the Premier League.

They also won three titles and failed to qualify for the Champions League just once, in the 2009/10 campaign.

4 City won three Premier League titles during the nine-year period in which their offences took place Credit: Getty

The club won a further FA Cup, Community Shield and three League Cups as well as reaching the semi-finals of the Champions League in 2016.



talkSPORT understands Premier League clubs are set to contact chief executive Richard Masters to stress the need for a conclusion to the case before the end of this season including appeals.

Independent Football Regulator latest

Following the confirmation of the independent commission's verdict, several other bodies could also look through the case against City.

Amongst them is the Independent Football Regulator, which was created in September 2025, two-and-a-half years after City were first charged.

Explaining how the regulator could become involved, Jacobs added: "The Independent Football Regulator was not around when this case started.



"It is now and they have the power and the ability to effectively re-review directors and owners.

4 The Independent Football Regulator could re-review City's owners and directors as well as looking into the case Credit: Getty

"So as this case comes to a close, sources tell me the Independent Football Regulator wants to also comb through everything regarding the owners and individual directors to determine whether any other action is necessary.

"The same applies to the FA as well. With Chelsea, it was a Premier League settlement plus an FA settlement plus a UEFA settlement.



"It’s going to be very interesting to see whether other regulators and bodies read the evidence and feel the need to act."

Chelsea were handed a record £10.75million fine and a suspended transfer ban in March for breaching Premier League rules regarding payments to agents.

Independent Football Regulator statement

The chair of the Independent Football Regulator, David Kogan has also released a statement regarding City's case.

He stated: "The independent commission’s decision raises serious issues.



"The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals.

"This includes taking account of findings made by the leagues. However, as the proceedings remain ongoing between Manchester City and the Premier League we will await further developments.

"We hope it can be resolved quickly for the sake of fans. For now, we have no further comment."

Sports.title: Golf star Phil Mickelson checked into addiction treatment facility because of 'family trauma'
Sports.content:
Phil Mickelson entered an addiction treatment center amid ongoing personal issues, according to a report.

The professional golfer, 56, is said to have checked into the undisclosed facility recently to seek 'treatment for family trauma and addiction,' a spokesperson for Mickelson told TMZ.

The six-time major champion, who has previously opened up on his struggles with a gambling addiction, is believed to have already left the center.

The Daily Mail has contacted Mickelson's representatives for comment.

The news comes after Mickelson stepped away from professional golf on the LIV Golf circuit and at this year's major championships.

He missed the start of the LIV Golf season, returned for one tournament in South Africa in March, but then stepped away again, even pulling out of the Masters and the Open Championship.

Phil Mickelson entered an addiction treatment center amid ongoing personal issues

Mickelson is pictured with his wife, Amy, at the 2012 Ryder Cup gala in Illinois

At the time, Mickelson cited an unspecified private family matter involving his wife, Amy, for his absence.

Mickelson has been married to Amy, 54, for almost 30 years after tying the knot back in November 1996. The couple share three children together in Evan, Sophie and Amanda.

The left-handed legend has been candid about his struggles with gambling, previously opening up on his addiction in 2023.

He said at the time that he had 'crossed the line from moderation into addiction which isn't fun at all.'

'The money wasn't ever the issue since our financial security has never been threatened, but I was so distracted I wasn't able to be present with the ones I love and caused a lot of harm,' he said.

He also described how this 'lack of presence' has been 'so hurtful' for his family, saying he's been 'often' told throughout his addiction, 'You're here, but you're not with us.'

'It affected those I care about in ways I wasn't aware or could fully understand,' Mickelson said. 'It's like a hurricane is going on outside and I'm isolated in a shelter oblivious to what was happening.'

'When I came out there was so much damage to clean up that I just wanted to back inside and not deal with it,' he added.

The golf icon has been married to wife Amy for close to 30 years. They share three children

Mickelson and Amy are pictured with their children, Evan, Sophie and Amanda, after his victory at the 2013 Open Championship

Mickelson has also made headlines this year for a series of alleged scandals and bombshell sexual misconduct accusations.

In June, Golf Digest reported that Mickelson had been removed as a member of The Farms Golf Club in Rancho Santa Fe, California, amid allegations of inappropriate physical contact with a female staff member.

According to multiple sources, Mickelson approached the employee in the clubhouse, made non-consensual and inappropriate physical contact with her, and he was confronted by club officials mid-round before being told to vacate the premises.

A representative confirmed he had resigned from the club.

A separate report from Skratch later painted the incidents as part of a deeply entrenched pattern of behavior. Mickelson had previously departed two other high-end clubs - the Madison Club and The Bridges, also in Rancho Santa Fe - with sources at both allegedly saying personal conduct was a primary factor.

Mickelson hit back at the allegations through his attorney, Tom Clare, at the time.

'There is a great deal of misinformation circulating and, while Phil's full attention is devoted to a private family health matter, he has retained defamation counsel and is determined to hold accountable any publication or individual trafficking in speculation or false rumors,' Clare said in a statement.

Mickelson's spokespeople also claimed that he has 'never been expelled from a golf club' and that the decision to leave said clubs was 'his alone.'

The golfer and his wife are seen taking in the action on the Sunday of the 2021 Ryder Cup

Mickelson was accused of showing a photo of himself naked and erect to Ashley Perez (left) in 2015, then-wife of fellow golfer Pat Perez

Just over a week later, however, Mickelson was accused of showing a nude photo to a fellow professional's wife in a bombshell report on his private life published by Skratch - written by legendary golf writer Alan Shipnuck.

In the piece, Mickelson is accused of allegedly showing a naked photograph of himself with an erect penis to the then-wife of fellow Tour professional Pat Perez during a tournament in 2015.

Ashley Perez, who was married to Pat from 2014 to 2023, told the outlet the incident occurred during the Barclays tournament in New Jersey, when Mickelson arranged for the couple to join him at his villa at Liberty National Golf Course.

While Pat had excused himself to use the restroom, leaving Ashley and Mickelson alone on the patio, she claims the six-time major champion produced his phone and showed her a full-body image of himself naked and aroused.

'Phil says to me, 'I'm going to leave my bedroom door open tonight. When Pat falls asleep I want you to come see me',' Ashley told Shipnuck.

According to the outlet, she said she declined his advances and did not immediately tell her husband, saying she had not wanted to create a scene mid-tournament.

When Perez was eventually told, he confronted Mickelson - who the outlet reports ultimately apologized during a corporate outing at the Madison Club in La Quinta, California.

The allegation became central to Perez's now-notorious comments on Claude Harmon's podcast in November 2022, when he said: 'I have a different hate for Phil than most people.

Ashley Perez told Skratch that Mickelson apologized during an awkward 26-minute call

'Phil crossed the line with me that is just uncrossable and unforgivable. He knows that he screwed up. He apologized for the action, but I cannot forgive him for it.'

Ashley Perez says she has a recording of a subsequent 26-minute phone call between Pat and Mickelson. During it, she claims, Mickelson alternated between contrition and saying he could not remember the details of the evening. Shipnuck also reports he has listened to the recording.

When Pat told him he had shown Ashley 'a naked photo', Mickelson is alleged to have responded: 'You mean topless?'

Without fully admitting what had happened, Mickelson is said to have told the couple: 'I can't tell you how disgusted and embarrassed I am in myself.'

A spokesperson for the golfer told the Daily Mail earlier this year: 'Some of the allegations circulating about Mr. Mickelson are false, and others revisit mistakes he has already acknowledged, publicly or privately. Stacking the disputed claims next to the ones he has owned does not make them credible. It instead contributes to a false and misleading narrative.

'No person, no article, and no book can present an accurate, complete, or personal story of the life Mr. Mickelson and his family have lived. His story, struggles, and recovery belong to him and to the people who have shared it closely alongside him.

'Recovery is not a straight line. Throughout their 35-year relationship, his wife, Amy Mickelson, has supported Mr. Mickelson and their family with extraordinary grace, unwavering love, and the belief that people are measured not only by their failures, but by what they do to make them right.

'Mr. Mickelson's priority is to become the husband, father, and man his family deserves. Right now, that means giving his full attention to a private family health matter. He understands that parts of his life are public, but his family's private matters are not.'

Sports.title: The six things Steve Borthwick must do to overhaul England and win the World Cup - with one year to go: Get Jack Willis and Shaun Edwards in, crack down on clubs, find midfield muscle... and a new captain?
Sports.content:
The last time Steve Borthwick appeared in public was deep beneath the Estadio Unico Madre de Ciudades in Argentina.

Borthwick has been England’s head coach for almost four years, addressing the media hundreds of times, but this was his crankiest appearance of the lot. Asking about England’s four yellow cards in their chaotic 31-24 victory over the Pumas, I was on the receiving end of a rare, spiky Borthwick response.

‘I love it,’ he said. ‘You’re my negativity committee. It’s lovely coming in and talking to you again.’

Emotion is rare in Borthwick’s press conferences – to the frustration of many English fans – so his retort took everyone by surprise. So, on a positive note, I asked whether his team is on track to win the World Cup? ‘Wow!’ he said. ‘Positivity!’ But right now, most people’s answer to my question would be: ‘No.'

Borthwick said he was happy with the progress in his young squad in his final address, leaving those in the room in a state of bemusement. I enjoyed Borthwick’s change of character – a bolt of emotion can’t do any harm – but not everyone appreciated his tone.

England had just had their worst ever Six Nations, had lost to Italy for the first time, and had been walloped by the Springboks two weeks previously, in a thumping that showed just how far Borthwick's side are from the top.

Steve Borthwick insists his team are on track to win the World Cup. Most England supporters would say otherwise

With Thursday marking one year to go until the World Cup, England are clinging on to fifth place in the world rankings.

They are a long way off South Africa, New Zealand and France but the lopsided World Cup draw – Wales, Tonga and Zimbabwe in Group F, followed by a likely last-16 clash with Italy – means they should avoid the heavyweight teams en route to next year’s final.

Despite that worst-ever Six Nations, the RFU have backed Borthwick with a token contract extension and now the focus is on how they can maximise their chances of an upset Down Under. A year out from the World Cup, this is what Borthwick needs to do to get England firing...

1. Flex their muscle

England are not blessed with world-class depth so keeping frontline players fit will be key. The likes of Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Fin Smith are central to English hopes and Borthwick should take a hardline approach with clubs to ensure their stars are not overplayed.

England's best players routinely go over their 30-game-a-season limit, increasing the risk of injury. It is a sorry reflection of an overcrowded fixture calendar.

Borthwick has the power to call the shots through the enhanced contracts and he should adopt a hardline approach over player availability. There is a high risk of angering clubs if Borthwick becomes too bullish over their selection, but it is a risk worth taking.

England need to ensure their world-class stars like Immanuel Feyi-Waboso are fit and firing, not burned out

2. Fill the midfield hole

Despite being three years into the cycle, England have still not worked out their best backline combinations.

No13 is one of their biggest problem positions. Ollie Lawrence has dropped out of the squad altogether and needs to rediscover his top-end speed for Test rugby.

Tommy Freeman has been pulled around the backline but he remains the squad’s best winger – unless the likes of Noah Caluori or George Hendy can break through at Test level.

Henry Slade is the latest incumbent of the jersey but Borthwick has never been entirely convinced by the Exeter star, who was left out of the 2023 World Cup squad.

Joe Marchant is now eligible for selection after returning from France and he could be fast-tracked if he discovers his best form at Sale.

Tommy Freeman is an option to fill England's problem position at No13 but he is still Borthwick's best winger

3. Give Edwards a chance

France’s decision to terminate Shaun Edwards’ contract has left some people questioning the Englishman’s stock. Yet there is no question he brings a winning mentality and has a wealth of insight on one of England’s biggest rivals.

As Ben Kay said this week: ‘If you speak to anyone who has worked with Shaun, they all say he made you feel you could do something that little bit more. That can be invaluable.’

Edwards, one of the most decorated coaches in rugby history, remains on the market long-term but is already under the RFU umbrella in his role as a consultant with England's women's side.

Borthwick has nothing to lose by testing out another short-term consultancy arrangement during the autumn.

Shaun Edwards, one of the most decorated coaches in rugby history, remains on the market long-term but is already under the RFU umbrella as a consultant with England's women's side

4. Fix the captaincy

Maro Itoje looked red hot on the opening round of the PREM but England now have fierce competition in their lock stocks.

With George Martin, Alex Coles and Ollie Chessum in fine form, skipper Itoje is no longer a guaranteed starter.

Jamie George has been a fine understudy but he is retiring next year and he too faces competition.

The captaincy has been dominated by Saracens players since Dylan Hartley lost the armband in 2018 but the balance of power has shifted.

Leicester's Chessum would be a popular candidate but perhaps it is time to empower the core of Northampton stars and look towards Smith.

With the likes of Ollie Chessum (left) and Alex Coles (second left) in fine form, Maro Itoje (right) is no longer a guaranteed starter

5. Get Willis

The ‘exceptional circumstance’ clause has long hung over the RFU’s stance on not selecting overseas-based players.

This week, Jack Willis was named the Top 14’s player of the season for the second straight year, captaining a Toulouse team that stars Antoine Dupont and Thomas Ramos.

Borthwick has toed the party line and refused to engage in debates about Willis.

But the flanker has been playing exceptionally well and he would walk into England's team as the starting No 7.

Jack Willis (centre, to left of trophy) is captain of the best team in France - but England still refuse to budge on their policy of letting overseas-based players represent their country

6. Establish an identity

During the Six Nations, Borthwick changed his entire backline throughout the tournament.

Against Ireland he selected Alex Mitchell, George Ford, Henry Arundell, Fraser Dingwall, Ollie Lawrence, Tommy Freeman and Freddie Steward. Against France he went for Ben Spencer, Fin Smith, Cadan Murley, Seb Atkinson, Tommy Freeman, Tom Roebuck and Elliot Daly. Neither would be his first-choice backline this autumn.

There is no doubt that certain players suit certain opponents but Borthwick needs to double down on a playing philosophy as the team’s DNA.

The attacking display in France for the final round of the Six Nations should be the blueprint – despite the night ending in a 48-46 defeat.

Sports.title: Inside Ferran Soriano's role in Man City scandal: Premier League sources reveal how 'aloof' Spaniard 'patronises' other clubs, how his fingerprints are on key documents and why he left some Etihad staff feeling like outsiders
Sports.content:
Inside Ferran Soriano's role in Man City scandal: Premier League sources reveal how 'aloof' Spaniard 'patronises' other clubs, how his fingerprints are on key documents and why he left some Etihad staff feeling like outsiders

In the small talk preceding one of the few interviews he has ever granted to the British press, Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano joked to us about how he didn’t need to impress journalists as much in this role as he did in Spain, during five years as an executive at Barcelona.

The Spanish press were his route to Barca’s members, or socios, who vote the club president in every four years, Soriano explained, in a hotel meeting room overlooking New York. ‘But in Britain, you're less interested in people like me.’

Little did he know. In the Copenhagen auditorium where European football club chiefs had gathered on Tuesday, Soriano found himself confronted by Sky’s Rob Harris and facing one of the vanishingly few moments when City can’t explain themselves through pre-prepared club videos.

‘I have nothing to say, thank you,’ said Soriano, who seemed to imagine that turning his back on the reporter would do the job. But Harris, one of the most indefatigable journalists on the long road to Tuesday’s City judgment, kept at it. Soriano scratched his nose, picked up his bag and left.

Confronting Soriano has been one of the few means of reaching behind the highly polished City veil. The BBC’s Dan Roan has approached him this way several times, too.

And though the 59-year-old stares ahead implacably each time, his job is the one that looks most vulnerable if City’s appeal fails. For a long time now, people have been very 'interested' in him.

Though Abu Dhabi and the court of its Crown Prince are at the heart of what the Premier League’s explosive verdict has described as almost £900million in ‘sham’ revenues, Soriano’s prints are certainly on some of the key documents which led to the verdicts.

Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano's job looks vulnerable if City's appeal against the Premier League fails

Rob Harris of Sky confronted Soriano in Copenhagen this week but was brushed off by the City executive

When there was a concern about City failing Financial Fair Play rules after forking out £9.9million to sack Roberto Mancini in 2013, it was Soriano, according to hacked documents published by German newspaper Der Spiegel, who suggested their Abu Dhabi sponsors cover off the heavy cost by paying City the pre-agreed bonus for winning the FA Cup in 2013… even though they lost to Wigan Athletic in the final.

City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak entered that email exchange, proposing that ‘we could do a backdated deal for the next two years, paid up front’. When chief financial officer Jorge Chumillas questioned whether the backdating suggestion would be possible, another leading executive, Simon Pearce replied: ‘Of course. We can do what we want.’

It was Soriano who sent an email, also published by Der Spiegel, that stated City needed to fight Financial Fair Play but must ‘do it in a way that is not visible, or we will be pointed out as the global enemies of football’.

Soriano's monotone video statement to City employees on Tuesday, declaring that the financial impropriety the club have been found guilty of ‘could not happen, did not happen’, even led to some on social media inaccuaretely speculating it was AI generated, partly because he does not blink once during the three-minute speech.

For City staff wondering what the future holds, it was miserably short on encouraging detail.

‘Bank statements, money transfers and witnesses’ would put things right, Soriano said, raising the inconvenient question of why, if such documents actually exist, no one had thought to present them to the commission panel in the first place.

It seems safe to say that few around the Etihad Stadium will be asking Soriano any challenging questions at the watercooler, given the uncompromising and difficult reputation he has always carried among the troops at the club. His predecessor Garry Cook, who presided over four years of ‘sham’, was at least personable.

But Soriano was detached, aloof and when he recruited a cadre of Spanish executives – a club within a club – some of the British employees were left feeling like outsiders. As Pep Guardiola arrived with his own Spanish entourage, it was a Spanish clique, in which being a Spanish speaker helped.

City's British executives joked that that you needed to be an FOF ('Friend of Ferran') or be considered of direct value to the Abu Dhabis, if you wanted to keep your job at City.

Soriano's unblinking three-minute video speech to City employees led some fans to inaccurately speculate it was AI-generated

Soriano alongside City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak after the club's Champions League triumph in 2023

Soriano certainly has a high sense of his own business acumen and had a book published on how to excel in football management, entitled 'Goal', three years before arriving at the Etihad.

The book’s subtitle, ‘The ball doesn’t go in by chance’, is an unfortunate one in retrospect for Soriano, who expounds within its pages on how you need to be one of the five or six biggest clubs in the world to get cut-through.

He cautions against cheating, telling the story of a British talent-spotter whom he found videoing an Under 13s game at Barca’s academy. After the individual was questioned at length, it emerged ‘he was gathering information for Liverpool FC’.

A cautionary tale, says Soriano, who also tells his readers to ‘limit risk’ – citing an obscure 13th century philosopher to reinforce the point. ‘The ability to make the right decision at the right point of the curve sorts the best people from the worst,’ Soriano advises. All immensely loaded in retrospect.

Those who have sat around the table with Soriano at Premier League board meetings describe an individual with great self-confidence whose belief he knows best has left smaller clubs feeling patronised.

'Put a black pepperpot on the table and he'll argue it's white,' says one executive. 'He's the one who thinks he's moving the pawns around the table,' says another.

His book came too early for Soriano to discuss his three years as the helm of Spanish airline Spanair from 2009, a year after leaving Barcelona. A plane crash at Madrid airport coupled with the effects of the 2008 financial crash left the company on its knees and it folded in 2012 with him still in charge.

Soriano was initially fined £8.6million for his role in the bankruptcy and banned from ‘managing other people’s wealth’ for two years, along with other board members, after they were found to have delayed filing for bankruptcy and continued issuing flight tickets as the company’s losses mounted.

But that court judgment was later overturned by judges who ruled there had been an intent to save the company from Soriano and his board members in the period before it went bust.

In New York, Soriano (pictured in 2013) foresaw only great things for himself and City. Now his future in football could be on the line

Now, he and his fellow City executives find themselves appealing the judgment of another adjudication panel and his future in football is on the line. In the New York hotel room, he foresaw only great things for himself and City.

We asked him that day in 2013 if he felt disquiet about the Financial Fair Play controls which established clubs like Manchester United, who had spent decades building up their business, seemed less vulnerable to.

'You know, this is arguable,’ he said. ‘But from our perspective, we want to be sustainable. When a young boy or a marquee signing comes to our club, we want him to know there are some people who are going to tell him, “This is City, this is how we play, this is how we behave”.’

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo WALKS OUT on Portugal: Star, 41, leaves camp after missing training again amid row with manager and vows to 'tell the truth' in cryptic statement
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has sparked claims he could retire from Portugal duty after he sensationally stormed out of Portugal's training camp amid a row with manager Jorge Jesus.

The star, 41, said in a statement on Instagram that he was heading home as a result of Jesus's comments in a tense press conference on Wednesday. It came after he failed to train with his Portugal team-mates for the third consecutive session.

Jesus appeared to have confirmed Ronaldo would not start the Nations League clash with Denmark, after the captain was left on the bench for the entirety of the 2-1 win over Norway on Sunday.

The Portugal boss, who also coached Ronaldo at Al-Nassr, admitted the player was 'angry' with him but insisted there were no issues between the two despite simmering tensions.

Ronaldo said: 'After the national team coach's press conference, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp.

'In due time, I will tell all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to my departure from the national team, to which I have always dedicated myself.

Após a conferência de imprensa do Selecionador Nacional, e no seguimento de uma conversa com o Presidente da Federação Portuguesa de Futebol, tomei a decisão de deixar o estágio da Seleção Nacional.



A seu tempo, direi a verdade a todos os Portugueses sobre as razões que… pic.twitter.com/j8Qrws9KTS — Cristiano Ronaldo (@Cristiano) September 30, 2026

Cristiano Ronaldo has confirmed he has left Portugal's camp amid a row with Jorge Jesus

'Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates.'

Portugal responded with a statement of their own, which read: 'Cristiano Ronaldo has left the national team camp. Our preparations for the next games continue with our 24 players with maximum focus on the results.'

Ronaldo had been seen leaving the Parken Stadium in Copenhagen while the rest of his team-mates trained. His private jet flew to the Danish city from Madrid and the player boarded the plane a short while after it landed.

The tension seems to have boiled over following Jesus' press conference. The manager said: 'There was no incident whatsoever.

'Any player - and I was a player myself - when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don't get on, no-one is happy about that.

'Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It's nothing to make a fuss about.'

Jesus also suggested Goncalo Ramos would keep his place in the side ahead of Ronaldo for the Denmark game on Thursday. 'If I need [Ronaldo], he'll come on,' he said. 'If I don't need him, he won't.'

Ronaldo had held showdown talks with Jesus in the morning, in addition to the head of the Portuguese FA following being an unused substitute in the win over Norway.

It was the first time in 18 years that Ronaldo has not featured at all for Portugal – aside from injury or suspension absences.

At full-time on Sunday, Ronaldo stormed straight down the tunnel and did not return to thank the travelling fans alongside his team-mates.

Footage of the moment Ronaldo left the team camp has emerged on social media

Jesus had originally planned to bring on the veteran striker for a 30-minute cameo but then decided to leave him on the bench.

Reports in Portugal claimed the talks between Ronaldo and Jesus were 'calm and cordial', but his decision to leave the squad suggests otherwise.

The shocking move means that Ronaldo will not be involved in his country's next game against Denmark.

It is an inauspicious start to the relationship between Jesus and Ronaldo, who opted not to retire from international duty after the World Cup.

Only a week ago, Ronaldo reiterated his commitment to the cause, saying: 'I had a conversation with our president, with our coach (about his future).

'I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want, and will finish when I feel like I'm not doing anything here.

'I think I can give to the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football.

'This is a new young generation. But for me the basic point is to be able on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games.'

Ronaldo will turn 42 in February and has scored three goals in five games for Al-Nassr so far in the Saudi Pro League this season.

Jesus and Ronaldo worked together successfully for a year when the 72-year-old was in charge of Al-Nassr but they could be on a collision course if the forward's playing time remains limited.

The 41-year-old was an unused substitute in Portugal's game with Norway on Sunday

Roberto Martinez stepped down after Portugal's 1-0 World Cup defeat by Spain and when Jesus was announced as his successor, he was asked the Ronaldo question.

Jesus insisted: 'As long as he's playing and is in a condition to be selected, I will pick him, within certain limits and under the conditions that I consider best for the national team.'

Ramos, 25, scored the winner against Norway on Sunday and is considered by many to be the natural evolution up front for Portugal.

But it seems as long as Ronaldo is around the national side, the five-time Ballon d'Or winner's playing demands will continue to be an issue for the new boss.

Sports.title: Man City's major sponsor Etihad considers legal action against Premier League after claims the airline was at the centre of 'sham' sponsorship deals
Sports.content:
Man City's major sponsor Etihad considers legal action against Premier League after claims the airline was at the centre of 'sham' sponsorship deals

Etihad Airways – the principal sponsor of Manchester City – is considering legal action against the Premier League after it was implicated in its bombshell ruling that the club breached its financial rules.

In an explosive statement, obtained by Daily Mail Sport, that further escalates the war dominating English football, the Abu Dhabi-based airline ruled to be at the centre of a series of ‘sham’ inflated sponsorship deals actually funded by City’s owners, says it ‘categorically rejects’ the findings of the competition’s commission and warns it is now seeking legal advice on next steps.

On Tuesday, the Premier League published the long-awaited, seismic verdict of an independent panel which stated that the club had disguised funding of more than £830million via a series of commercial deals between 2009 and 2018, when it won eight trophies. It found that of the £949.94m City claimed to have brought in, only £119.25m was legitimate, with the rest coming from owners the Abu Dhabi United Group and that in total it cooked the books to the tune of £900m.

While Etihad were not named in the judgement, it is the longstanding sponsor of City’s stadium, kit and training centre in a relationship with the club that stretches back to 2009. In 2011 it penned a £400m, 10-year deal that has since been extended.

City will appeal the devastating findings, in which they were found guilty on all substantive charges, and which could result in points deductions, relegation transfer bans. They have until Friday to do so.

But in another seismic development, state-owned Etihad – worth around $5billion – has now gone into battle.

The Abu Dhabi-based airline ruled to be at the centre of a series of ‘sham’ inflated sponsorship deals actually funded by City’s owners, says it ‘categorically rejects’ the verdict

They say that ‘at no time’ did the Premier League engage with them during the process and point out that they were never given a right of reply or an opportunity to ‘provide relevant information’.

They add that the ruling has ‘created damaging implications for Etihad’ and warn that the Premier League ‘must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented’.

The development came hours after Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Manchester, said he would be ‘really concerned to lose’ City’s owners, who have heavily invested in transforming areas of east Manchester close to the club’s stadium.

Football’s independent regulator, which has the power to kick out owners it deems unfit, said yesterday that the decision ‘raises serious issues’ and restated its powers to ‘assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives’, adding that it would ‘use these powers where appropriate’, while Burnham warned subsequently that it would be wrong to jump to conclusions.

An Etihad spokesperson said: ‘Etihad categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements. The Premier League’s public communication of the Commission’s findings, following a period of selective leaks and reporting, has further created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings.

They added: ‘At no time did the Premier League reach out to or engage with Etihad in the process associated with the Commission’s opinion. Etihad was therefore never given the opportunity by the Premier League to be represented, to provide relevant information, or to ensure the accuracy and fairness of information relied upon in reaching conclusions that may now be interpreted as reflecting adversely on the airline.’

In what is clearly a warning to competition bosses, the statement went on: ‘Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly. The lack of clarity and transparency, together with the selective disclosure of information, has created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the published decision. The Premier League must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented.’

The spokesperson reaffirmed the airline’s commitment to City which ‘remains strong’.

‘We stand with the Club, its supporters and our wider Etihad community as Manchester City challenges the Commission’s conclusions through the processes available to it,’ it added, before concluding: ‘Etihad will seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests.’

Earlier, Burnham had hailed City’s owners, who arrived in 2008.

‘They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester,’ he added. ‘‘I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad and the campus around it, but also into the city.’

‘I can’t intervene more in the process. It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail, but obviously it’s ongoing, and because it’s still contested by Manchester City, then I think it’s right that I don’t say much more.’

Burnham, an avid Everton supporter, campaigned for his club when they fell foul of the Premier League’s spending rules in 2023-24.

‘I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time,’ he said, ‘and with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled. So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I’d had before becoming prime minister.’

The Premier League has been contacted for comment.

Sports.title: Ricky Hatton left £30MILLION estate after his tragic death, new figures reveal, as son Campbell claims family are 'completely in the dark' amid dispute over late boxer's finances
Sports.content:
Ricky Hatton reportedly amassed a £30million fortune before his death last year, though uncertainty remains over how the boxing legend's estate will be distributed.

Hatton, who died aged 46 last September, won multiple world titles before using his fight earnings to build a business empire worth more than £20million, with at least another £10m tied up in property investments, according to The Sun.

Trustees were appointed to manage Hatton's estate after he took his own life in September last year.

However, sources close to the family claim communication with the trustees has since broken down, with one describing the situation as a 'complete mess', according to an earlier report in The Sun.

It was thought Hatton had intended for his fortune to pass to his three children, Campbell, 25, and daughters Millie, 14, and Fearne, 12. However, a year after his death, the family are still waiting to learn how and when the estate will be distributed.

Campbell told The Sun on Wednesday: 'My family is still completely in the dark. We’ve had no involvement in my dad’s finances for over 15 years.'

Hatton, who died aged 46 last September, won multiple world titles before using his fight earnings to build a business and property empire

It was thought Hatton had intended for his fortune to pass to his three children, Campbell, 25 (above), and daughters Millie, 14, and Fearne, 12

During his successful boxing career, Hatton used his fight earnings to finance a string of businesses, many of them linked to property investments in his hometown of Hyde, as well as in Leicestershire, London and Kent.

One source said Hatton was 'determined to ensure that he had a financial legacy from his incredible career'.

'Everyone who knew and loved Ricky would give anything to have him back. But during his life he's done a great job of providing for the people he loved the most, his children,' the source added.

Earlier this month, the Daily Mail reported that Hatton's house had been sold for £1.5m this year after £350,000 was knocked off the original asking price.

The house, where Hatton was found in September last year, was put up for sale shortly before his death for £1.85million but was later taken off the market following his tragic death.

The mansion then went back on offer for £1.75million, then £1.65million before it was sold for £1.5million.

It was described by the estate agent as being a 'landmark modern residence offering luxury, space and unrivalled lifestyle features'.

It said that the five-bedroom six-bathroom property, which was built in 2010, had been 'impeccably designed'.

One source said Hatton was 'determined to ensure that he had a financial legacy from his incredible career'

Hatton put his own stamp on the property, decorating it with personal touches including a traditional telephone box in the garden and an array of Manchester City memorabilia. Among its more unusual features are seats salvaged from the club's former Maine Road stadium.

It has extensive landscaped grounds with greenbelt views, plus a leisure suite with a heated indoor pool and jacuzzi.

A private gym and cinema room complement a games room and bar area, which is separated from the pool by a striking glass wall.

The principal bedroom suite features a walk-in dressing room, a luxurious en suite bathroom, a crushed-velvet chaise longue and dark patterned wallpaper.

Elsewhere, the property offers multiple reception rooms and expansive open-plan living areas centred around a high-specification, dark-panelled kitchen.

Situated in the sought-after area of Gee Cross in Greater Manchester, the estate is equipped with advanced security features, including CCTV.

The estate agents said: 'This is a rare opportunity to acquire a truly outstanding home in one of the North West's most prestigious and sought-after residential locations.'

For confidential support, call Samaritans on 116 123, visit samaritans.org or visit thecalmzone.net/get-support.

Sports.title: Moment Arsenal star Leah Williamson concedes bizarre penalty after handling the ball in the area as Gunners throw away two-goal lead against Paris FC
Sports.content:
Leah Williamson gave away a bizarre penalty as Arsenal threw away a two-goal lead to draw with Paris FC in the Women's Champions League.

Renee Slegers' side have struggled to find the back of the net this season, but Alessia Russo ended her goalscoring drought with a clinical finish in the 41st minute.

Georgia Stanway then joined her Lioness team-mate in getting her first goal of the campaign in the 50th minute, her first since signing for the north London club from Bayern Munich in the summer.

But Paris FC bided their time, scoring a wonderful goal on the counter 20 minutes later before a miscommunication between Williamson and Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez led to a penalty in the 87th minute.

It appeared Williamson thought Rodriguez had thrown her the ball, and she handled it to place it on the edge of the six-yard box to take the goal kick herself.

The problem was that Rodriguez had in fact kicked the ball to Williamson and, with play considered live, the referee judged it to be handball and pointed to the penalty spot.

WOW! What on earth has happened here? 😮



Arsenal's Leah Williamson concedes a bizarre penalty to give Paris FC a penalty 👀



📺 Watch the UEFA Women’s Champions League live on @DisneyPlusUK pic.twitter.com/T3MWzaFzAC — ESPN UK (@ESPNUK) September 30, 2026

Arsenal vice-captain Leah Williamson gave away a bizarre penalty as Arsenal threw away a two-goal lead to draw with Paris FC in the Women's Champions League

According to IFAB's Laws of the Game, a goal kick is in play once the ball is stationary and 'is kicked from any point within the goal area by a player of the defending team'. Replays showed the ball had come to a stop after Rodriguez threw it onto the pitch before kicking it to Williamson, meaning the referee's decision was correct.

Williamson looked visibly devastated by the incident as Maeline Mendy stepped up to convert the equaliser.

After the match, Slegers came under scrutiny for choosing to skip the post-match press conference, instead sending assistant coach Aaron D'Antino to meet the media.

D'Antino said: 'We didn’t think it was a penalty, we don’t think the goal kick had actually been taken for what we had seen. But it goes to VAR and apparently that’s a penalty.

'It's just passing the ball to Leah from what I remember seeing, the ball was still rolling and she was moving it to Leah for her to take the goal kicks as we normally do.'

Slegers is under pressure heading into this weekend's match against champions Manchester City, with Arsenal having won just one of their opening four WSL games and only managing a narrow 1-0 win in their Champions League opener against HB Koge last week.

After making statement signings in the summer, including star midfielder Stanway and World Cup winner Ona Batlle, Arsenal were widely expected to challenge for the title this season.

They are now seven points behind league leaders City, and defeat at the weekend could effectively end their title hopes before the race has properly begun.

Sports.title: Dock points for NINE years, force Abu Dhabi owners to sell up and a walk of shame down to League TWO: Our experts have their say on Man City's fate after club found guilty of £900m 'sham'
Sports.content:
Dock points for NINE years, force Abu Dhabi owners to sell up and a walk of shame down to League TWO: Our experts have their say on Man City's fate after club found guilty of £900m 'sham'

English football was left stunned on Tuesday with the verdict that Manchester City cooked the books to the tune of £900m in a nine-year period peppered with ‘sham’ sponsorship deals, all in a bid to pump money into the club and swerve Premier League spending rules.

City were found guilty of ‘all charges related to serious breaches’ of the regulations and the majority of those in relation to its failure to co-operate with the competition’s probe.

The club will appeal against the verdict, but with a sanctions hearing due before that appeal is heard, our experts have their say on what the punishment should be...

IAN HERBERT: The owners must be forced to sell... but rivals should say no to compensation

The Premier League should relegate Manchester City and make the provision for them to face a 20-point deduction in each of the next three seasons. Fines and points deductions will be immaterial to them and straight relegation would mean them enjoying a joyful next campaign thumping everyone in the Championship. That should not be permissible.

City’s typically aggressive response on Tuesday – alleging bias against them by describing the adjudication panel as a ‘Premier League commission’ – should be deemed an aggravating factor, as should another drawn-out appeal, were that to fail.

The Independent Football Regulator must force a sale of the club whose Abu Dhabi owners have brought British football into disrepute and breached a signed undertaking to run City with integrity. The club should be stripped of their titles.

For the benefit of the game, other clubs should sign an amnesty agreement, agreeing not to further line lawyers' pockets by seeking compensation.

City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and CEO Ferran Soriano have both pleaded the club's innocence

OLIVER HOLT: Start again in League Two - and yes, they should be stripped of titles

Like a lot of people, I suspect, my views on what should happen to City are hardening as new details of their wrong-doing are released. The scale of it emphasises the extent of the advantage they gained.

It also emphasises how difficult it was for those abiding by the rules to compete with City. If City's appeal fails, they should be expelled from the Premier League and made to start again in League Two.

Instinctively, I don't like the idea of stripping a club of titles won but I don't see any alternative in this case. The fault in those punishments is that the fans, who are blameless in all this, pay the price.

But the ownership should be made to pay a price, too. They cannot be allowed to remain as custodians of a great club they have brought so low.

TOM COLLOMOSSE: Guarantee relegation - then make the system fairer

Speed is essential here. For too long, too many commentators have responded to every development in this saga with ‘Oh, it will take years.’ Enough of that, for Goodness sake.

We have already taken far too much time to reach this point and waiting for more months or – God forbid – years for the outcome will do untold damage, not only to the Premier League but to English football. Of course, Manchester City have the right to appeal. But if someone is found guilty of a crime, the sentence arrives before the appeal. If the opposite happens in this case, it will lead only to more chaos.

Sergio Aguero's famous goal against QPR in 2012 gave City their first league title since 1968

The punishment should come swiftly and should be a points deduction this season large enough that relegation is virtually guaranteed. That should be followed by a points deduction next season, and a fixed compensation bill to all affected clubs – as proposed by former Aston Villa CEO Christian Purslow. This is far more effective than stripping titles.

Finally, we need a more equitable system of financial rules. It feels uncomfortable that clubs like Tottenham and Manchester United can underperform season on season yet continue to spend vast sums on transfers just because they generate huge revenue off the pitch.

A fairer system will go a long way to stopping any repeat of the Manchester City case.

KIERAN GILL: One big points deduction... and a multi-window transfer ban

If Manchester City are to win on appeal, it needs to be based on the actual evidence, not on them trying to find a technicality to do with impartiality or whatever else they can conjure. Their reputation is already in the mud after that verdict from the independent commission.

Their only way back is by winning fairly; not by continuing to try to thwart the investigation. If their guilt is upheld, then they should not be a Premier League club for at least one season.

So in my mind, a hefty points deduction, circa 60-70 points, would be sufficient for a start. Along with a multi-window transfer ban, the stripping of the titles won (they would be tainted anyway and I would not re-allocate those titles to the runners-up), and I could not see how their ownership could remain the same.

Too harsh? If ultimately guilty, City will have been found to have deliberately sabotaged so many years of football for not only their own supporters but us all.

LEWIS STEELE: Dock points for nine years... and City's current stars need answers

They should be docked points nine years in a row (given that’s how many years they were cheating for). A simple relegation is like a slap on the wrist: they would waltz the Championship and be fighting for Europe again within 18 months.

Elliot Anderson is among the Man City stars who may want answers from the club's ownership

They have duped their rivals for a decade so should be punished accordingly. City fans — many of whom are in denial — are right to feel aggrieved but their anger should not be directed at the Premier League but the men that have run their club into the ground.

I also feel sorry for the likes of Enzo Maresca, Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez etc — the people who have just joined the club and been lied to by the owners (it seems). Surely they have a claim?

MATT BARLOW: Play in the Championship next season - and put an asterisk next to all their titles

Cheating on such a vast and systematic scale demands a severe penalty with sporting consequences. Otherwise, what’s the point of anybody following the rules?

Money is no object to Manchester City’s owners. It defies the essence of sport if they can effectively pay to play by different rules. City should be expelled from the Premier League and all the titles won during the contaminated era should be asterisked. Swindon were denied entry to the top flight in 1990 for breaking financial rules.

I’m not sure how Chelsea escaped sporting penalty for their recent case, but that’s another story. City should start next season in the Championship. I can't see a point in sinking them any further down the EFL food chain just to watch them squirm.

But all future accounts should be subject to scrutiny by football's authorities to make sure they do not reoffend. I don't think we should start meddling to redistribute titles, for where does that begin and end? But I expect there will be clubs seeking compensation. It's easy to see why they will be aggrieved but at the same time a very depressing prospect.

Man City could be playing in the second tier for the first time since the 2001-02 season, when Eyal Berkovic and Shaun Goater were part of the squad which won promotion as champions

RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: Repay the rest of the pyramid by putting them in League Two

How to solve a problem like Manchester City? Turn them into a solution. To my mind, one season to the Championship isn’t severe enough for cheating that stretched across nine and has had residual benefits up to the present day.

So here’s an idea: a walk of shame to match the sham and one that feeds a financial boost to the lowest reaches of the pyramid.

The thought hinges on expulsion from the Premier League, if the guilty verdict remains intact after the appeals process.

Measures could be taken in the interim to prevent a tainted champion for 2026-27, such as a severe points deduction, with the expulsion occurring next summer (an optimistic timeline, perhaps).

The question then would be one of where to insert the club, which falls on the EFL. My suggestion is an immediate drop to League Two, guaranteeing City spend at least three seasons in the EFL before securing enough promotions to return to the Premier League.

The interest in the EFL in that period will be huge, as will the financial reward for each club they visit on their way back.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.
