World.title: Liberia: How Chief Justice Gbeisay’s Judiciary is Bringing the Gavel Closer to the Ordinary in Bong County
World.content:
Dafuwah hasn’t made headlines with landmark rulings. What’s drawn attention instead is something smaller and, in some ways, harder to quantify that the way he runs his courtroom. Where the law allows for it, he’s known for slowing down before assigning winners and losers — asking questions, hearing both sides out fully, and testing whether the dispute in front of him can be settled through dialogue rather than confrontation

GBARNGA, Bong County — Ask most Liberians what the word “court” conjures, and the answer rarely involves comfort. For decades, the courthouse has stood in the public imagination as two separate buildings occupying the same address: one for those who can pay their way through the system, and another — slower, colder, more intimidating — for everyone else.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

That divide wasn’t invented by any single scandal. It was built up over years of war, weak institutions, whispered accusations of bias on the bench, case backlogs that stretched on indefinitely, and legal fees that put the process out of reach for the people who needed it most. A farmer, a market seller, a motorbike taxi driver weighing whether to file a complaint wasn’t just asking “am I right?” They were asking whether they could survive the process long enough to find out.



A Different Kind of Magistrate

That backdrop makes it easier to understand why people in Gbarnga have started talking about Stipendiary Magistrate Richard M. Dafuwah, who took over the city’s Magisterial Court roughly a year ago from his predecessor, Daniel Dolokelen.

Dafuwah hasn’t made headlines with landmark rulings. What’s drawn attention instead is something smaller and, in some ways, harder to quantify that the way he runs his courtroom. Where the law allows for it, he’s known for slowing down before assigning winners and losers — asking questions, hearing both sides out fully, and testing whether the dispute in front of him can be settled through dialogue rather than confrontation.

People who’ve watched him work describe a magistrate who treats the poorest litigant with the same attention as anyone else. One resident familiar with the court’s proceedings put it simply: coming before Dafuwah, a person doesn’t feel dismissed for being ordinary — he lets them explain themselves fully before he acts. Another resident described the effect as almost as important as any verdict: being taken seriously restores a person’s faith that the process is actually working for them.

The Health Workers’ Case

The clearest test of that approach came when Bong County’s health worker protests spilled into legal territory. After a night in police custody, the workers’ leader was brought before the Gbarnga Magisterial Court — a moment that could easily have hardened into a standoff between striking workers and the government.

Instead, accounts from the community describe Dafuwah working to de-escalate the situation, engaging both sides directly rather than letting the confrontation deepen. It’s a small case study in what advocates of court-based mediation argue is possible: using the authority of the bench not to punish, but to create space for people to find their own resolution — without ever abandoning the law that governs the outcome.

That distinction matters. Mediation isn’t a replacement for adjudication, and no one — including Dafuwah’s admirers — argues it should be. Serious crimes, constitutional questions, and cases that legally demand a formal ruling still have to go through the full judicial process. But plenty of disputes that land in a magisterial court don’t need that kind of weight brought down on them. Sometimes what’s needed is simpler: someone willing to actually listen before deciding.

Justice as a Relationship, Not Just a Ruling

There’s a practical reason this matters beyond any single case. In a place like Gbarnga, the parties to a dispute don’t disappear from each other’s lives once a judgment is entered. They still share a market, a church, a school, a water source. A ruling can settle who’s legally right. It can’t necessarily repair what broke between two neighbors — but a resolution both sides had a hand in shaping just might.

That’s the argument residents make when they describe what they’ve seen from Dafuwah: that treating people with dignity and giving them room to be heard doesn’t soften justice — it expands what justice is capable of doing. As one community member framed it, people don’t just want a ruling; they want to be seen and treated with respect along the way, and that’s what they say they’ve gotten from him.

A Bigger Story Than One Courtroom

Dafuwah’s rising local reputation lands at a moment when Liberia’s Judiciary, under Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr., has been pushing to make courts more present — and more credible — outside Monrovia. In September 2026, the Judiciary formally seated 73 newly appointed magistrates across all 15 counties, a move officials framed as extending access to justice into the country’s most remote areas.

Earlier, in June 2026, Gbeisay announced a performance-based evaluation system meant to reward professionalism and accountability among judges and magistrates annually.

Dafuwah’s rising local reputation lands at a moment when Liberia’s Judiciary, under Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr., has been pushing to make courts more present — and more credible — outside Monrovia. In September 2026, the Judiciary formally seated 73 newly appointed magistrates across all 15 counties, a move officials framed as extending access to justice into the country’s most remote areas

Those are administrative moves, made from the top. But their success or failure will be measured almost entirely at the bottom — in rooms exactly like the one Dafuwah presides over. For most Liberians, the Supreme Court in Monrovia is an abstraction. The magistrate down the street is the actual, physical face of the justice system: the person who decides, in real time, whether the law is something that protects them or something that happens to them.

That’s precisely why a single magistrate’s demeanor carries outsized weight. A citizen who leaves a courtroom feeling heard walks away more willing to trust the next institution they encounter. A citizen who leaves feeling dismissed carries that suspicion into every future interaction with the state — and, in the worst cases, may decide that formal institutions aren’t worth the trouble at all, pushing disputes back into the community where they can curdle into retaliation and violence instead.

The Limits of Popularity

None of this means Dafuwah should be judged, or judge himself, by how well-liked he is. A magistrate’s job isn’t to be popular — it’s to apply the law, and sometimes that means handing down decisions that disappoint the very people who’d otherwise praise him. A year on the bench is a short track record, and his long-term legacy will rest on the consistency of his rulings, his independence from outside pressure, and his fidelity to due process — not on goodwill alone.

But the goodwill itself is worth paying attention to, because of what it reveals about what Liberians have been missing. The admiration building around Dafuwah isn’t really about him as an individual. It’s a proxy for a much larger and older demand: fairness, access, timeliness, and the basic experience of being taken seriously — regardless of how much money or influence a person carries into the room.

What Comes Next

The real test of Liberia’s judicial reform push won’t be the number of magistrates seated or systems announced. It will be what happens after those magistrates put on the robe: whether citizens feel safe walking into their courtrooms, whether the poor believe they’ll get a fair hearing, whether political and financial pressure gets resisted, and whether officers of the court can tell the difference between a dispute that needs mediation and one that demands a formal ruling.

In Gbarnga, those questions are still being answered one case at a time. Dafuwah’s tenure is young, and its ultimate verdict — pun intended — will be written over years, not months. But for now, his court offers a glimpse of something Liberians have long been told to expect and have too rarely experienced: a justice system that treats ordinary people as though they belong inside it.

For a country still working to convince its own citizens that the courthouse door swings open for everyone, that glimpse — however modest, however local — is not nothing.

World.title: Liberia: MFDP Commences Executive Budget Hearings for FY2027 Today as Several Entities Lined Up
World.content:
Monrovia, September 30, 2026 – In an effort to have the 2027 National Budget submitted on or in time so as to enhance its full implementation, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP) has scheduled today, Thursday, October 1, 2026 for the kick-off of the budget hearing processes.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The Executive Budget Hearing is a legal requirement under the Public Financial Management (PFM) Act, wherein the Budget Policy and Coordination Committee consult with all Ministries, Agencies and Commissions (MACs) on their programs and budget justifications for the next fiscal year.



According to a statement issued by the MFDP, the exercise is another critical phase in the Government of Liberia’s national budget formulation process.

By law, MFDP must submit the national budget to the Legislature no later than October 31 of every year. In a bid to achieve this and especially to ensure that allocations are not arbitrary, there will be a thorough consultative process to ensure efficiency and effectiveness. During the hearings, MACs will be made to defend their budget to convince the panel of experts whether there is a need for addition or subtraction.

The process also among other things, aims to ensure that the FY2026 Budget align with the government’s 5-year development plan, the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID).

The hearings, coordinated through the National Budget Committee (NBC), will allow spending entities to present and justify their proposed programs, priorities, expenditure requirements, and planned activities for Fiscal Year 2027.

The process is in line with the statutory mandate requiring the MFDP to consult with spending entities on their programs, commitments, and budgetary priorities before the preparation and submission of the National Budget.

The opening session on Thursday will focus on the Ministry of Mines and Energy, the Special Presidential Project Coordinating Committee (SPPCC), and the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC), bringing together key institutions responsible for managing Liberia’s mineral and energy resources, coordinating priority presidential development projects, and overseeing public procurement and concessions.

During the hearings, participating institutions are expected to outline their proposed programs and activities, provide justification for their budgetary requests, and respond to questions concerning their priorities, implementation plans, and resource requirements.

The Executive Budget Hearings are scheduled to run through Friday, October 9, 2026, and will cover a broad range of sectors and spending entities across government.

World.title: Liberia: Concerned Members of Gold and Diamond Brokers Union Back Omar Sekou Kamara for Organization’s Presidency
World.content:
Monrovia — A group of elders and concerned members of the Gold and Diamond Brokers Union (GDBU) has endorsed Omar Sekou Kamara for president of the organization ahead of its upcoming election.

Speaking on behalf of the group, Joseph D. Jallah said their decision was based on what they described as Kamara’s experience, commitment, integrity, and willingness to serve the interests of members.

“We stand before you today as elders and a group of concerned and committed members of this Union to publicly express our support for Mr. Omar Sekou Kamara,” Jallah said.



He said the group believes leadership of the union should go beyond holding office and should focus on listening to members, respecting differing views, promoting unity and collectively addressing challenges confronting the organization.

According to Jallah, the group has observed Kamara’s commitment to transparency, professional development and advocacy on issues affecting members of the union.

He stressed that the endorsement was not intended to undermine any of the other candidates contesting the presidency.

“Our endorsement of Mr. Kamara is not against any individual or group because we respect all candidates who have offered themselves for service,” Jallah said.

He added that the group believes Kamara would provide accessible and accountable leadership while representing members’ collective interests and promoting fairness within the union.

Jallah urged members of the GDBU to participate in the election and cast their ballots for Kamara, saying the union needs leadership focused on unity, progress, transparency and service.

Receiving the endorsement, Kamara thanked the elders and other members for their support and confidence in his candidacy.

He said his team would remain committed to what he described as a “One Union” vision aimed at improving the welfare of members and strengthening their representation within the brokerage sector.

Kamara said his agenda includes efforts to support the provision of clinics, schools and a market hall, while ensuring that members have effective representation before the government and the Ministry of Mines and Energy.

“On behalf of myself and my family, we say thank you for your unwavering support and for giving me and my team the trust to serve you,” Kamara said.

He pledged to remain engaged with union members across the country, from Grand Cape Mount County to Gbokougedeh and Lofa County, saying his team would work to represent members across Liberia.

The upcoming GDBU election is expected to determine the union’s next leadership and direction as candidates campaign for the support of members.

World.title: Liberia: CSO Groups Rally Support for Land Rights Act, Call for Increased Funding
World.content:
Monrovia – A conglomeration of civil society groupings under the banner of Civil Society Working Group on Land Rights Reform and the Multi-Actor Platform on Land Governance (MAP Liberia Land Platform) have called for stronger political will and increased budgetary support to accelerate implementation of the Land Rights Act (LRA).

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The call was made Wednesday, September 30, 2026 at a news conference held Monrovia. During the news conference, the groups unveiled the 2026 Policy Brief titled “Defending Land, Protecting Rights.”



The policy brief was produced by the Ducor Institute for Social and Economic Research and commissioned by the Sustainable Development Institute (SDI) and MAP Liberia Land Platform, with support from the International Land Coalition (ILC).

A History of Land Reform

Addressing the media and Liberians, Mr. Daniel Wehyee, Coordinator of Land Program at SDI and Mr. James Yasiah, Executive Director of Rights and Rice Foundation, traced the country’s land history from the 1926 Firestone Agreement, which covered one million acres at six cents per acre, to subsequent large-scale concessions that, according to the groups, contributed to dispossession, rural neglect, and the conditions that fueled Liberia’s 14-year civil war.

The groups recalled that post-war land reform, led by the Governance Commission under former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, culminated in the passage of the Land Authority Act in 2016 and the signing of the Land Rights Act by former President George Weah in September 2018.

Gains Made

According to the policy brief, the Land Rights Act has recorded several significant achievements.

They disclosed that approximately 70 customary communities, comprising about 380,000 citizens, mostly in rural Liberia, have completed the process required to qualify for land rights and are set to receive deeds for the first time.

Also, an additional 150 communities, involving approximately 800,000 citizens, are currently undergoing the formalization process, while key reforms have been introduced, including a Parcel Verification System aimed at reducing fraud and boundary disputes.

“A Digital Scanning Center has been established to preserve land records. A new standardized deed form with enhanced security features has been introduced. There have been modern surveying technologies, including drones and Geographic Information Systems (GIS), are being deployed. The Liberia Land Authority is collaborating with the Liberia Revenue Authority on property valuation, with support from the World Bank,” read the statement by Wehyee.

The policy brief noted that implementation of the Land Rights Act contributes to peace-building, inclusive governance, investment confidence, and stronger climate and environmental governance.

Challenges

Despite the progress, the CSOs identified several major challenges affecting implementation of the Land Rights Act.

Low Budgetary Support

The groups said inadequate government funding has made implementation heavily donor-dependent, with the momentum now threatened by the dissolution of USAID, which they described as a major donor in Liberia’s land sector.

Slow Formalization Process

The organizations also pointed to the slow pace of community formalization. With an estimated 600 to 700 clans nationwide, they said that, at the current rate, it could take many years for communities across Liberia to fully realize their land ownership rights.

Overlapping Institutional Mandates

The groups highlighted overlapping mandates among several government institutions, including the Liberia Land Authority, Forestry Development Authority, Environmental Protection Agency, Ministry of Mines and Energy, and the newly established Liberia Carbon Marketing Authority.

Limited Capacity and Public Awareness

Other challenges include limited technical capacity within relevant institutions and inadequate public awareness of the Land Rights Act.

Recommendations

The policy brief stressed that Liberia does not need to weaken the Land Rights Act but rather needs stronger coordination and greater investment to ensure effective implementation.

It called on the government and development partners to increase investment in customary community formalization, expand public awareness and education on the Land Rights Act, improve land data administration and management and strengthen county-level land services to bring land administration closer to communities.

“The LRA does not block investment, it ensures that investment proceeds on clear, lawful, and stable terms,” the policy brief stated.

The brief further noted that secure land tenure places communities in a stronger position to participate in addressing climate change and emerging opportunities in carbon marketing.

The statement was issued by the Civil Society Working Group on Land Rights Reform, Rights and Rice Foundation, and Sustainable Development Institute.

World.title: Petrol Hits K31.46, Diesel K33.27 As Tax Relief Ends, While Hichilema Pushes To Scrap Monthly Price Changes
World.content:
The Energy Regulation Board (ERB) has raised pump prices for October, pushing petrol to K31.46 a litre and diesel to K33.27, after six months of tax relief on fuel came to an end.

Petrol rose from K25.29 and diesel from K26.86, adding more than K6 to every litre. Kerosene moved from K27.02 to K29.76 a litre, while Jet A-1 climbed from K28.71 to K31.85. The new prices took effect at midnight, following the expiry of the tax-relief period at the end of September.

ERB board chairperson James Banda said the increase was driven mainly by higher international petroleum prices, the depreciation of the Kwacha and the reinstatement of excise duty. The Board said the revised prices were set after weighing international prices, the prevailing exchange rate and applicable taxes.

Over the review period, the average price of petrol rose from US$104.94 to US$121.58 a barrel, while diesel went from US$150.92 to US$160.88. Kerosene and Jet A-1 moved from US$125.30 to US$144 a barrel. The Kwacha also lost ground against the United States dollar, slipping from K19.28 to K19.76, and Mr Banda said sustained tensions in the Middle East kept upward pressure on international prices throughout the period.

Mr Banda said Government had suspended excise duty and zero-rated Value-Added Tax (VAT) on petroleum products from April to September 2026, and that those measures had held the pump price down. He was clear about what would have happened without them.

“In the absence of these interventions, petroleum prices would have been materially higher,” he said.

He said the measures also helped keep Zambia’s petroleum prices among the lowest in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) regions, although they cost Government revenue it would otherwise have collected.

Government has resolved to reinstate excise duty from October to cushion the immediate impact on consumers, with VAT on petroleum products returning on 1 December 2026. Mr Banda said the country’s position in the region had not been lost.

“Notwithstanding the adjustment, Zambia’s petroleum prices remain competitive within the region,” he said.

The pump price rise came on the same day President Hakainde Hichilema told a delegation in Abu Dhabi that monthly fuel price changes are no longer working for the country. Mr Hichilema said the adjustments were creating uncertainty for businesses and households, and that frequent changes made planning difficult and complicated the management of the economy. Zambia is now considering longer pricing periods of two or three months.

The President raised the matter when he met Ahmed Bin Thalith, chief executive officer of ADNOC Global Trading, the trading arm of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), who led a delegation to the meeting. Afterwards, Mr Hichilema summed up what the two sides had discussed.

“We discussed how best to stabilise fuel prices and move away from monthly price adjustments,” the President said.

He said Government was keen to work with partners such as ADNOC on long-term supply arrangements that bring greater stability to fuel prices. The Head of State accepted that some of the factors driving prices, including global conflicts that disrupted international supply chains, were beyond Zambia’s control, but said the pricing mechanism itself could be improved.

“We may not control every factor that drives fuel prices, but we can make our pricing mechanism more predictable and business-friendly,” Mr Hichilema said.

A steadier mechanism, he said, would help businesses plan better instead of constantly having to adjust to changes in fuel prices.

Mr Bin Thalith said more investment in Zambia’s fuel infrastructure could secure the country’s domestic demand and create a surplus to supply neighbouring countries. He said ADNOC’s interest rested on its earlier experience of supplying Zambia, particularly in difficult periods, and on its record of honouring contracts in East Africa. ADNOC wanted a long-term partnership with Zambia rather than month-to-month arrangements, he said.

The company is also exploring ways to support local firms such as Indeni in managing and expanding the country’s petroleum terminals, while improving operational flexibility and capacity.

For motorists and transporters, the immediate position is the October price list. Petrol stands at K31.46 and diesel at K33.27, and VAT is due back on fuel on 1 December.

World.title: United Capital Fertilizer to expand capacity
World.content:
United Capital Fertilizer Zambia Company Limited has disclosed that the firm has plans of expanding its existing fertilizer manufacturing facility.

Oroma Resources Limited, on behalf of United Capital Fertilizer Zambia Company Limited, Company Consultant, Maxwell Nkoya, says the proposed expansion has been estimated at 1.5 billion United States dollars and would significantly increase the company’s fertilizer production capacity.

He was speaking during a stakeholder’s engagement meeting in Chilanga as part of the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) for the proposed expansion of the company’s existing fertilizer manufacturing facility in the district.

Mr Nkoya explained that the expansion would increase the approved urea production capacity by double, from the current 300 thousand tonnes to a total of 600 thousand tonnes per year.

He further disclosed that the project would also introduce a new ammonium nitrate production capacity of 400 thousand tonnes per year.

Chilanga Town Council Chairperson, Buumba Mulunda said the proposed expansion has the potential to contribute positively to the local economy through increased employment opportunities and enhanced economic activity.

Mr Mulunda, however, called on the company to ensure that carbon emissions and other environmental impacts associated with the expansion were effectively managed to safeguard communities and the surrounding ecosystem.

Council Secretary, Stephen Malenga said investors remain important partners in enhancing service delivery and development in the district.

Mr Malenga urged business entities to remain compliant with the payment of property rates and obtain the requisite trading certificates from the local authority.

World.title: Chinsali to get 10 megawatts power plant
World.content:
Arc Power has announced plans to put up a 10 megawatts power plant in Chinsali District, Muchinga Province.

Arc Power Country Director Emmanuel Chilufya, says the project is part of its contribution to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He disclosed that the firm has partnered with the utility company, ZESCO to put solar plants across the country.

“In June this year, the company signed an agreement with Kiyona Energy Limited a subsidiary of ZESCO Limited to develop solar projects across the country and Chinsali District is one of the selected areas,” Mr Chilufya said.

The country director said this when he paid a courtesy call on the Muchinga Provincial administration today.

Mr Chilufya said land has just been secured in the Industrial Park from the local authority and handed over to ARC Power.

He added that the company will conduct a feasibility study for three months and is expected to conduct the ground breaking ceremony in the first quarter of 2027.

Mr Chilufya said Arc Power is an African company supported by the World Bank through the International Monetary Fund (IMF), stating that it pre-finances projects.

He disclosed that the company has an agreement with Kiyona Energy Limited to finance projects up to 60 million US Dollars.

Mr Chilufya said the company’s first project of 14 megawatts is in Chongwe, while the second will be in Chinsali, Muchinga Province.

And Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary, Brian Sichande has described a 10 Megawatts solar power project as a milestone for Chinsali District and the province at large.

Mr Sichande said the investment falls under the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

“As Muchinga Province, we are happy to have this noble investment under the Grow Zambia Agenda,” he said.

Mr Sichande said President Hakainde Hichilema is committed to ensuring access to electricity among community members.

He noted that climate change has been affecting power production, as the country largely depends on hydro power generation.

Mr Sichande said government is working hard to ensure solar plants are developed to cushion the power deficit.

The 10 Megawatts solar electricity generation project is under an agreement between Arc Power and Kiyona Energy Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of ZESCO.

World.title: Nalolo farmers start redeeming inputs
World.content:
Acting Nalolo District Agricultural Coordinator (DACO) Patience Munalula, says only 20 out of 500 farmers under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) have started redeeming farming inputs for the 2026/2027 farming season.

Mrs Munalula says the 20 farmers are from Namabunga area near Senanga District, who sold their maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) in Senanga.

She said the remaining farmers are still waiting for the physical deposits to commence, as there is no FRA shed in Nalolo District.

Mrs Munalulu said lack of an FRA depot in the district has disadvantaged farmers as it delays them from accessing inputs to plant early.

“Our district predominantly starts planting early along the flood plains before the plains are flooded, or in case of drought. Delayed access to inputs affects our production,” she said.

Meanwhile, Nalolo District Commissioner, Namatama Mupo said there is need to follow up on the shed being constructed in Muoyo area at Makwibi Primary School under the Pilot Programme for Climate Resilience (PPCR), so that it can serve as an FRA shed.

Mrs Mupo said once completed, the facility will make it easier for farmers to access FRA services within the district.

World.title: Shangombo women, youths equipped with human rights advocacy skills
World.content:
Women, youths and persons with disabilities in Shangombo District have been equipped with knowledge and tools on human rights mentorship and advocacy.

The training is being implemented under the Participatory Power Project by the Action Governance Forum, with financial support from the European Union (EU).

Speaking in an interview with the media, Action Governance Forum Executive Director, Justine Mushoke, said the training is meant to equip communities with the right information on human rights, governance and advocacy.

“This training is important because it will equip the community with the skills and necessary knowledge on issues to do with human rights,” Mr Mushoke said.

He explained that the project is designed to amplify the voices of marginalized groups in communities, particularly women, youths and persons with disabilities.

Mr Mushoke said the project will help create a culture of consultation between institutions and community members on issues of governance and human rights, adding that the trained individuals will be empowered to hold duty bearers accountable.

Meanwhile, Shangombo Town Council Secretary, Abwino Banda, said the training re-echoes the Government’s policy of empowering communities with knowledge on governance matters to enable them become self-sufficient.

“The meeting supports Government’s policy of empowering communities with knowledge on governance matters in order for them to make meaningful contributions to their communities,” Mr Banda said.

Mr Banda said the knowledge acquired will help the participants identify challenges in their respective communities and assist in the selection of Constituency Development Fund (CDF) projects.

He however, expressed displeasure at the negative attitude of some community members towards developmental meetings.

“I would like to urge all participants present to actively participate in engagement meetings, the attitude towards meetings is bad,” he said.

And Human Rights Commission District Focal Point Person, Mubita Simangolwa, said the meeting is critical in fostering development in communities.

He said he has learnt the importance of holding duty bearers accountable and transparent in the execution of service delivery.

“As a Human Rights District Focal Person, I am honoured to be part of this training. The knowledge gained will help us promote and protect human rights in the district,” he said.

And Robert Kamuya, a youth participant, has appreciated the Action Governance Forum for incorporating the youths of Shangombo in the project, saying it will broaden their perspective on human rights and help them identify and claim their rights.

World.title: Mwanza Demands ECZ Account For Suspended Vote Count And Stolen Mandevu Ballots
World.content:
Democratic Progressive Party president Antonio Mwanza has demanded that the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) publish a detailed report on why it suspended the counting and announcement of results during the general election. He said the credibility of the process will stay in question until the commission accounts for what happened in those missing hours.

Mr Mwanza said he had no doubt that President Hakainde Hichilema won the election and would always have crossed the 50 per cent plus one threshold. His quarrel, he said, was not with the winner but with the way the contest was run, and with an electoral body he believes cannot act independently because of how it is set up.

“The outcome of the election was never in doubt,” he said. “But the election itself raised very critical issues that we must address going forward.”

The first of those issues was the suspension of counting on what the commission described as security grounds. He said the ECZ had never told the public how widespread those concerns were, nor what took place between the moment counting stopped and the moment it resumed.

“The Electoral Commission of Zambia did not give us a detailed account of what happened between this period,” Mr Mwanza said.

He then turned to Mandevu constituency, where no election was held after the commission said ballot papers and other electoral materials had been stolen. Weeks after the polls, he said, the public still did not know whether anyone had been apprehended for the theft.

He also raised the death of a Socialist Party election agent. He said neither the commission nor the Zambia Police had explained what happened to him, and warned that the same failures would return at the next national vote unless all three matters were answered.

“If we don’t get to the bottom of this and to the extent of how widespread it was and to what extent it affected the outcome of the elections, we will have a repeat of this in 2031,” he said.

Mr Mwanza was careful to separate the question of who won from the question of how the result was produced. He pointed to the Christian Churches Monitoring Group (CCMG), whose members include the Jesuit Centre for Theological Reflection, the Zambia Conference of Catholic Bishops, the Council of Churches in Zambia and the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia. He said he respected its finding that the President won.

“There’s no doubt about him winning the election,” he said. “We’re talking about the credibility of the process.”

For the opposition leader, the root of the problem lies in how commissioners are appointed. ECZ commissioners are appointed by the President, who is also a candidate in the same election the commission is meant to referee, and he said that placed the body in an impossible position.

“It is extremely difficult for the Electoral Commission of Zambia to act in an independent, impartial manner when they are appointed by a President who also happens to be part of the election process,” he said.

His party is proposing that commissioners be selected by an independent and impartial body through an accountable and transparent process, with their appointments ratified by Parliament. Only then, he said, would the commission have the confidence to enforce the rules against everyone, including the governing party.

He said the conflict showed most plainly in the commission’s failure to enforce the Electoral Code of Conduct on media coverage. The code requires public media to give equal, fair and balanced coverage to all contestants. Yet in his view every state outlet, from ZNBC to ZANIS, Times of Zambia and Zambia Daily Mail, leaned towards the ruling party.

“It is not the first time,” Mr Mwanza said. “It has always been like this from time immemorial. And this must change.”

He blamed the editorial policies of publicly owned media houses, which he said left their journalists no room to give the opposition fair and balanced airtime or space.

The second structural failure, he said, was the campaign timetable. Mr Mwanza said he accepted its purpose, which is to keep rival presidential candidates apart and prevent clashes. The problem was that the sitting President, who is also a candidate, is exempt from it.

“The President is given a free will to campaign and to be anywhere he wants,” he said. “That disadvantages the other candidates who don’t have that free will.”

He said opposition candidates were at times turned away from areas because their timetables placed them elsewhere. In a campaign of about 90 days, where every hour counts, he described enforcement of the electoral code as “extremely selective”.

“He cannot be a candidate but is given preferential treatment by virtue of him being the President,” he said. “The election must be free, must be fair, and everybody must be on an equal footing.”

Mr Mwanza made three proposals. First, the ECZ must publish its report on the suspended count and the scale of the threats it cited. Second, commissioners must be appointed by an independent body and confirmed by Parliament. Third, the timetable must bind every presidential candidate, including the incumbent, and public media must be compelled to give all contestants fair coverage.

He added that the commission was also under-resourced, lacking the money and staff to carry out voter education across the country. Reform of its governing law, he said, must come with the funding to match.

The Democratic Progressive Party did not field candidates in the general election. Mr Mwanza said registering the party took more than a year, leaving it too little time, manpower and money to mount a credible challenge against the United Party for National Development (UPND).

The party has instead begun preparing for 2031, and Mr Mwanza said electoral reform would be central to that effort. His demand for a full report now sits with a commission that has yet to publicly account for the suspended count, the stolen Mandevu materials or the death of the Socialist Party agent.

World.title: Zambia keeps changing drivers and never fixes the car
World.content:
Zambia keeps changing drivers and never fixes the car

In April 2017, police broke into the Lusaka home of the country’s main opposition leader in the dead of night, fired tear gas and carried him away on a charge of treason. His offence was that his motorcade had failed to give way to the presidential convoy on a road in Western Province. Hakainde Hichilema spent more than four months in custody before the State quietly dropped the case.

Nine years later, that same man is President, freshly returned for a second term. And the runner-up in the election he has just won, Brian Mundubile, sits in custody on a treason charge, with a sedition charge added for good measure. The State says it is still gathering evidence.

If there is a single image that captures what has gone wrong in Zambian politics, it is this one. The faces change. The furniture stays exactly where it was.

Antonio Mwanza, the Democratic Progressive Party leader who sat out the polls, put it bluntly in a long radio interview this week. There are no good men when it comes to power, he said, only good institutions or bad ones. It is the most useful sentence any Zambian politician has spoken since the results were declared, and it should be read as an indictment of every party that has ever held State House, including the one Mr Mwanza once served.

Consider the record. Kenneth Kaunda built the University of Zambia and the University Teaching Hospital, and then built a one-party state to protect himself. Frederick Chiluba rode to power on the promise of multiparty freedom and then tried to buy himself a third term, until churches, lawyers and students stopped him in 2001. The Patriotic Front turned the Public Order Act into a padlock on opposition rallies. The UPND spent a decade on the receiving end of that padlock and promised, loudly, never to use it.

Now look at what has happened since polling day.

On polling night, the Electoral Commission of Zambia suspended counting and the announcement of results on security grounds. Counting later resumed, and a clear winner was declared. Nobody seriously disputes that President Hichilema won. Church monitors said so. Mr Mwanza says so. This column says so.

But nobody has explained what happened in the hours when the count stood still. Nobody has told the voters of Mandevu, who did not vote at all because ballot papers were stolen, whether a single thief has been caught. And on 24 August, the last day on which any losing candidate could file a petition challenging the result, the courts of the Republic were shut on “security reasons” that have never been set out in public.

The Law Association of Zambia said it best: the right of access to the courts is meaningless if the courts can simply be closed at the precise moment citizens most need them. That is not a partisan complaint. It is a description of a door slammed in the face of the law itself.

Then came the arrests. Opposition leaders, former Members of Parliament and campaign figures have been picked up, some in circumstances their lawyers and families only learned of later. Where the law requires an appearance before a court within 48 hours, detainees have waited. Where public figures with fixed addresses could have been served a simple call-out, the police have preferred the drama of a night arrest.

The Government says it had been investigating some of the accused for three years. Yet the prosecutions chief has been quoted as saying the State is still collecting evidence. Both statements cannot comfortably be true. If the evidence exists, put it before a judge. If it does not, open the cell door. There is no third option in a constitutional democracy.

And now, as if on cue, comes the oldest song in the Zambian hymn book. A ruling party Member of Parliament has floated the removal of presidential term limits. Cadres have taken up the chorus. The line, as always, is that it is not the President asking. It is “the people”. When that fails to persuade, the line becomes “let Parliament decide”, which is another way of saying “let us decide, because we have the numbers”.

Zambians have been here before. They were asked about term limits by the Mung’omba Constitution Review Commission and said two terms. They said it again in 2001, in the streets, in green ribbons. They have said it at every review since. A people who have answered the same question the same way for a quarter of a century are not confused. They are being ignored.

To his credit, President Hichilema has said on more than one platform that nobody deserves a third term. He should say it again, now, from the podium, in words that leave no room for interpretation. Silence from the Head of State is not neutrality. In this country, silence has always been read as permission.

What makes all of this so dispiriting is not that the UPND has turned out to be wicked. It is that it has turned out to be ordinary. It has inherited a presidency with the power to appoint judges, electoral commissioners, ambassadors, police chiefs and almost every head of a public institution, and, like every party before it, it has found that power far too comfortable to surrender.

The ECZ is appointed by the President, who is also a candidate. The prosecutions office answers to a system the President heads. The public broadcaster, funded by every taxpayer, tilts towards whoever holds State House, as it has done since independence. The courts can be closed with a notice and a phrase. None of these arrangements was invented by the current Government. All of them have been used by it.

That is the real crisis. Zambia keeps changing the driver and leaving the car exactly as it is: faulty brakes, a steering wheel that pulls to one side and a speedometer the driver is allowed to reset. Each new driver swears he will fix it. Each one discovers that the faulty car suits him perfectly well while he is the one behind the wheel.

The cadres understand this better than anyone. Mr Mwanza tells of friends who walked Lusaka’s streets with him five years ago and are now building blocks of flats in Silverest and posing with pigs and fish ponds. We have seen this before too. The MMD had its instant businessmen. The PF had its instant businessmen. Where are they now? Their fortunes lasted exactly as long as their party did.

There is a lesson in that for the UPND, and it is not a moral lesson. It is a practical one. Every law passed for comfort in power becomes a weapon in the hands of the next Government. The treason charge that held Mr Hichilema in 2017 is the same instrument now holding Mr Mundubile. The cyber laws the UPND once denounced are now turned on its own detractors. A Constitution amended to suit one President will one day serve a President the UPND fears.

So what should be done?

First, take the appointment of electoral commissioners away from the President and give it to an independent panel, with confirmation by Parliament. Second, bind every presidential candidate, the incumbent included, to the same campaign timetable and the same rules on public media. Third, give the judiciary financial independence so that no administrator can lock its doors on a deadline day. Fourth, require the prosecution to have a case before it takes a liberty. And fifth, leave Article 106 exactly where it is.

None of this requires the UPND to lose power. It only requires the party to govern as though it one day will.

President Hichilema has five years left. He knows, better than any President before him, what it feels like to sit in a cell on a charge the State cannot prove. He can be the leader who finally fixes the car. Or he can be the next name on a long list of men who were certain the rules would always favour them.

Zambia has already seen how that list ends.

By Kingsley Mwila

World.title: Zambia, UK to enhance trade relations
World.content:
Minister of Finance and National Planning Situmbeko Musokotwane, says Government is open to more trade and investment between the United Kingdom and Zambia.

Dr Musokotwane says the United Kingdom and the Zambian government have long standing cooperation with the UK having several investments in the country.

He said this when British Trade Commissioner, Alastair Long and British High Commissioner Rebecca Terzeon paid a courtesy call on him at his office where they had a cordial discussion to enhance cooperation and open investment opportunities for Zambia.

Dr Musokotwane said the discussion was centered on specific investment areas adding that Britain has expertise and capital to invest in Zambia.

He stated that various proposals have been put across to the British High Commission delegation.

“This comes at a time when the focus in Zambia is how to get the economy to grow so that young people can get jobs as well as business opportunities for Zambians,” he said.

Dr Musokotwane added that the British business community can take advantage of some of the targets on the Grow Zambia Agenda that include beef, mining, sugar and forestry.

And British Trade Commissioner, Alastair Long, said the United Kingdom is committed to investing and contributing to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Long noted that Zambia has great potential to grow with the coming of the Grow Zambia Agenda being spearheaded by President Hakainde Hichilema.

He further said Zambia has taken some significant steps to stabilize the economy and prepare itself for a bright future.

“The UK is really proud of our relationship, we are also incredibly proud of the investment relationship,” Mr Long said.

And British High Commissioner to Zambia, Rebecca Terzeon said UK will continue to invest in Zambia saying British international investments in the country date back to many decades ago.

World.title: Botswana: Botswana Criticised for Slaughtering 23 Elephants for Independence Celebrations
World.content:
Botswana has authorised the killing of 23 elephants and other wildlife for meat as part of celebrations marking the country's 60th anniversary of independence, drawing criticism from animal rights and conservation groups.

The government had approved the culling of 23 elephants ahead of the celebrations, with the meat to be distributed across eight districts. The programme also included the hunting of other wildlife species such as kudu, impala and wildebeest.

The Elephant Protection Society warned that using elephants for celebratory feasts could undermine conservation efforts and encourage poaching.

The decision has also sparked concerns over hygiene and disease amid a foot-and-mouth outbreak. Local officials are calling for the meat to be processed and distributed more safely.

Botswana has more than 130,000 elephants and defends regulated hunting as a way to manage human-wildlife conflict and generate funds for communities and conservation.

The government's stance on hunting is controversial. Supporters of Botswana's hunting policy, however, said that international criticism fails to fully account for the challenges faced by rural communities living near large elephant populations.

They said elephants could destroy crops and property and endanger people, especially as expanding human settlements push communities closer to wildlife.

World.title: South Africa: City Power Warns of Cable Theft Fires - South African News Briefs - October 1, 2026
World.content:
press review

City Power Warns of Cable Theft Fires

Johannesburg City Power has raised concern over repeated vandalism and attempted theft of electricity infrastructure at its Central Substation, reports EWN. The utility said three fires have been reported at the substation this month. The latest left large parts of the Johannesburg CBD without electricity, a day after power was restored following a two-week outage. City Power spokesperson Isaac Mangena said six fires have been recorded at the substation since January, with four confirmed to have involved cable theft and vandalism.

Tshuma Faces Extradition Proceedings

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Zimbabwean-born British national Ndodana Tshuma is set to appear in the Johannesburg Magistrates' Court for extradition proceedings after the United Kingdom requested his arrest and extradition over the alleged murders of his wife and two daughters, reports SABC News. Separately, his plea and sentencing proceedings in South Africa were postponed to October 21 as negotiations with the State remain unresolved. Tshuma has pleaded guilty to unlawfully possessing a firearm and ammunition and entering South Africa illegally. He will remain in custody until his next court appearance.

Cape Town Boosts Firefighting Capacity

Cape Town is strengthening its firefighting capacity ahead of what the city expects to be a long, hot and dry summer, reports EWN. The Fire and Rescue Service has added 100 new cadets and 35 junior firefighters. The city plans to spend more than R25 million on additional resources in the coming financial year, including nearly R6 million for specialised vehicles. The city attended almost 31,000 fires during the 2025/26 financial year and introduced 11 wildfire 4x4 vehicles designed to reach difficult terrain. Safety and Security Mayco member JP Smith said dry vegetation, strong winds and limited, unpredictable rainfall are expected to increase fire risks. The dam levels are currently around 75% and should provide sufficient water for firefighting operations.
