World.title: Saskatchewan mayor stepping down now that 'Queen of Canada' cult is gone
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Brad Miller signed up to be the mayor of Richmound, Sask., he never dreamed his tiny southwestern village would be overrun by a cult.

After three years and many sleepless nights, the cult is finally gone.

Miller says he's stepping down on Oct. 15 in hopes that the village can start a new chapter. He is about halfway through a four-year term that was set to end in November 2028.

"We fought a lot of battles and wars, and I think it's just time," he said. "Somebody else can step up and take the reins, and maybe turn a new leaf."

Miller was elected as Richmound's mayor seven years ago. The village of 118 people is roughly 60 kilometres northwest of Maple Creek, near the Alberta border.

"Running for mayor in a small village or town should be a fairly easy thing," he joked.

But for Miller, it was anything but easy. He said he's also dealt with property fraud, disputes over the seniors centre and navigating the financial impact of the pandemic.

"Nobody knows the hours that I put in," Miller said. "It was day after day, week after week, month after month. And I don't think anybody should have to go through that."

WATCH | Like 'living next to dormant volcano' Richmound resident says: Having cult in town like 'living next to dormant volcano,' says Richmound, Sask., resident | Duration 2:23 Tensions are high in the small southwest Saskatchewan village of Richmound, nine months after the 'Kingdom of Canada' set up camp in an old school.

Richmound made national headlines on Sept. 15, 2023, when Romana Didulo, the self-proclaimed "Queen of Canada" and her Kingdom of Canada followers moved into an empty school in the village.

She is known as a QAnon conspiracy theorist who started to amass a following during the pandemic.

For two years, the group refused to pay utilities, pumped raw sewage into a children's playground and threatened Miller and others with public executions.

The former school where members of the Kingdom of Canada cult lived for almost two years. (Shawn Mullin)

Through it all, Miller was public about how the cult affected his town and continually sought help from the government and RCMP.

"I think Brad needs to be commended for how he handled it, you know, [being] blindsided with this," said Doug Steele, the MLA for Cypress Hills, who represents the area.

"This is a first-time situation, and I think they did quite well. It was pretty stressful for that community."

The RCMP raided the school on Sept. 3, 2025, arresting and removing members of the cult after receiving a report one of its occupants had a gun.

The Saskatchewan Health Authority declared the building "unfit for human habitation" and issued a public health order forcing the eviction of its occupants.

WATCH | Sask. village mayor upset Crown stayed charges against cult leader: Sask. village mayor upset Crown stayed charges against cult leader | Duration closed caption 2:24 Crown prosecutors have stayed the charges against a cult leader whose group occupied a former school in Richmound, Sask., a southwest Saskatchewan village.

Didulo was charged with failing to comply with an undertaking and intimidating a justice system participant. The Crown stayed her charges last March.

Miller said he's very disappointed in the justice system for that decision.

'A bright future'

Since the cult was pushed out, things are relatively back to normal in the village.

"Well, for the village of Richmound, I feel great that we finally won the war," Miller said. "And I think there's a bright future."

Scott Earl and his wife, Mel, are among those helping the community start over.

The couple moved to town a week before the cult did.

"We like to watch a lot of those documentaries about cults," Scott Earl joked. "Never thought [I'd] live through one."

Earl said it wasn't the fresh start he was expecting, but he's excited to be a part of a new future for Richmound.

"Everybody's bringing in new ideas to build the community, and I think we need to focus on those things rather than always looking in the rearview mirror."

He's the project co-ordinator for Grow Together, an initiative to build an all-seasons domed greenhouse.

"The idea behind the project is to have the villagers initiate some action by coming into the greenhouse, volunteering their time to either weed, plant, water," Earl said. "And by doing that, they'll be able to take a harvest from the greenhouse as well."

Richmound has a corner store, but the nearest grocery store with fresh produce is a 50-minute drive away.

Scott Earl, from left, Mel Earl, Richmound Coun. Renee Glass and Miller at the proposed site for an all-seasons greenhouse. (Shawn Mullin)

"This is to try and help with food insecurity that we're battling across Canada right now, and to give rural Saskatchewan an advantage on being able to sustain ourselves," Earl said.

Grow Together plans to dehydrate any leftover food to create dry soups or food packs that can be donated to other food banks in the area.

The project got started using a $10,000 grant to address food insecurity. Fundraising initiatives continue, and Earl said they're only at two-thirds of the current fundraising goal.

The group is placing an order for the structure this month and is hoping the greenhouse can be up and operating by July.

Earl said he's sad Miller won't be marking the greenhouse's opening as mayor.

"He was an ambassador for the town — always friendly, engaging, willing to put the best efforts for the village forward," he said.

"It's kind of sad to see Brad step down because after going through all that, I think he should have had at least a few years of down time, where things are going in the right direction."

Miller is planning on staying in Richmound, where he lives with his wife. He said he's looking forward to watching the future community growth from the sidelines.

World.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is in 'high spirits' for Thursday's launch to the International Space Station
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

All eyes will be on the weather Thursday morning, as Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk prepares to launch to the International Space Station (ISS).

Kutryk, 44, will be a mission specialist for NASA’s Crew-13 mission to the ISS, alongside Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov from Roscosmos. NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins will serve as commander and Luke Delaney will be the pilot. They are heading to space on SpaceX's Crew Dragon.

The weather at Cape Canaveral, Fla., is expected to be a little variable, with chances of showers and potential thunderstorms.

Initially, Kutryk was to fly on a Boeing CST-100 Starliner, but after the company suffered major setbacks, he was reassigned to SpaceX.

NASA has also been dealing with a potential issue on the ISS, as first reported by ArsTechnica on Monday.

Canadarm2, which is used to catch some spacecraft and during spacewalks, is able to move around on the ISS like an inchworm, However, after conducting one of these "walk-off" manoeuvres, engineers detected "some communications errors." In a statement to ArsTechnica, NASA said that they and SpaceX were working to ensure there wouldn't be any GPS interference between Crew Dragon and the station during docking.

At today's press conference, Lorie Glaze, NASA's associate administrator for human spaceflight said, "I was lucky enough earlier today to get to speak with Jessica. Luke, Josh and Sergey. They are ready to fly."

Dana Weigel, manager, Low Earth Orbit Program, echoed Glaze: "I also talked with the crew this morning when they were in crew quarters. They're doing great. They're ready to fly. A lot of smiling faces."

CSA astronaut Joshua Kutryk and the other members of Crew-13 participate in training at SpaceX facilities in Hawthorne, California, in preparation for their six-month mission to the International Space Station. From left to right: Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, NASA astronaut Luke Delaney, and CSA astronaut Joshua Kutryk. (Canadian Space Agency, SpaceX)

The mission comes just six months after CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen’s trip around the moon as part of the Artemis II mission.

Canada has a lot to be proud about, Mathieu Caron, director of CSA’s astronaut office, told CBC News' Karen Pauls ahead of the press conference.

"I think what people really need to remember is: Why do we have access to that incredible world-class laboratory?... Because Canada contributed the mobile servicing system, which is a complex robotic system that allowed the space station to be built."

The crew will do a traditional walk-out from their quarantine facility at roughly 7:40 a.m. Thursday.

After that, they will head out to the pad and ascend in the elevator to their Crew Dragon capsule and undergo preparations for launch.

On a personal note, Kutryk's wife Heather will be giving birth to their third child while he's in orbit.

"So we'll look at which labour code applies," Caron said at the press conference, laughing.

Once they launch, they will catch up with the ISS in a few hours.

"If the launch does go tomorrow as planned, this will be the fastest Dragon mission to station around eight hours or so," said Weigel.

WATCH | Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk talks space travel: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk talks space travel | Duration 9:23 Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk is in training to go to space one day. He says private space companies have an important role to play in the future of space travel.

If the weather doesn't co-operate Thursday, the next launch opportunity is Friday morning.

"We always ensure that we fly only when we're ready," Glaze said.

And Kutryk is ready.

"He's so ready," said Caron of the CSA. "And hopefully the weather will co-operate tomorrow. So … you know, for him, for his family and for the mission at hand, really, we're [in] very high spirits."

World.title: UCP MLA says he’s voted in favour of Alberta holding binding referendum on independence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A sitting MLA with Alberta’s governing United Conservative Party says he has voted in favour of proceeding with a legally binding referendum on whether the province should leave Canada.

Red Deer-South MLA Jason Stephan confirmed how he voted in this fall’s referendum to CBC News at a town hall he hosted Tuesday night at the Alberta Sports Hall of Fame in Red Deer.

“My reason for preferring Option 2 [on the question about separation], which I have had that position for a long time, is I would love nothing more than for Canada to fix itself,” he told CBC News. “Currently we do not see that happening.

“I've always supported having a referendum on independence because I want Ottawa to be compelled to fix the things that are broken, and they will not change things unless they are compelled to do so.

“We had a prime minister that more than doubled the national debt. I want to see respect, discipline. I want to see a better government."

During the event, Stephan said his position on the independence referendum issue has long been publicly known.

Stephan, who left his role as Premier Danielle Smith’s constitutional affairs adviser in the spring , has been outspoken in the last few months in his message to “get Ottawa’s attention.” He has written op-eds and newsletters and urged Albertans to sign a petition calling for a referendum on whether Alberta should separate from Canada.

Question 10 of the upcoming referendum asks "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"

Voters can choose between Option 1, which is “Alberta should remain a province of Canada,” and Option 2, “The government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.”

About 100 people turned out for a town hall in Red Deer, Alta., on Sept. 29, 2026 to talk about Alberta's upcoming referendum. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC)

CBC News asked Stephan, who said he has already mailed in his ballot ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum, how he would vote with regard to separation if Option 2 is successful this fall.

“I've never said that I want Alberta to separate,” he said. ”I've actually always said that I'd love to see Canada fix itself. That's what I'd love. We have this awesome potential, and we have so poorly managed it and underachieved, and that makes me very sad.”

Stephan said his best-case scenario is that Canada “becomes the most free and prosperous nation on Earth, that Alberta is treated fairly [and] that our constitution is fixed.”

When asked if he feels in line with his party caucus’ position of wanting to remain as a sovereign Alberta within a united Canada, he said he’d “like to see united.”

“That's my hope, but there's some work to do there. And again, I think the federal government needs to do a lot more, unfortunately.”

Town hall

Stephan said he sent an invitation to people who live in his constituency for Tuesday’s town hall to discuss the 10 questions in the upcoming referendum.

“In Question 10, some good people ... had different opinions,” he said. “It's good to have a civil discussion on those questions.

“If Albertans choose Option 1, I respect and honour that.

“I'm glad that we're having this referendum because I honestly think that it's got Ottawa's attention,” he said, noting that Prime Minister Mark Carney recently visited Red Deer .

In a recent newsletter to constituents, Stephan writes about Question 10 and notes it is not a referendum question on independence but rather a referendum on whether to have a future referendum.

“In fact, Option 1 and Option 2 can be true at the same time,” the newsletter reads. “A voter can want Alberta to remain a province of Canada AND want Alberta to hold a future referendum on independence to compel Ottawa to fix what it has broken.”

Tuesday's event had a mix of perspectives. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC)

Tuesday’s town hall attracted about 100 people and the crowd had a mix of opinions, both for and against separation. Some sported Alberta flags and separatist merchandise. Some voiced opinions about confusing wording, others expressed worry about businesses leaving and what happens next if Albertans say no to staying in Canada.

One attendee asked if there is any possibility of the UCP caucus trying to get Premier Smith to support Option 2, which was met with applause.

Smith has said she is voting for Option 1.

At an unrelated news conference in Calgary on Wednesday, Smith was asked if she is still in control of her party since Stephan said he voted for Option 2.

“We have a big-tent party,” she replied. “And big tent means that different MLAs are able to express different views. But the position of our party, our caucus and our government remains clear.

“Albertans are going to have a chance to tell us if they differ in their views on Oct. 19.”

World.title: After day of delays, witnesses say Tennessee unable to carry out execution of Christa Pike
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tennessee officials were unable to carry out the execution of Christa Gail Pike for a 1995 murder on Wednesday, media witnesses said, after the lethal injection was halted for hours as courts considered a last-minute appeal.

Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned an appeals court ruling that stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start.

Officials appeared to give Pike two doses of pentobarbital.

At 7:46 p.m. prison officials closed the curtain to the media room. They raised the curtain three minutes later. Pike could be heard loudly snoring, and the curtain was closed again at 8:06 pm.

Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at about 8:53 p.m. At that time there was an announcement to escort media witnesses out of the area.

People gather during a protest against the death penalty at the Tennessee State Capitol on Sunday in Nashville. (George Walker IV/The Associated Press)

Tennessee Department of Correction spokesman Dorinda Carter told media witnesses she was unable to immediately provide information about what happened.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday to the U.S. Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit court and district court.

The motion also asserted that the Department of Correction should begin lifesaving measures. "Failure to provide such care constitutes deliberate indifference to legitimate, serious medical needs."

Pike and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, were convicted of stabbing and beating 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility, in Knoxville in 1995.

Pictures of murder victim Colleen Slemmer is seen at a news conference in Nashville, Tenn., on Sept. 30. (George Walker IV/The Associated Press)

The case garnered widespread attention in part because a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer's body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the "satanic panic" of the 1980s and 1990s.

She was initially scheduled to die by lethal injection in the morning, and witnesses had already gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay. That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike's allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing.

But later in the day, the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the execution to proceed. The Supreme Court's conservative majority did not explain their order, while the three liberal members signed a dissent that said Pike's claims deserved a closer look.

A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction then said it would proceed with the execution ahead of a midnight cutoff.

Legal flurry

After the stay was issued, Tennessee's attorney general immediately appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. Witnesses and media remained at the prison while the high court considered the case.

In its appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, the attorney general's office wrote that halting the execution at the last moment traumatized Slemmer's family and rewarded "abusive delay tactics" by Pike's lawyers.

Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in the dissent that the decision to vacate the stay interfered with the Sixth Circuit court's handling of the case and "unnecessarily prevents that court from giving due consideration to Pike's claim."

In this image from video provided by WBIR-TV, Pike cries after being sentenced to death on March 30, 1996. (WBIR-TV/The Associated Press)

Pike does not deny committing the killing, but her supporters have argued the state should consider her age at the time, mental illness and a history of severe sexual abuse that included being raped from the time she was a toddler.

"It is inconceivable that in the 21st century, the criminal justice system is poised to execute a survivor of rape and child sexual abuse whose jury never had the opportunity to consider those facts in weighing the defendant's moral culpability," her lawyers wrote in a filing to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Renewed debate

As the execution date drew near, it renewed debate over the death penalty for young offenders.

Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike's death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds sentenced to death in Tennessee have had their sentences vacated.

After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn't "put the brakes on."

"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done," Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.

"Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."

Victim's mother awaits execution

Slemmer's mother wants the lethal injection to go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.

"Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run," May Martinez said in a telephone interview.

Martinez said a group helped raise money so she and her husband could travel from Florida to witness the execution. She didn't respond to a message on Wednesday after the execution was halted.

May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, leaves Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on Sept. 30. (George Walker IV/The Associated Press)

Martinez said her daughter's age also should matter in deciding Pike's fate.

"Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," Martinez said, noting that her daughter would have turned 51 earlier in September.

The 1995 killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995.

Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.

Executions of women rare in U.S.

Tennessee has not executed a woman for at least 200 years, according to Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Older records can be spotty, though, so it's difficult to know precise details about the last woman who was put to death there.

It's a rarity across the U.S. Since 1976, 18 women have been put to death in the country, representing about one per cent of all executions, according to the centre.

Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the U.S.

In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the U.S. government put a female inmate to death.

Pike would be the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year after Florida carried out an execution on Tuesday.

World.title: Stelco's U.S. owner touts right to idle operations at Hamilton steel plant as PM vows legal action
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The chief executive officer of Stelco’s American parent company says he has every legal right to idle production at a steel mill in Hamilton, Ont., resulting in up to 500 layoffs, due in part to the bitter trade war between Canada and the U.S.

His remarks follow comments from Prime Minister Mark Carney that Ottawa will "use all powers that we have" against Cleveland-Cliffs as it pursues the company to the "fullest extent of the law."

In an interview with CBC News on Wednesday, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves called Stelco’s ability to freely sell steel produced in Hamilton to U.S. buyers an "underlying condition" to terms it agreed to when it purchased Stelco in 2024. Those include maintaining "significant employment levels in Canada" and "significant operations in Hamilton."

"We had [the] USMCA [United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement] in place . . . we had the ability to sell into the United States," Goncalves said. "That was an underlying condition for me to acquire Stelco.

"I would not have acquired the Stelco if I knew that Canada and the United States would become what they became — enemies in trade."

WATCH | Carney says Canada will do all it can to ensure Stelco meets obligations: Stelco 'betrayed' Ontario workers with layoffs, Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:16 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada will 'use all the powers that we have' to ensure that Stelco meets its 'legal obligations for employment.' The company, which is owned by U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs, announced plans on Monday to idle some production at its Hamilton plant, putting hundreds of workers out of a ‌job.

Layoffs linked to trade war

Stelco, owned by Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs, directly linked its plan to cut up to 500 jobs with U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada.

The Trump administration imposed 50 per cent tariffs on foreign steel under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act last year. Canada has retaliated with duties on many U.S.-made steel products.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Carney singled out Goncalves for "applauding" Trump's move to impose punishing tariffs on Canadian steel imports to the United States.

Goncalves said on Wednesday that his support for Trump was not at odds with his support for steel workers in Canada. He also said he had not received notice of a lawsuit from Canada’s federal government.

"America first is not America only," he said. "Canadians need to understand that people like me that invest money in Canada are not going there to screw them up. We are there because we believe in the country. We believe in the people. We believe in the workforce."

Cleveland-Cliffs acquired Hamilton-based Stelco in a $3.4-billion cash-and-stock deal that closed in November 2024. In a news release announcing the deal, Stelco's then-CEO Alan Kestenbaum stated the transaction "keeps national interests at the forefront and recognizes the importance of the workforce."

The Stelco Hamilton Works production facility is seen in an aerial view. Stelco Holdings Inc. said on Monday that it plans to idle part of its Hamilton plant. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

CEO defends move

Carney said he was "very disappointed" by Stelco’s decision to lay off workers as it temporarily halts cold-rolled steel production in Hamilton.

Goncalves defended the move, stating foreign steel imports to Canada have put pressure on Stelco by tightening the domestic market.

"We do not have a market that could accommodate all the participants in the marketplace, mainly the two big ones, Stelco and ArcelorMittal Dofasco, together with a number of tonnes of imported steel coming through the borders, and sell that altogether in the Canadian domestic market.

"So we have decided to go ahead and concentrate on hot-rolled products."

When pressed on whether Stelco was turning away orders, the CEO responded that there were no orders: "We can't turn down something that does not exist."

A source inside Stelco told CBC News the company has customers wanting to place orders. Another industry insider said Canada’s steel industry at large continues to get orders of flat-rolled galvanized steel. CBC News is not naming these sources due concerns related to their respective employers.

The prime minister said on Tuesday that there is "money on the table from the federal government" to help companies like Stelco blunt the impact of the ongoing trade war.

Goncalves said the financial lifeline offered by Ottawa was not what his company needed.

"The problem is not lack of money. It's not like Stelco is running out of cash," he said, noting the core issue is the lack of a firm Canada-U.S. trade deal.

"There's no money that could resolve that."

World.title: Passengers foil bid to crash Dubai-Tel Aviv flight after co-pilot stabbed pilot, Israel says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Passengers on a FlyDubai flight reached Israel safely on Wednesday after passengers and crew foiled a co-pilot's attempt to crash the aircraft, Israeli officials said, in a struggle that began when he stabbed the pilot and sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds.

Passengers and crew entered the cockpit, overpowered ‌the co-pilot and enabled a second pair of FlyDubai pilots who were aboard the flight to land the jet safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, Israeli officials said.

More than 10 hours later, the passengers arrived at Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion International Airport aboard a replacement aircraft, with several describing the episode as a miracle and recounting a frantic struggle to prevent a catastrophe.

"I just can say that it was a miracle. It was awful, crazy, and we thank God that we survived it. We didn't think we will make it, but thank God we are in Israel. We are back home. And we are happy to see everyone here," passenger Lital ​Shachaf said.

The flight from the United Arab Emirates diverted to Saudi Arabia after transmitting emergency signals earlier in the day. The airport in Tabuk reported that a FlyDubai flight made a distress call at 8:44 a.m. local time, before landing safely at 9:45 a.m.

Motive under investigation

Israeli officials said the attacker's motive aboard Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv remained under investigation. Israel and the U.A.E., which includes Dubai, signed the Abraham Accords normalizing relations in 2020.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot alleged to have committed the stabbing was being questioned by Saudi authorities, though it wasn't clear if that was taking place in the hospital.

WATCH | Passengers subdue attacker on Israel-bound flight: FlyDubai pilot tried to crash Israel-bound flight, says Netanyahu | Duration closed caption 2:34 A FlyDubai flight descended into chaos when the pilot was stabbed inside the cockpit, sending the aircraft plunging. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says the attacker intended to crash the plane, which was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

Netanyahu identified the captain as Smit Machchhar, an Indian citizen, and noted his "extraordinary bravery."

The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was hospitalized in stable condition.

"Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu said on X. "He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals."

Israel's Foreign Ministry said the people on board were from Israel, India and the U.A.E. The U.S. State Department said four passengers had American citizenship.

Flights suspended

FlyDubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while an investigation takes place. Saudi authorities also said an investigation was underway.

The plane ​diverted over Jordanian airspace toward Saudi Arabia, transmitting a general emergency signal ​and then another emergency signal that indicated possible unlawful interference several minutes later, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.

The aircraft's data appeared to ⁠show that it had suddenly and rapidly descended by nearly ‌14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before the first emergency signal, Flightradar24 said.

Passengers on the FlyDubai aircraft bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates, which was diverted to Saudi Arabia following an emergency signal, arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv on Wednesday. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)

The emergency signals triggered a major security response in Israel, which has no official diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, where the plane landed.

The passengers were eventually retrieved by another aircraft, landing in Israel on Wednesday evening.

"I was sitting next to the window … 15,000 feet we fell down and you're in shock," passenger Peleg Italy told CBC's Willy Lowry after arriving in Tel Aviv. "You don't know what happened."

Italy said while he couldn't see the front of the plane from his seat, he saw people running toward the cockpit and soon the plane levelled out. "So we started flying up, and we were, like, whoa. But then the plane shifted back to normal, and everyone was squished under the G-Force."

In this still photo from video, passenger Peleg Italy describes his experience on board the FlyDubai flight as it suddenly plunged. (CBC)

Panic on board

"People started yelling and shouting that's there's blood and there's a stabbing," passenger Adam Polo told CBC News Network's Andrew Nichols from Tel Aviv. He said his fellow passengers were panicking because they could feel the plane was falling, they didn't know what was going on and there was no way to communicate with anyone on the ground.

Polo said they eventually realized the pilot had gotten the door to the cockpit open, the alleged attacker was subdued and another pilot got control of the aircraft.

The incident highlighted the potential risks on a route that has become popular among Israeli nationals since the U.A.E. and Israel normalized ties six years ago.

Polo said there was indeed some concern on board when they heard the plane was going to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, but that the concern was short-lived.

"They welcomed us in a very, very nice way. They gave everyone medical treatment, they gave us food and something to drink, sweets for the kids," Polo said.

Passengers aboard the flight described panic and then relief. (Ohad Zwigenberg/The Associated Press)

The incident came weeks before Israel holds elections on Oct. 27, with security among the top issues in the wake of the deadly Hamas-led mass attack of Oct. 7, 2023.

Netanyahu ordered authorities to "ramp up" security on both Israeli and foreign carriers flying into the country.

"Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots' identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check," Doron Spielman, ​a Netanyahu spokesperson, told Reuters.

Israel has not experienced a hijacking in decades but maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world, including on Israel-bound flights. During the 1960s and '70s, Israelis were targeted in a string of hijackings and airplane attacks by militants, including a 1972 incident in which Netanyahu, then with the Israel Defence Forces, was struck in the arm by a bullet during a rescue operation.

Friends and family wait to greet the passengers as they arrive back in Tel Aviv following the diverted flight. (Michal Yaakov Itzhaki/Reuters)

FlyDubai cautions against 'speculation'

In a statement, FlyDubai said two replacement aircraft were deployed to Tabuk to transport the passengers and crew, and it cautioned against early "speculation" about the incident.

"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation. We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts," the statement read.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said he spoke with his counterpart in the U.A.E and they agreed to work together "against extremist elements seeking to harm security and undermine stability in the region."

The general Civil Aviation Authority of the U.A.E said it was investigating a security incident.

FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates airlines. It operates daily return ⁠flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv and normally uses airspace over Saudi Arabia and Jordan.

The carrier's fleet relies entirely on variants of the 737 — a twin-engine, single-aisle aircraft that is widely used by airlines around the world. It has nearly 100 of the planes, including 69 of the Max 8 variant.

Though rare, there have been alleged and confirmed incidents of pilot murder-suicide before. It was concluded that a Germanwings pilot deliberately crashed a plane in the French Alps in 2015, killing all 150 people on the aircraft.

The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board concluded that an EgyptAir pilot in 1999 downed a plane into the Atlantic Ocean after taking off from New York — a finding that the Egyptian government disputed.

World.title: Colombia seeks to tighten checks on public protests
World.content:
Colombia’s government published a draft decree that seeks to tighten regulations on public protests.

The draft was published weeks before labor unions and social organizations plan regional anti-government protests ahead of a national strike that is set for November.

The draft seeks to update the Decree #3 of 2021, which was issued months before a national strike that was violently repressed by the police and the military.

In an attempt to prevent another bloodbath, the decree seeks to regulate authorities’ response to protests and the coordinated use of force in response to acts of vandalism and violence.

The decree regulates dialogue between the protesters and law enforcement authorities to promote the peaceful nature of protests.

The decree additionally limits the use of police intelligence against those organizing and participating in the protests.

Last but not least, the decree seeks the effective prosecution of those arrested during protests through increased surveillance and a permanent police presence.

The decree comes amid social tensions that surged after the far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and announced counterrevolutionary measures that seek to undo reforms by his leftist predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro.

Swelling student protests have been publicly accused of being fueled by insurgencies and De la Espriella has warned that police may enter universities if they find evidence they are used to prepare acts of vandalism or terrorism.

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: The Spectator likens Milei's Falklands push to Galtieri's
World.content:
The Spectator likens Milei's Falklands push to Galtieri's

30th Wednesday, September 2026 - 23:01 UTC Full article

An opinion column published on Wednesday in the British weekly The Spectator likens Argentine President Javier Milei's campaign over the Falklands to that of dictator Leopoldo Galtieri in 1982, with the difference, its author argues, that the current government is using legal rather than military means. The piece, by law professor Andrew Tettenborn, is an argument of opinion rather than a report of new facts.

The columnist calls “lawfare” — the use of legal instruments for political ends — the arbitration Argentina announced on Monday over the Sea Lion oil project. He argues that the real aim is to reopen the sovereignty question, that Milei sees the United Kingdom as weak and divided, and that he is seeking a distraction from domestic difficulties. These are the author's assessments; he also directs personal characterisations at British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and at Milei himself.

The legal core of the column is its most concrete part: the author argues that Argentina's claim is in substance a territorial sovereignty dispute and that the international law of the sea tribunal has made clear it does not see that as its role. In previous cases, tribunals constituted under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea have declined to rule on sovereignty disputes, as in the 2015 arbitration between Mauritius and the United Kingdom over the Chagos Islands. The procedure Buenos Aires has announced is an Annex VII arbitration; from the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, Argentina would only seek provisional measures while the arbitral tribunal is constituted.

The column contains inaccuracies. It places the environmental lawsuit against the project in Buenos Aires and suggests it was filed with Milei's tacit approval; it was filed on September 1, before the presidential address that launched the campaign, by the Falklands War Veterans Centre of La Plata and an association of environmental lawyers before the federal court in Río Grande, Tierra del Fuego. Nor is it confirmed that the criminal complaints cover Rockhopper executives, as the text states.

Tettenborn advises the British government to reject the claim and “hold our nerve”, and argues that international courts have lost impartiality. The British statement issued the same Wednesday, however, expressly invokes the Law of the Sea Convention as the legal framework for oil activity in the archipelago.

Argentina argues that unilateral exploitation contravenes UN General Assembly resolutions 2065 and 31/49 and that the residents' wishes do not settle the dispute. In the 2013 referendum, on a 92% turnout, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: London rejects Argentina's arbitration and questions its "reliability" as a partner
World.content:
London rejects Argentina's arbitration and questions its “reliability” as a partner

30th Wednesday, September 2026 - 22:59 UTC Full article

MLA Roberts this morning working the Labour Party Conference with Minister of Overseas Territories and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting

The British government has rejected Argentina's decision to initiate international arbitration over the Sea Lion oil project and said Buenos Aires' campaign over the Falklands “raises questions about Argentina's reliability as a partner for the United Kingdom”. It is the first time London has extended the dispute to the bilateral relationship as a whole.

The statement, signed by Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for the Overseas Territories Uma Kumaran and released on Wednesday, describes the recourse to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea as “the latest attempt to undermine the rights and livelihoods” of the archipelago's residents. It says they “have freely and democratically chosen their future” and have the right to develop their natural resources “without intimidation, coercion or interference from others”, and that hydrocarbon activity is regulated under local law “in full accordance with international law, including UNCLOS”. These are UK government positions, contested by Argentina.

According to the text, London told Argentina's ambassador to the United Kingdom this week that efforts to obstruct economic activity “are not acts of responsible international engagement” but “deliberate attempts to undermine the prosperity and economic security of a self-governing people”. The statement concludes that the United Kingdom will continue to stand “shoulder-to-shoulder” with the archipelago's government and will “robustly defend” its wishes, its economy and its right to self-determination. On X, Kumaran wrote: “The Falkland Islands are British.” Rockhopper Exploration, the project's British partner, said it would press ahead with Sea Lion and called Argentina's claim “illegitimate”, according to the Buenos Aires Herald.

President Javier Milei on Monday ordered the start of arbitration proceedings under Annex VII of the Convention and gave London two weeks to prevent exploitation in the basin north of the archipelago; if it does not, Argentina will seek provisional measures from the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. Buenos Aires argues that unilateral exploitation contravenes General Assembly resolutions 2065 and 31/49 and causes “irreversible and irreparable” harm to its rights. In previous cases, tribunals under the Convention have declined to rule on territorial sovereignty disputes.

Argentina also has 60 administrative proceedings open, with no penalty applied, and three criminal complaints against ten companies. None of the allegations has been proven. In the 2013 referendum, on a 92% turnout, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Trump and six tech companies sign a voluntary artificial intelligence safety accord
World.content:
Trump and six tech companies sign a voluntary artificial intelligence safety accord

30th Wednesday, September 2026 - 19:10 UTC Full article

The document, titled “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities”, was posted by the president after a lunch with industry executives

US President Donald Trump and the heads of six technology companies signed a voluntary accord at the White House on Tuesday under which the companies commit to ensuring the safety of their own artificial intelligence systems. Trump called it “morally binding” and said it was “almost like a constitution”.

The document, titled “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities”, was posted by the president on his Truth Social network after a lunch with industry executives. It was signed by Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Elon Musk.

According to the text, the companies are responsible for the safety of their own technology, will implement safeguards so models operate as intended, will quickly detect and fix problems and will work with independent auditors to verify their systems do not access other technical systems in unintended ways. The accord sets no consequences for breaches. Trump also announced a board to oversee the area, without naming its members, and the appointment of a government official to lead on the issue in the coming days.

Zuckerberg described it as “a start”; Pichai as “historic and consequential”; and Amodei as a way “to win safely”. Specialists consulted by the BBC were critical. Kimberlee Weatherall, a law professor at the University of Sydney, said the accord lets companies “define what counts as safety” and called it “deeply unimpressive”. Jeannie Paterson of the University of Melbourne warned that self-regulation could mean “only minimal safeguards”.

The accord comes amid calls from parts of the industry and from experts for tighter oversight of the technology. According to the BBC, OpenAI cancelled the release of one of its models on Monday over safety concerns.

The same day, Trump signed an executive order requiring federal agencies to replace “artificial intelligence” with “Super Intelligence” or “SI” in official correspondence, websites and reports, and tasking his science and technology adviser with proposing a legal definition within 60 days. In his address to the UN General Assembly last week, the president said the word “artificial” made the technology “sound fake”.

Trump reiterated his support for the expansion of data centres, whose construction has become a sensitive issue ahead of November's midterm elections: a Marist poll for NPR and PBS found 65% of registered voters oppose having them built in their area.

The accord puts into practice the position Washington set out in New York against calls for common rules. There, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for “a single set of global principles and standards”, while Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei rejected any pre-emptive regulation.

World.title: Pilot stabs another on a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight and passengers subdue him
World.content:
Pilot stabs another on a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight and passengers subdue him

30th Wednesday, September 2026 - 18:10 UTC Full article

The pilot identified as the attacker has been arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu

A pilot on a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv stabbed another pilot in the cockpit on Wednesday and, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, “apparently tried to crash the plane”. Passengers and crew members subdued him, and the aircraft made an emergency landing in Tabuk, in north-west Saudi Arabia, with all 174 passengers safe, 166 of them Israelis.

Flight FZ1073, a Boeing 737 MAX, had taken off from Dubai at 03:05 GMT. Near the Israel–Jordan border it first declared a general emergency and, minutes later, transmitted the unlawful interference code used in hijackings. According to Netanyahu, the aircraft lost about 5,200 metres of altitude in under two minutes before diverting. It landed in Tabuk at 06:58 GMT. The Israeli Air Force sent fighter jets towards the aircraft.

Netanyahu said he had spoken with a passenger who, together with a crew member, broke into the cockpit and overpowered the pilot “while he was attempting to sabotage the aircraft's systems”; another crew member stabilised the plane. Flydubai said the aircraft was secured by on-duty crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed it. The pilot identified as the attacker has been arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to the prime minister. Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, identified the injured pilot as Emirati.

Imagens de passageiros capturam o pânico a bordo de um voo da Flydubai após o co-piloto esfaquear o piloto, levando a aeronave a uma descida rápida de 17.000 pés. Passageiros correram em direção à cabine de pilotagem enquanto o co-piloto omanense começou a esfaquear o piloto.… — FREE BUBBLE (@FreeBubble40637) September 30, 2026

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz called the incident an “attempted jihadist terror attack”. The airline said the motives “are unknown” and subject to a formal investigation, and urged people to “refrain from premature speculation”. No authority has announced charges.

Several passengers said the plane began to drop and that screams came from the cockpit before three to five men went in to subdue the attacker. All were flown out on a replacement aircraft sent by Flydubai, which landed in Tel Aviv in the afternoon.

The incident comes weeks before Israel's elections. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called it a terror attack; opposition leaders Yair Lapid and Avigdor Liberman accused the government's camp of seeking political advantage. Transport Minister Miri Regev called for Flydubai flights to be suspended. Former Israeli ambassador to the United Arab Emirates Amir Hayek urged instead that the airline be allowed to investigate, and President Isaac Herzog said Israel would keep acting “together with our Emirati partners”.

Flydubai operates ten daily flights in each direction between Dubai and Tel Aviv, a route opened after the 2020 Abraham Accords, under which the UAE recognised Israel.

World.title: Foundering of Argos Georgia with the loss of 13 lives, MAIB report points to hatch failure
World.content:
Foundering of Argos Georgia with the loss of 13 lives, MAIB report points to hatch failure

30th Wednesday, September 2026 - 07:29 UTC Full article

Image of Argos Georgia. (Courtesy of Argos Froyanes Limited)

Argos Georgia sinking, air photo from MOD

The marine accident investigation report refers to the loss of Argos Georgia, 23 July 2024, which occurred approximately 190 nautical miles east of Port Stanley. The Accident Investigation report 19/2026 includes what happened, subsequent actions taken and recommendations.

Argos Georgia was a longline fishing vessel registered in St Helena. The vessel foundered while on passage from Port Stanley in the Falkland Islands to fishing grounds near the island of South Georgia. Of the 27 people on board, 13 lost their lives.

The investigation found that the line hauling hatch in the starboard side of Argos Georgia opened unexpectedly. This allowed significant quantities of water to enter the vessel, causing it to list to starboard and founder.

Safety issues



• Cause of loss: The manual securing mechanism for the line hauling hatch had likely not been applied and the hatch could not be closed by the crew. This led to the vessel progressively flooding, loss of stability and foundering.

• Technical and operational failures: The hatch’s drive mechanism had an unidentified design weakness, while open weathertight doors, vulnerable electrical systems and inaccessible manual controls allowed flooding to spread.

• On board emergency response: The crew’s response was unstructured, and delays in declaring distress and abandoning ship reduced rescue time. Poor evacuation control, extreme conditions and liferaft damage increased cold water exposure and loss of life.

• Shoreside management deficiencies: The company lacked effective systems for controlling safety-critical risks and for assessing, escalating and responding to flooding, abandonment and distress emergencies in severe weather and remote waters.

Recommendations

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is recommended to amend Merchant Shipping Notice 1873 (F) – The Code of Practice for the Construction and Safe Operation of Fishing Vessels of 24m Registered Length and Over – to include design requirements for shell door arrangements that, as a minimum, require automatic locking arrangements capable of securing doors in the closed position.

Argos Froyanes Limited is recommended to implement a documented safety management system across its fishing vessels.

The Falkland Islands Government, Directorate of Emergency Services and Islands Security is recommended to enhance the Falkland Islands maritime search and rescue communications capability so that direct and reliable contact can be established with vessels in distress within the Falkland Islands maritime search and rescue area of responsibility.

World.title: Milei opens Argentina Week at the OECD and will meet Macron at the Élysée
World.content:
Milei opens Argentina Week at the OECD and will meet Macron at the Élysée

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 21:50 UTC Full article

Friday will feature panels on energy and critical minerals, technology, artificial intelligence, international trade and fisheries. Milei will also receive an award from the Paris Economic Forum.

Argentine President Javier Milei will lead Argentina Week in Paris from Wednesday, a gathering aimed at attracting European investment, with its main day on Thursday at the headquarters of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, ending that evening with a private meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace.

The schedule released by the Argentine presidency opens on Wednesday with a welcome reception at the embassy. On Thursday, at the Château de la Muette, Milei will deliver the keynote address under the theme “Forces driving Argentina's growth: milestones and investment opportunities”, following a panel on the country's macroeconomic transformation led by Economy Minister Luis Caputo and Central Bank Governor Santiago Bausili. He will then meet provincial leaders and a group of business executives. The meeting with Macron is scheduled for 6:50 p.m., followed at 8 p.m. by a reception hosted by the French president for the delegation. The two leaders met in Paris, Buenos Aires and Nice between 2024 and 2025.

Friday will feature panels on energy and critical minerals, technology, artificial intelligence, international trade and fisheries. Milei will also receive an award from the Paris Economic Forum.

Twelve governors are travelling — from Neuquén, Mendoza, Corrientes, Chubut, Río Negro, Santa Cruz, Salta, Jujuy, San Juan, Catamarca, Entre Ríos and Chaco — along with Buenos Aires city head of government Jorge Macri. Santa Fe's Maximiliano Pullaro is not attending. The national delegation includes Presidential General Secretary Karina Milei, Cabinet Chief Diego Santilli, Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno and ministers Federico Sturzenegger, Mario Lugones and Juan Bautista Mahiques.

Participants include TotalEnergies chief executive Patrick Pouyanné; ENI's Claudio Descalzi; Glencore's Gary Nagle; Santander's Héctor Grisi; Louis Dreyfus Company chair Margarita Louis-Dreyfus; YPF's Horacio Marín; and International Energy Agency executive director Fatih Birol. Vaca Muerta, liquefied natural gas, lithium and mining are at the centre of Argentina's pitch.

Before the trip, Milei told the weekly Le Point that French investors were welcome “to come and fill their pockets in Argentina” and said his government “sanctifies property rights and the sanctity of contracts”. In a separate interview with the channel LCI, he said “Europe is sinking”.

The trip comes as financial indicators deteriorate: country risk rose above 640 points on Monday, its highest level of the year, in the same week the president questioned official activity and poverty statistics.

World.title: Lula remark on medical exams sparks controversy five days before the vote
World.content:
Lula remark on medical exams sparks controversy five days before the vote

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 21:37 UTC Full article

“Men don't like to have the prostate test. They don't like the touch. Women learn to receive touch from a young age. Men don't, they're full of hang-ups,” he said

A remark by Brazilian President and re-election candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva about men's reluctance to undergo prostate examinations has sparked a controversy in the final stretch of the campaign, after opposition figures linked it to child sexual abuse. Lula's campaign has taken the matter to the Superior Electoral Court.

Lula spoke on Monday at an event in Belém, capital of Pará state, after the first robotic prostate surgery carried out by the public health system in the country's north. “Men don't like to have the prostate test. They don't like the touch. Women learn to receive touch from a young age. Men don't, they're full of hang-ups. They don't know that when they get prostate cancer, they'll be touched a lot,” he said. In the same speech he recalled that his mother died of cancer.

Liberal Party deputy Nikolas Ferreira responded on X: “A little girl doesn't learn to receive any touch, Lula!” Other figures from the party, whose candidate is Flávio Bolsonaro, joined the criticism, and messages linking the remark to the abuse of minors spread on the platform.

Lula's coalition filed an action on Tuesday with the Superior Electoral Court against Ferreira's posts, accusing him of attributing a sexual connotation to the statement. According to the campaign, the president was speaking about public health and comparing male reluctance over prostate exams with the gynaecological check-ups women undergo from puberty.

The first round of Brazil's election takes place on Sunday, October 4.

World.title: France woos Mexico as a stronger trade partner, citing US uncertainties
World.content:
As the two nations celebrated 200 years of economic relations a French trade minister encouraged Mexico to deepen its ties with his country as a means to diversify its markets and supply chains, thereby reducing pressure on its strained trade relationship with the United States.

During the presentation of the France-Mexico Economic Report 2026 on Tuesday, French Minister Delegate for Foreign Trade and Economic Attraction Nicolas Forissier emphasized that France and Mexico share a commitment to multilateralism and to rules-based trade relations

Closer modern ties between Mexico and France followed the May 22 signing of the Modernized Global Agreement between Mexico and the European Union (EU), updating an agreement that had been in effect since 2000. The aim is to expand trade and investment, eliminate most remaining tariffs, and improve access to services, investment, and public procurement. It effectively eliminates tariffs on 99% of products traded between the EU and Mexico, significantly facilitating agricultural trade.

This joint stance is fueled by global trade uncertainty, as the U.S. Trump administration continues to pressure Mexico to meet its demands as part of negotiations to conclude the review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Free Trade Agreement (USMCA).

Forissier stressed the importance of securing supply chains, especially those linked to critical minerals and rare earth elements, given the risk that these resources could be used as tools for economic pressure.

He said that France views Mexico as a gateway to the Americas, while Paris seeks to position itself as a platform for Mexican companies to access the European Union, North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East.

Forissier urged French companies to increase their presence and investment in Mexico and called for greater investment from Mexican companies in France to solidify a mutually beneficial economic relationship.

Around 700 French companies already operate in Mexico, including 37 of France’s 40 largest companies, supporting 215,000 direct jobs, according to a report presented by the French Embassy.

Cumulative French investment in Mexico between 2006 and 2025 totaled $13.6 billion, while bilateral trade reached $7.9 billion last year.

The 2026 report indicates that over 50% of the French companies surveyed source more than half of their purchases from Mexican suppliers.

With reports from López-Dóriga Digital and Reporte Indigo

World.title: Court deals setback to controversial gas terminal on the Gulf of California
World.content:
The start of construction on a liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal in the northern state of Sonora has been temporarily halted by a federal court, even though a government port authority granted the project 36 hectares last year.

The Amigo LNG terminal — planned for Catalina Bay south of Guaymas, Sonora on the Gulf of California — would receive natural gas from the United States by pipeline, cool it into a liquid for shipment and export it by tankers to Asian markets.

A federal judge in Sonora granted a definitive suspension that temporarily bars the previously authorized construction while the court reviews an amparo (a constitutional rights challenge) filed by the environmental group Nuestro Futuro.

Last week’s ruling, which followed a Sept. 18 hearing, does not cancel the project or revoke Amigo LNG’s separate agreement with the Guaymas National Port System Administration (ASIPONA Guaymas), a federal port authority.

But the case does add to mounting opposition against LNG development in the Gulf of California, also known as the Sea of Cortez.

Dubbed the “aquarium of the world” by French ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau, the gulf is home to a rich variety of marine life and includes a UNESCO World Heritage area.

In April 2025, ASIPONA Guaymas granted Amigo LNG rights to use 36 hectares in Catalina Bay, according to documents obtained by the newspaper El País.

Awarded directly, without a public bidding process, the agreement allows the company to build and run an LNG terminal in the area.

El País reported that developers chose Mexico because similar terminals have faced stricter environmental rules and opposition on the U.S. West Coast.

The project would process at least 250,000 tonnes of LNG in its first year. That figure would rise to 3.7 million tonnes a year beginning in its 10th year — a volume equivalent to 50 to 60 large LNG carriers.

Environmental groups, citing concerns similar to those raised in a separate legal challenge that ended in a victory for whales, warn that added traffic could increase underwater noise and collision risks for marine life. The gulf is also home to the critically endangered vaquita.

They also say public documents regarding the Amigo LNG terminal did not provide enough information to fully assess risks to marine life and coastal communities.

Mexico’s Agency for Safety, Energy and Environment (ASEA) said it believes the suspension could remain in place until the court resolves the amparo.

The project cannot begin construction while the suspension remains in force.

Amigo LNG is one of several proposed projects intended to move gas from Texas’ Permian Basin through Mexico and across the Pacific to Asian markets.

With reports from El País, La Silla Rota and Global Energy.mx

World.title: 2027 midterm elections in Mexico: Who are Morena’s top picks for governor?
World.content:
An ex-chief of the federal government’s Financial Intelligence Unit and a former state attorney general are among 17 men and women selected as the ruling Morena party’s presumptive candidates for gubernatorial elections next June.

Sixteen of the 17 presumptive candidates were selected via surveys conducted by Morena, the main party of the “fourth transformation” (4T) political movement led by President Claudia Sheinbaum. The presumptive candidate in San Luis Potosí was selected by consensus.

The 10 women and seven men selected by Morena were designated as “state coordinators of the transformation and national sovereignty.”

Seven of the coordinators were announced on Monday, while 10 others were previously unveiled.

It is almost certain that the 17 coordinators will subsequently be named as Morena’s gubernatorial candidates in the 17 states where gubernatorial elections will be held on June 6, 2027.

It is likely that the Labor Party (PT) and the Green Party (PVEM) will support most, if not all, of the candidates selected by Morena. Both the PT and the PVEM are allies of Morena.

Morena’s 17 presumptive gubernatorial candidates are listed below in alphabetical order by the states they are seeking to govern. Morena already governs 12 of the states where gubernatorial elections will be held next year. MND will cover prospective candidates from other parties in future articles.
