World.title: Defence raises questions about cop who was member of Kevin Smith’s flock
World.content:
Late pastor of Pathways International Restoration Ministries, Kevin Smith.

THE detective sergeant who cried repeatedly on Tuesday while giving evidence in the Andre Ruddock murder trial in the Home Circuit Court in Kingston breathed a sigh of relief on Wednesday as she was released as a witness after defence attorney Anthony Williams ended his cross-examination of her.

Ruddock is on trial for murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 throat cutting of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner at the Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James.

On Wednesday, the witness was more composed on the stand as Williams quizzed her on the happenings at the church where Gardner and two male members were killed. One of the men was killed allegedly by the late pastor of the church, Dr Kevin Smith. The other man was shot and killed by the police after he attacked lawmen with a knife.

The detective sergeant was the initial investigator assigned to the case before it was turned over to a more senior cop.

On the day of the incident, the pastor was said to have taken a Glock pistol from a female member of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) who was also a member of the church. The pastor used that firearm to shoot at the police.

When the incident was brought to an end, the police carted away numerous individuals, including Smith and the members of his church, to a police station where criminal charges were laid against them.

The female cop, who had a close relationship with Smith, was among those who were arrested. She was charged for breaching the Disaster Risk Management Act (DRMA) during COVID-19 lockdowns when no one, except for essential workers, was supposed to be on the road. Under the Act, large gatherings were prohibited.

Williams, who is one of two attorneys representing Ruddock, along with Venice Brown, asked the witness whether any other charges were laid against the female police member of Smith’s flock.

The attorney enquired if the cop was ever referred to the Inspectorate and Professional Standards Oversight Bureau (IPROB), which is a disciplinary unit within the JCF.

“Is this arm of the JCF responsible for complaints and investigations into the conduct of any member of the JCF?” Williams asked.

The witness told him that to the best of her knowledge that was, in fact, so.

The attorney wanted to know why the cop wasn’t referred to IPROB, but no definitive answer was given to that question.

The witness told the court that when the female constable was arrested, she was taken to an area of the church which looked like living quarters where she handed over a bag that contained her private Glock pistol, handcuffs, a video recorder, personal items, as well as her police uniform.

“As indicated to me, it was a private firearm,” the witness said.

Williams asked her if the constable’s hands were swabbed, and the witness said she personally did not swab her hands but gave instructions for that activity to be carried out; however, she could not speak to the outcome of the swabbing.

“When you first saw her on the 17th of October 2021, did she say anything to you?” Williams asked.

The witness responded in the affirmative, saying that she did speak to the cop, and that she said several things.

The lawyer sought to find out if whatever was said was indicative of her involvement at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries.

“In light of the several utterances, did it lead you to carry out any further investigation?” the attorney asked.

“Yes, sir, certainly,” the witness said, before explaining that she was not the person who charged the constable.

She explained further that she did not know who exactly charged the constable for breaching the DRMA.

The trial continues today with a new witness. The seven members of the jury are expected to view photographs of the scene at the church as described by the six witnesses who have taken the stand so far during the trial which started two weeks ago.

World.title: Kabaka Pyramid still has lots to say
World.content:
Kabaka Pyramid.

There is still a rebel in Kabaka Pyramid. Fifteen years after the Rebel Music era first introduced audiences to that particular side of his artistry, the Kingston-born musician has chosen to revisit familiar territory — but he is not quite the same man who entered it.

Though the lyrical sharpness and the instinct to make music that says something beyond simply sounding good remains, time and a few battles of his own have added new layers to the story.

That evolution is recognisable in his latest single A Warrior’s Pain, a collaboration with American rappers R-Mean and Styles P.

The track serves as the foundation for Rebel Music 1 & 2, a new lyrics tape marking 15 years since the beginning of the entertainer’s Rebel Music chapter.

For Kabaka Pyramid, the return was not the result of an elaborate master plan. In fact, it was almost accidental.

“We knew the 15-year anniversary of Rebel Music was approaching and also the 10-year anniversary of the Accurate mixtape,” he explained. “So my team and I were floating around ideas since the start of the year. We were keeping it simple — samples and hip hop drums,” he said. “I just wanted something that inspired me to be lyrical.”

That instinct reignited something the artiste said had perhaps become dormant.

“It felt like I had suppressed a part of my craft and it needed to be reawakened,” he said outlining that the first few tracks were a hit with his manager, who remarked that they sounded like the

Rebel Music days.

“That moment was when we knew what had to be done,” he said. “Everything flowed easily from there.”

That renewed focus on lyricism sits alongside another important thread in Kabaka Pyramid’s current work — vulnerability.

On A Warrior’s Pain, the entertainer brings together reggae and hip hop through a shared appreciation for substance, storytelling, and resistance. But beneath the lyrical exchanges and musical chemistry, A Warrior’s Pain speaks to a more personal kind of battle

Kabaka Pyramid points to his own struggle with confidence in his voice and singing ability as part of the experience informing his contribution.

“I was always being told I need more melody, songs need to be more catchy, simplify the music,” he said. But, rather than resist the criticism, he used it as motivation.

“So I put in the hours to train myself and be ready for anything when called upon,” he explained. “Overcoming challenges is the best way to build confidence and strength comes from there naturally.”

That growth is perhaps one of the clearest differences between the Kabaka Pyramid of the early days and the artiste he has become.

“The message is still the same, just more mature now,” he said. “I think more people can relate to what I’m saying. It’s not music only for hip hop heads that love to dissect lyrical patterns.”

With that said, Kabaka Pyramid shared that the response to reggae and conscious music from international audiences continues to surprise him, particularly in Africa, Europe, Japan, and the United States. This is sees as not cultural appropriation, but an opportunity to observe how others interpret and conduct business around Jamaican music.

“When others incorporate our music I like to learn from them, and see what aspects they connect with and also how they conduct the business of touring,” he said.

There is, however, one boundary: “If you sample my record I want what is rightfully mine,” he said with a laugh.

World.title: Green calls for regional farmworker framework
World.content:
Belize’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise, Rodwell Ferguson (left) speaking on Wednesday during a plenary session on “Unlocking private sector partnerships and expanding investments in agriculture and fisheries development” during the Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 conference at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny. Looking on is Floyd Green, Jamaica’s agriculture minister. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CORAL SPRING, Trelawny — Agriculture Minister Floyd Green is calling for a regional structure to facilitate the movement of agricultural workers across the Caribbean, pointing to Dominica as a model for easing constraints on farmers and boosting production.

“I think we need a framework, a framework that works for the movement of agricultural workers across the region,” he said.

He noted that Dominica has already established a framework for agricultural migrant workers which has enabled the country to bring in about 200 workers, benefiting roughly 80 farmers and contributing to a significant increase in productivity.

Green was speaking during Wednesday’s plenary session on “Unlocking private sector partnerships and expanding investments in agriculture and fisheries development” at the Caribbean Week of Agriculture 2026 conference. It was held at Ocean Coral Spring Hotel in Trelawny.

The session, on the fourth of the six-day conference, followed a question from the floor about region-wide difficulty finding workers for agriculture.

Green said the Caribbean should reconsider its traditionally insular approach to agricultural labour.

“If given the opportunity, just as they are given the opportunity to go to Canada and to go to America and they work and they return home…what about the region?” he asked.

He said a regional mechanism could allow workers to take up agricultural employment in neighbouring territories while providing farmers with access to people willing to work within the sector.

Green acknowledged that such an arrangement would require proper oversight, but said Dominica’s experience provides a model worth examining. He said he intends to raise the matter at the Caribbean Community’s Council for Trade and Economic Development (COTED).

At the same time, Green said the region must make greater use of technology as the profile of the agricultural workforce changes.

“One of the challenges with the young people going into agriculture now, they want to be owners. They don’t want to be workers,” he said, stressing the need to provide them with tools that can improve efficiency and productivity.

Green cited agricultural drones as one example of how technology can reduce reliance on manual tasks.

Through the Rural Agricultural Development Authority (RADA), Jamaica has invested in four drones which farmers may rent. They come with trained drone pilots. The College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) is also training drone operators, while Jamaican company Sky Crop has begun assembling agricultural drones locally.

Green also pointed to the growing use of small walk-behind tractors, which can enable individual farmers to more efficiently manage their operations.

He said artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies should form part of the region’s response as agriculture adapts to changing workforce patterns.

Belize’s Minister of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise Rodwell Ferguson said his country has experienced a similar shift.

He recalled that three to four decades ago, Belize relied on agricultural workers from neighbouring Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. That has changed as more young Belizeans have gained access to secondary and tertiary education, including university and postgraduate studies.

“Young people are getting the opportunity to go to high school, sixth form, universities, [do] master’s degree, doctorate degree. And so maybe it is a good reason for the advent of the AI because it’s a time when we are having labour shortage, and no matter what we do, we can’t convince those young people to go and do agriculture,” he said.

Ferguson said the changing aspirations of young people are also reflected in schools.

In Belize, he said, agriculture is compulsory in first and second form but becomes an elective in third and fourth form. By then, participation can fall to about five students.

Ferguson said smart agriculture could help make the sector more attractive to young people while helping Belize meet its food production needs.

“It is critical. It is crucial because we must be able to feed ourselves,” he said.

World.title: UNITED BEHIND INFANTINO
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) speaks with British Virgin Islands Football Association President Avanell Morton during the launch of the island’s new technical centre on Saturday. (Photo: FIFA Media)

The Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) will not be alone in backing FIFA President Gianni Infantino with fellow Caribbean associations of Trinidad and Tobago, British Virgin Islands, Antigua and Barbuda, and St Kitts and Nevis also on board.

Infantino recently completed his tour of the Caribbean at the weekend with many critics believing the trip was used to try to secure votes as he seeks to remain FIFA president for another four years ahead of the body’s congress in Morocco in March.

Infantino, 54, has led FIFA since 2016 and has faced increased scrutiny over the past few months after his controversial plan to sell stakes in FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cup, to private investors. This plan was eventually scrapped last month after widespread backlash. Infantino’s recent Caribbean visit was his second in a matter of weeks after attending the Caribbean Football Union Presidents’ Meeting in the Dominican Republic. He was advised prior by his FIFA vice-president and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani to stay away from the event.

His first stop was in Kingston on Friday where he met with JFF officials, including President Michael Ricketts, and attended the Reggae Boyz’s 3-2 win over Guatemala in the Concacaf Nations League at the National Stadium.

As the Jamaica Observer reported on Sunday, the JFF will back Infantino in the upcoming elections with the board of directors in favour of him staying.

Ricketts told the Observer in August that he would support Infantino, given what he describes as massive support he’s given to football, particularly in the Caribbean.

Ricketts reiterated his support for Infantino after his one-day visit to the island.

“I think Infantino has done so very well for football globally,” he said. “I remember when I got into football as the president, the support from FIFA was medial to say the least.It has been a lot better now and we are just very grateful and we are looking forward to further improvements so that we can impact not just football but the social well-being of every boy and girl who plays the sport.”

Also in Kingston during Infantino’s visit was Trinidad and Tobago Football Association (TFFA) Kieron Edwards who also attended the game on Friday. Trinidad’s senior men’s team played Haiti at Sabina Park a day before.

In 2020, FIFA appointed a normalisation committee to manage the TTFA’s affairs due to serious financial issues. However, it was lifted in 2024 with Edwards being named president.

Edwards says FIFA has helped to reshape football in his country.

“FIFA is our largest supporter when it comes to our infrastructure,” he said. “Even our leagues, when we look at our women’s league now, [it’s a] full professional league, playing for seven months for the year, over 12 teams. That was only [possible because of] the continued support of FIFA in terms of our games. When it comes to the support of FIFA in terms of growing football, not just in Trinidad and Tobago but across the Caribbean and Concacaf, it’s been tremendous so far.”

Edwards says he has no doubts that the TTFA will be backing Infantino at the elections next year.

“We would have given President Infantino our full support and we have not wavered with that. Things do come up, changes, you have to have discussions, you have to have dialogue but the support is there 100 per cent behind the President always.”

British Virgin Islands (BVI) Football Association president Avanell Morton has also thrown his support behind Infantino.

Infantino visited BVI on Saturday and opened the new BVI Technical Centre, which was funded by FIFA.

“What more can he do? He’s doing a fantastic job already. He’s doing a fantastic job in the entire region,” Morton said.

The Antigua and Barbuda Football Association (ABFA), led by President Ickford Roberts, is also in favour of Infantino staying on as president. Infantino visited the island on Saturday and met with Roberts and Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who announced that a new football stadium would be built with FIFA support.

“[Infantino’s] transformative policies, from ground-breaking investment in grassroots infrastructure to the historic expansion of World Cup access, have elevated the aspirations of emerging football nations into attainable realities,” the ABFA said in a statement recently. “By listening with genuine humility and acting with decisive conviction, he has forged a legacy of inclusivity that transcends the sport itself, affirming that every nation, regardless of size, deserves equal voice and fair opportunity on the world stage.”

Infantino also visited St Kitts and Nevis on Saturday, where he attended the launch of a new technical centre with St Kitts and Nevis Football Association President Atiba Hattis president giving his support.

Infantino could have as many as 25 Caribbean votes behind him if all of the region’s FIFA member associations support his bid.

No one has signalled intentions to challenge Infantino with nominations closing on November 18, but it’s understood that Montagliani is seen as a credible opponent who would receive the backing of Europe (UEFA) and the Asian Football Confederation.

World.title: Dinner @ OMNIA SKY LOUNGE
World.content:
(Photo: Aceion Cunningham)

Nestled atop Parkway Plaza in Ocho Rios, Omnia Sky Lounge has quickly become more than just a dining spot — it’s the embodiment of Jamaican flavour, international influences, and vibrant nightlife. Since its grand opening in April 2024, this rooftop haven has been captivating locals and tourists alike with its unique blend of great food, lively music, and inviting ambience.

For owner Doneisha Johnson, the journey to creating Omnia Sky Lounge is rooted in her travels, taking cues from stunning rooftop lounges in Indonesia and Los Angeles. Her previous venture, a Loud Fashion store in Ocho Rios, serendipitously provided the perfect platform — the rooftop space above the store — to birth a new concept. She envisioned a place that brought together food, music, ambience, and entertainment in a seamless, memorable offering.

“It was about creating something different. A place where people don’t just come to eat, but to immerse themselves in an unforgettable experience,” Johnson said.

Omnia Sky Lounge embraces the tagline ‘Dinner With a Vibe,’ aiming to transcend the typical dining experience. Whether guests come for a celebratory occasion, a casual night out, or an exclusive event, the lounge promises an atmosphere that lingers in memory long after the night ends.

The concept is clear and intentional — a fusion where the essence of Caribbean cuisine meets international flair, showcased in a setting alive with music, thoughtfully crafted cocktails, and a welcoming environment.

The menu showcases contemporary Caribbean dishes infused with Jamaican flavours — seafood, chicken, pork, curry goat, and pastas — all prepared with Omnia’s distinctive twist. Alongside enticing bites is an impressive beverage selection featuring signature cocktails, premium spirits, wines, Champagne, and bottle service.

Feedback has been overwhelmingly positive, cementing Omnia as a destination for locals and visitors, with the lounge becoming a favoured spot for special occasions like birthdays, weddings, corporate events, and family reunions.

“Seeing customers return and recommending us has been extremely rewarding. Sometimes I stand back and remember when Omnia was simply an idea in my head. Seeing people choose us for something as important as their wedding makes the challenges of entrepreneurship feel worthwhile,” Johnson expressed.

Johnson has ambitious plans for Omnia’s growth, aiming to enhance the existing space with an additional level and dedicated event areas. An exciting new concept centred on regulated cannabis is also under consideration, pending licensing and approvals.

“Our plans include adding another upper level above the kitchen area and two dedicated event spaces at the rear of the property. The goal is to continue developing Omnia into a complete dining, entertainment, events, and lifestyle destination. Long term, I definitely see the Omnia brand expanding beyond Ocho Rios,” Johnson added.

Johnson also expressed gratitude to her loyal customers, dedicated staff and excitement for the future.

“We’re proud of what we’ve built, excited about what’s ahead, and still building. My vision is for Omnia Sky Lounge to become a must-visit destination when people come to Ocho Rios and Jamaica,” Johnson concluded.

Text & Photos: Aceion Cunningham

World.title: Post match brawl mars Vauxhall’s win over Charlie Smith in Walker Cup
World.content:
Screengrab of video showing crowd gathered on Charlie Smith High School field following alleged brawl following Walker Cup round-of-16 match on Tuesday (Original Video: andrewilliamsmedia Instagram)

Vauxhall High School’s dramatic Walker Cup round-of-16 victory over Charlie Smith High School was followed by a reported post-match disturbance, with videos circulating online appearing to show alleged stone-throwing, fighting and damage to property after the game.

Vauxhall High secured their place in the next round of the competition after overcoming the hosts in a tense penalty shootout, but the celebrations were overshadowed by events that unfolded after the final whistle.

Footage shared online appears to show chaotic scenes at the venue, with reports that students and teachers from Vauxhall High were injured during the incident. There are also reports that the Vauxhall team was unable to leave the venue for more than an hour due to difficulties accessing an exit.

In one video, a man can be heard saying that people at the venue were unable to leave because stones were being thrown.

“They are throwing stones and we cannot leave,” the man said before turning the camera towards another man behind a gate, who he said had refused to open it.

Another video appears to show two men engaged in a physical confrontation on the field, while separate footage shows a coaster bus with shattered windows as students disembarked.

Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) competition director Ewan Scott confirmed that the governing body was aware of the incidents and said a full investigation would follow.

“A thorough investigation will be conducted,” Scott said, following reports submitted by the schools.

The disturbances marred what has otherwise been an impressive campaign for Vauxhall, who have emerged as one of the competition’s surprise performers after entering the knockout phase with a 2-0 victory over Norman Manley High.

Their latest victory came in another closely contested encounter, with neither side able to find a winner after 90 minutes before Vauxhall held their nerve from the penalty spot.

The result also provided another reminder of the intensity surrounding the Walker Cup, particularly with several of Jamaica’s traditional schoolboy football powers competing in a revamped knockout format.

World.title: Sugar tax shortfall
World.content:
The new sugar sweetened drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year.

The Government collected $3 billion less than it had budgeted from the local special consumption tax (SCT) during the April-June quarter, with the Ministry of Finance pointing, in part, to non-compliance following the introduction of the sugar-sweetened drinks tax.

But the country’s fiscal watchdog, the Independent Fiscal Commission (IFC), says the explanation does not go far enough.

The IFC said information provided by the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service (MoFPS) was inadequate to determine whether the explanation for the 35.5 per cent shortfall was reasonable.

According to the IFC’s latest statement on fiscal performance that was tabled in Parliament last week, the Government collected $5.52 billion in local SCT during the first quarter of the 2026/27 financial year, well below the $8.57 billion that had been budgeted.

The resulting $3.04-billion gap was the largest shortfall recorded under the local SCT heading among the production and consumption taxes for the quarter.

The ministry attributed the underperformance to several factors, with the introduction of the new tax on non-alcoholic, sugar-sweetened beverages forming only part of its explanation.

“The shortfall reflects lower-than-expected collections from new revenue measures in Q1 (quarter one), due in part to non-compliance by some firms in remitting SCT for May 2026 following the introduction of the sweetened drinks tax. Changes in production and consumption behaviour in anticipation of the scheduled tax increases announced under the FY [financial year] 2026/27 revenue measures also contributed to the shortfall.

“Lower remittances from Petrojam Limited, together with weaker-than-expected performance in the automotive, petroleum distribution, and beverage/tobacco industries, further reduced SCT collections,” the ministry told the IFC.

However, the IFC was not satisfied that the explanation provided enough information to properly assess the reasons for the shortfall.

The new sweetened-drinks tax came into effect on May 1, two months into the fiscal year. The Government had initially proposed a charge of two cents per millilitre on non-alcoholic sweetened beverages, but subsequently changed the structure following consultations with industry. The revised measure applies SCT at 22 cents per gram of added sugar or sweetener.

The Government had said the measure was intended not only to raise revenue but also to support public-health objectives. It was originally projected to generate $10.1 billion during the fiscal year.

The implementation itself also encountered administrative challenges. Tax Administration Jamaica extended the deadline for beverage manufacturers to complete licensing under the new SCT regime to May 15, after the tax took effect.

The local SCT shortfall formed part of a wider revenue gap during the quarter. Central Government revenue and grants came in $28.7 billion, or 9.8 per cent, below budget, while tax revenue was $18.8 billion, or 6.9 per cent below target.

The IFC noted that nearly $9 billion of the overall $28.7-billion gap was related to timing differences, including tax revenue that had been projected for April but was collected in March as some companies paid early, and a $2.9-billion transfer from the National Housing Trust that was budgeted for June but was received in September.

The delayed implementation of the Environmental Protection Levy also contributed to the revenue shortfall. The IFC estimated that the delay resulted in approximately $700 million in revenue not being collected during the June quarter and projected a $1.8-billion revenue fallout for the 2026/27 FY if implementation remained delayed.

The legislation for the Environmental Protection Levy was passed by the Senate last Friday with the higher 0.85 per cent levy set to take effect on October 1.

World.title: Spain’s warning on drug pricing deals
World.content:
Presented by EFPIA By CLAUDIA CHIAPPA with DOMINIC GIANNINI

Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum.

SNEAK PEEK

— Europe must band together to tackle drug pricing pressures rather than being picked off one by one, Spain’s Health Secretary Javier Padilla Bernáldez tells Morning Health Care.

— Parliament’s environment committee will vote on its opinion for the Biotech Act.

— EU health ministers meet in Dublin.

Welcome to Thursday’s Morning Health Care! Kudos to all those who made it to the 6am hike ahead of another jam-packed day at the European Health Forum in Gastein. I won’t throw Claudia under the bus, but I, for one, proudly took the lie-in. For those who opted for the walk, at least their stride shouldn’t have been impacted by this news that air pollution can impact marathon times — thanks to the clear air of the Austrian Alps.

Get in touch: [email protected], [email protected]. 

DRIVING THE DAY

LET’S COME TOGETHER: Spain’s Health Secretary Javier Padilla Bernáldez has called for Europe to band together in the face of U.S. drug pricing pressures rather than seeking bilateral agreements. As pressure mounts on Germany to strike a deal with the Trump administration, Padilla Bernáldez argues any such deal risks weakening the European market.

Right now: “When [most favored nation] emerged, there was a consensus that the main strength of the European Union was being more people with a higher degree of universal health coverage, and the weakness was having a fragmented market,” Padilla Bernáldez told Morning Health Care at the European Health Forum in Gastein, Austria. “If you go bilateral, you are losing this main strength.”

The context: Europe is grappling with how to respond to the Trump administration’s most-favored-nation drug pricing policy, which risks delaying the launch of new medicines in Europe. Companies fear launching in Europe will risk a lower matched price in the U.S., limiting profits in that lucrative market.

Is the breakfast club no more? Countries initially seemed to be on the same page about the best way to respond to the pressure — as a team. Back in June, 11 countries, led by Sweden, first met to debate how to protect EU prices and agreed they were stronger when working together rather than pursuing individual deals. The Beneluxa group — a health care alliance uniting Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Austria and Ireland — also urged Europe to protect its solidarity-based health systems and warned against “uncoordinated, individual national responses.”

Sweden continues to lead discussions on drug pricing and reimbursement amid geopolitical pressure, within an EU alliance of authorities that carry out this work known as NCAPR. (The next meeting is Oct. 9.) But some may be breaking ranks.

Art of the deal: U.S. diplomats and pharma companies are eyeing deals with EU countries similar to the one Washington struck with the U.K., which will see the National Health Service pay more for medicines.

Germany has been in talks with U.S. officials over the price of its medicines, following the Section 301 investigation. It has not announced an agreement but is considering rewarding drugmakers with higher prices if they invest locally.

France this week announced a new deal with the pharmaceutical sector on drug pricing, to provide “more clarity and predictability to pharmaceutical companies.” “France is making a clear choice to invest in the future,” the government said Tuesday. Health Minister Stéphanie Rist said access to medicines was at the heart of the policy, while Public Accounts Minister David Amiel said "the resources released throughout the life cycle of medicines must make it possible to finance innovation and the treatments of tomorrow."

Bad idea? Padilla Bernáldez warned that countries are giving up Europe’s main strength, its potentially large market, by thinking that they will be treated “in a positive way by the bully government of the United States” — but “I don't think it's going to happen.”

No comment, but: The U.S. government didn’t respond to a request for comment, but when it announced its trade probe into Germany’s drug pricing policies, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the U.S. was “calling on Germany to pay its fair share for the innovative treatments its people use.”

We’ve seen this film before: “When we talk about procurement in Europe, there are always countries with big economies that think — and maybe that’s true — that they are … going to get a better price if they are going on their own,” Padilla Bernáldez said. “Maybe France and Germany think they are going to calm the United States by going on their own. It doesn't work like that.”

Muddy deals: Yannis Natsis, head of the European Social Insurance Platform, representing payers, agreed that “going it alone is no solution.” “It remains unclear what French patients and taxpayers will get in return for accepting higher prices,” he said. “Even less clear is what pharmaceutical companies are committing to in return, beyond benefiting from those higher prices.”

Yes, but: Renew MEP Stine Bosse said the new French deal has “the right instinct.” But she warned that Europe should act as one in rewarding innovation and manufacturing. Her fear is that multiple sets of rules or bilateral deals will make the EU “more vulnerable” — “we become an even less predictable place for the companies we want to invest here.” Patients will pay the price, she said, and Europe’s competitiveness will suffer. "Europe must act as one, or we will be picked off, one by one."

It’s a common sentiment in Gastein: Valentina Strammiello from the European Patients’ Forum supported the European Commission coordinating a discussion that included patients’ voices, saying it was important that stakeholders were brought together to find a solution. “Otherwise, keeping working in isolation doesn't lead to any solution,” she said.

Also pro-EU: Nathalie Moll, head of pharma lobby EFPIA, said that Europe risks losing out “as a whole” if countries put policies in place to attract manufacturing to their country. “The problem in Europe is … that there isn't enough Europe. And here we need to be smart as a region in how we consider competitiveness and what tools we put in place to attract the investment, and not fragment ourselves even further than we are today.”

What now? Ministers had asked the Commission to conduct an impact assessment of Trump’s policies at their last meeting, which Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi handed back to member states in August — although it found it was too early to assess the impact on Europe. The ball is now in the Council’s court.

Rolling coverage: EFPIA’s Moll said it was “really important” the impact of MFN on Europe is "monitored very closely, so that we can respond to it in the right way," adding there needs to be “continuous assessment.” Europe also had to look at solutions it could implement quickly, and this should include scrapping clawbacks and cost containment measures, she added.

BIOTECH ACT

TIME TO VOTE: The environment committee is set to vote on its opinion on the Biotech Act today. Socialists and Democrats MEP Nicolás González Casares, who wrote the draft opinion, has called to scrap or limit the proposal to extend some biotech patents. This is only an opinion since the health and industry committees lead on the proposal.

Talking about the Biotech Act: Padilla Bernáldez has used his appearance at Gastein to defend Spain’s proposal to create a “European Coordinated Market Access Toolbox” to help drugs reach the market earlier. Countries could work together to estimate demand and coordinate negotiations with companies or launch collaborative procurement.

But: Companies could have commitments such as ensuring supply continuity, maintaining European manufacturing capacity, submitting national pricing and reimbursement applications on time, and ensuring equitable launch and access.

Reciprocal commitments: Moll at EFPIA said there also needed to be reciprocal commitments on the part of states. “One of the commitments has to be to increase the value that is given to innovative medicines, so there needs to be a recognition that these products bring value beyond the value to the patient, but also to the economy and in the socio-economic context,” she told Morning Health Care.

Speed up access: Moll has another proposal — an agreement to make medicines available on the market while national pricing and reimbursement negotiations are ongoing, meaning patients would have faster access to drugs. Companies would set an initial price before discussions would start, and if negotiations stalled, patients would be able to keep using the medicine through a non-reimbursed route. Moll admitted the idea was in its early phases and hadn’t been brought to governments.

COUNCIL

WELCOME: Ireland’s Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill will chair an informal meeting of EU health ministers in Dublin today, which will also include the EU health commissioner, the World Health Organization’s Europe director and the head of the European Medicines Agency.

Smile: Ministers were shown around Dublin’s National Institute for Bioprocessing Research and Training on Wednesday afternoon, and today’s meeting will kick off with a family photo.

On the agenda: They’ll hold closed-door discussions on innovation and improving patient outcomes; integrating care across the EU and strengthening medical ecosystems; and, of course, discuss global pressures and collective action.

Sneak peek: The Irish Council of the EU presidency wants to lean into Europe’s commitment to universal access to health for the whole population, rather than people’s ability to pay. “There's huge strength in that,” Muiris O’Connor, assistant secretary at the Department of Health, told Gastein via videolink. “We retain a core belief in science, and we purchase medicines and medical products at national scale right across the European Union. So I really think we have to remember just what is really strong about us and shore up the vulnerabilities.” A press conference is scheduled for 3.30 p.m.

UCPM

SANT, ENVI VOTE ON UCPM PROPOSAL: Lawmakers in the public health and environment committees will vote today on an EU proposal for a union civil protection mechanism, or UCPM, for health emergency preparedness and response.

What’s this about? In the next multiannual financial framework proposal, the Commission wants to expand the civil protection mechanism — created to strengthen cooperation for disasters — to include health emergency preparedness and response. The proposed budget for this was €11 billion, though it’s unspecified how much will go to the civil protection department DG ECHO versus the health preparedness authority DG HERA.

Behind the report: The health and environment committees are leading on this file. Their compromise proposes increasing the budget to over €12 billion and allocating funds across sectors: 40% for civil protection, 40% for health emergencies, and 20% for flexibility.

Some of the changes: The committee draft proposes a new focus on climate-risk assessment, scenario planning and stress testing; emphasizes a One Health approach and measures to build public risk awareness and community preparedness; calls for action to fight disinformation; and expands support for resilient health care systems and workforces, cross-border medical teams, patient evacuation and stockpiling of medical countermeasures.

Smooth sailing: Lawmakers are expecting a “straightforward” vote, after reaching a “balanced agreement” supported by EPP, S&D, ECR, Renew, Greens and The Left, said S&D's Leire Pajín, a co-author with ECR's Aurelijus Veryga.

WHAT WE’RE READING

The FT looks at how Australia is battling a black market for cigarettes after a decade of tax rises.

Patients switching to Novo's Wegovy pill from shots lose more weight, Reuters reports.

World.title: The €865 billion brainstorming session
World.content:
Ukraine’s prime minister is warning of a $20 billion defense funding gap as Russia intensifies its attacks and Kyiv struggles to protect its skies and keep the country running. Zoya Sheftalovich and Sarah Wheaton look at just how much pressure Ukraine is under — from its military finances to farmers struggling to get their grain out.



They also unpack the Commission and EU governments’ two-day brainstorming session on how a huge chunk of the next EU budget should work — and who may end up controling it.



Plus, the Commission’s attempt to build a sovereign alternative to Microsoft Teams is not exactly winning rave reviews.

World.title: Trump says diesel export ban is still on the table
World.content:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the administration, as well as European governments, would soon announce measures aimed at bringing down diesel prices.

President Donald Trump said Wednesday he hasn’t yet made up his mind on whether to impose a ban on diesel fuel exports, despite fierce pushback on the idea in recent days from the oil and gas industry and some of his own advisers.

The White House is facing growing pressure to take steps to bring down record high diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections, and Trump indicated last week he would be open to restricting exports. But members of his Cabinet and top industry officials argue that such a move would end up raising prices for all types of fuel, including gasoline, and they have scrambled to present alternative measures to the president.

“I’m thinking about it,” Trump said of the export ban at an Oval Office event. “I speak to [Energy Secretary] Chris [Wright] and [Interior Secretary] Doug [Burgum] about it a lot — they sort of think it’ll help diesel, but it might raise the price of other things.”

World.title: Securing coastal waters for small-scale fishers: Lessons from Ghana
World.content:
Amid continued debate over marine spaces, the question of who leads and shapes action has never been more critical to answer. The European Union’s (EU) Ocean Act presents a crucial opportunity to change the future of Europe’s seas equitably and sustainably, and lessons can be learnt from small-scale fishers thousands of kilometers away in West Africa.

Ghana faces immense economic pressures, and despite access to far less financial and scientific resources than the EU, the government has committed to strong protection of its coastal waters. It extended its Preferential Access Area (PAA) from six to 12 nautical miles, granting exclusive fishing access to local, small-scale fishers while barring destructive vessels, namely trawlers, from coastal waters.

Real-world evidence shows that well-enforced PAAs, where bottom trawling is prohibited, strengthen the resilience of small-scale fleets, accelerate fish stock recovery and protect coastal livelihoods.

Meanwhile, despite its global leadership in fighting illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing and its repeated commitments to global ocean protection, the EU continues to allow industrial bottom trawlers near-unfettered access to coastal waters. This comes at the direct expense of coastal communities and small-scale fishers who represent the vast majority of Europe’s fishing fleet.

Recent research highlights how a small group of large commercial owners, acting through fishing industry associations, has opposed stronger seabed protection in Brussels by questioning the science and warning of socio-economic disruption. Yet real-world evidence shows that well-enforced PAAs, where bottom trawling is prohibited, strengthen the resilience of small-scale fleets, accelerate fish stock recovery and protect coastal livelihoods.

Ghana may not offer Europe a ready-made blueprint for preferential access, but the country’s experience demonstrates that governments can make significant policy changes when the voices of affected communities, evidence and objective political leadership come together.

A decade on the frontlines — CaFGOAG’s story

In Ghana, small-scale fisheries are not simply an occupation; they are the foundation of coastal communities. In contrast to destructive trawl fleets, they are among the most energy-efficient animal-sourced food production systems, with low environmental impacts and outsized economic and social value. Yet fishers are experiencing declining catches, increasing costs and competition from industrial trawlers.

Industrial fishing, such as bottom trawling, has been a major driver of this decline, particularly through the “saiko” fish trade, where trawlers harvest juvenile and small pelagic species and illegally transship them at sea into adapted canoes for onward sale at local markets.

Our experience has demonstrated that political and economic complexity must never be an excuse for inaction.

The consequences extend beyond individual fishers: fish processors, traders and economies are devastated, with women feeling the impact most severely when landings crash. For the Canoe and Fishing Gear Owners Association of Ghana (CaFGOAG), the fundamental issue is not simply competition between fishing methods, but whether marine resources are managed to protect the ecological foundations of life at sea and protect livelihoods for coastal communities.

For over a decade, CaFGOAG has consistently called for stronger protection of Ghana’s inshore waters through an expanded PAA. Our experience has demonstrated that political and economic complexity must never be an excuse for inaction. Instead, it underscores the need for meaningful dialogue, robust evidence and direct participation of the people whose livelihoods are closely connected to the marine resources.

Small-scale fishers are central to Ghana’s progress. The case for extending the PAA was rooted in lived experience: fishers know their fishing grounds, seasonal patterns, changes in fish availability and the practical consequences of industrial fishing activity, in ways that complement scientific information.

It is paramount that fishers and their communities are directly involved in policy discussions, with community knowledge considered alongside scientific evidence. This approach, supported by the Transform Bottom Trawling Coalition and its members, such as Oceana and Blue Ventures, has helped advance efforts to promote PAAs in Ghana, Brazil, the Philippines and elsewhere.

Ghana’s progress toward extending the PAA from six to 12 nautical miles is a milestone for small-scale fishers worldwide. It now joins a growing list of countries that have adopted, or are in the process of adopting, similar measures.

The view from Portugal — MARSEMPRE’s story

Portugal is facing many of the same pressures. In Ferragudo, in the Algarve, Marsempre was established in 2021 to defend the village’s maritime cultural heritage and champion reform toward a more sustainable sea.

© OCEANA / Gorka Leclercq

Marsempre began pushing for stronger protection of the village’s fishing grounds after a major conflict, when an aquaculture project risked livelihoods by considerably reducing the fishing grounds. Since then, Marsempre has successfully worked with other stakeholders to create a national marine park in Pedra do Valado, which is also in the Algarve. It also continues to fight for the safeguard measures agreed with all local fishing associations, including extending the PAA for fishing vessels with low-impact fishing gear (traditional fleet) from six to eight nautical miles from the coast and to ban bottom trawling.

Restricting industrial fleets from coastal waters is not just an environmental measure; it is a vital lifeline for small-scale fishers, local food security and coastal economies.

For communities like Ferragudo, where small six-to-eight-meter boats using low-impact gear such as gillnets and octopus traps depend on access to nearby fishing grounds, extending this protected area would help safeguard the space and livelihoods of the local artisanal fleet.

Caution, protectionism of the status quo and the heavy influence of industrial lobbies frequently paralyze political action. But change is urgently needed.

Lessons for the EU

By embedding PAAs into member states’ maritime spatial plans, EU leaders can grant priority access to small-scale, low-impact fishers within territorial seas while strictly prohibiting destructive practices like industrial bottom trawling. Restricting industrial fleets from coastal waters is not just an environmental measure; it is a vital lifeline for small-scale fishers, local food security and coastal economies, including sustainable tourism and recreation. It is a chance to reframe coastal waters as a public good rather than a zone for competing industrial exploitation.

Momentum is already building: Ireland is set to protect its six-nautical-mile coastal zone, while fishing organisations in France, Cyprus and other EU states are advancing similar proposals. The Ocean Act can accelerate this progress and support Europe’s small-scale fisheries and coastal seas in recovering and thriving together.

World.title: Trolling Trump: Why Macron and Carney became ‘leaders of the resistance’
World.content:
According to former White House strategist and current MAGA influencer and podcaster Steve Bannon, there is. “They’re playing with fire,” he told POLITICO. “They’re totally dependent on us for trade.” He also added a dark warning about “the Alberta secession movement picking up momentum” — Bannon and other MAGA luminaries have been encouraging the oil-rich Canadian province to break away.

Bannon also cited the deal Trump recently struck with Denmark and Greenland as an example of U.S. power and Washington’s ability to get what it wants. “Our Greenland deal shows the reality of Canada’s inability to defend itself from being the next Ukraine — this time in the Arctic,” he said.

But Ivo Daalder, a former U.S. ambassador to NATO, draws a different lesson from the Greenland deal, which extends an earlier agreement dating from 1951 and does not give Trump control of the island, as he said he wanted. For Daalder, this deal shows that when allies stand their ground, the U.S. president backs down. “With that deal Trump literally got nothing,” he told POLITICO.

Donald Trump, Macron and Carney attend a working lunch during the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Evelyn Hockstein via Getty Images

“I think what’s happening is the allies are starting to understand how to play him,” said Daalder. “Now they’re ignoring his bluster, and do and say what they think is important for their own good. By doing so, they have as good a chance as any in getting what they want.”

It’s also not surprising that Macron was quicker to taunt Trump than other Western leaders, said Daalder. “He’s French, after all.” Even during the first Trump presidency, Macron was willing to go mano a mano with the U.S. president, squeezing his counterpart’s hand in a handshake until their knuckles turned white and refusing to let go even when Trump tried to pull away.

But the French president’s tone seems sharper now, his actions even more pointed. Fort his, Daalder points to Macron’s maneuvering of Trump this June into inking an interim deal with Iran at Versailles — a palace infamous for a treaty that ended one world war but led to another. Macron, Trump’s critics trumpeted, had pulled off an epic diplomatic “troll.”

World.title: Trump made ‘a lot of mistakes,’ sighs Portugal’s far-right leader
World.content:
Ventura, whose party has surged in recent election cycles, is often described as a Portuguese Trump for his confrontational tactics and heated campaign rhetoric targeting Portugal’s ruling elite. The Chega leader traveled to Washington, D.C. for Trump’s inauguration and borrowed the MAGA slogan during last year’s parliamentary election campaign, saying he wanted to “make Portugal great again.”

But with Portugal now among many European countries hit by increasing fuel prices caused by war in the Middle East, Ventura appears to be turning on his American role model — like other populist chiefs across Europe who have jabbed the U.S. president’s “erratic” war goals or walked back support in the face of a snowballing cost-of-living crisis.

“I wish this war didn’t exist, especially for Portugal, Spain, France, Italy. We are paying more than the United States the price for this war,” he said during the interview. “It’s not very fair that one country starts the war and the others pay for the costs.”

Residents and antifascist activists protest outside the Patriots’ event venue. | Marion Solletty/POLITICO

The former sports commentator turned leading politician — whose early steps in politics were marred by controversies over comments widely criticized as racist — has elevated his party from barely registering in the polls to becoming the largest opposition group in the Portuguese parliament. He secured a third of the votes in February’s presidential election.

His recent electoral gains place Ventura among several far-right leaders and parties currently surging across the continent. Representatives from several of his European allies, including France’s National Rally, Spain’s Vox, Hungary’s Fidesz and Italy’s League, traveled to the Ericeira event where they shared views closely aligned with the MAGA-boosted narrative that Europe is suffering civilizational decline because of uncontrolled immigration and crippling regulation.

Ventura urged like-minded European politicians to unite, including by working with parties currently not part of the continental Patriots alliance, such as the Alternative for Germany. The AfD was kicked out of the ID Group, one of the precursors to the Patriots, in 2024 over downplaying Germany’s Nazi past. Its stellar performance in this month’s regional elections in eastern Germany has highlighted a schism in Europe between far-right parties eager to soften their image and those, like the AfD, who are doubling down on their radical positioning.

World.title: Kanye West’s controversial concerts in Russia have finally been cancelled
World.content:
Most artists have avoided performing in Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine. But Kanye ‘Ye’ West would never stoop to putting himself in that category.

 

The controversial American rapper, who has been barred from several European countries, was due to perform in St Petersburg on 10 and 11 October, thereby becoming the biggest western act to play in the country since 2022.

Following earlier reports that St Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena said it would not host the rapper, as no rental agreement has been signed, Ye’s two dates have now officially been cancelled.

According to the Moscow-based organizer Say Agency, who confirmed the cancellation, refunds for purchased tickets will be available.

The agency, which had previously disputed the venue’s statement regarding rental agreements, did not elaborate further on the reasons behind the cancellation. However, according to the Russian media, the decision was made by the authorities. The organisers had begun selling tickets before obtaining the necessary approval, and the cancellation was decided following “a call from Moscow”.

Russian authorities are reportedly investigating the organizers for alleged fraud – as reported by the Kommersant newspaper, citing an anonymous source.

St Petersburg outlet Fontanka had previously reported that the concerts had not received all the necessary approvals and were going to be called off following a “call from above” in Moscow.

The cancellation follows opposition to West's booking from some Russian politicians wishing to rid the country of any Western influence. These include conservative Russian lawmaker Vitaly Milonov, who released a video statement in which he suggested West should perform traditional Russian songs instead of his planned setlist.

“Maybe after that he’ll stop his disgusting antics and become a normal person,” he said.

Conversely, some Russian politicians had hailed the announcement of West’s visit as a victory against “anti-Russian hysteria” - despite the rapper’s antisemitic past and comments glorifying Nazi Germany.

West’s antisemitic remarks began in 2022, when he made a series of offensive comments on social media which ended up getting him booted off both X and Instagram. The musician was dropped by his talent agency and fashion brands like Adidas and Balenciaga also distanced themselves from West.

West went on to post a picture of KKK robes, rescind his previous apology to the Jewish community, declare himself “a Nazi” and assert that he has “dominion over his wife”.

In February 2025, West started selling swastika t-shirts, and in May, he released a song titled ‘Heil Hitler’, which praised the Nazi leader. This led him to be stripped of a visa to enter Australia and faced withimmediate arrest in Brazil.

West apologised for his actions and took out a full-page ad in the Wall Street Journal earlier this year. He addressed his past antisemitic comments, reflecting on a "four-month-long manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behaviour" and saying that he “lost touch with reality.”

Still, many questioned the timing of his apology, considering it coincided with the release of his new album ‘Bully’ and the start of his world tour.

World.title: Can Canada be the EU's answer to 'unreliable' trade partners?
World.content:
With tariffs, export controls and politics turning trade into a geopolitical lever, the EU seems to be shopping for partners it can count on. Canada, a like-minded economy already tied to the bloc by a free-trade agreement, is pitching itself as one.

 

Ahead of the EU-Canada summit at the end of October, the two sides are discussing a partnership beyond the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).

Prime Minister Mark Carney proposed exploring an integrated market for financial services, alongside cooperation on payments, strategic minerals, energy, AI, and defence production. Nothing has been agreed on financial passports, mutual recognition of licences, or bank access.

Fabian Zuleeg, Chief Executive and Chief Economist at the European Policy Centre, says the summit must deliver more than words. "So by the time we get to the summit, we should really be concrete," he says.

A trade order under strain

The EU's problem is dependence. It relies on the US for technology and security, on Chinese supply chains for critical inputs, and on outside suppliers for energy, at a time when trade access is increasingly used as leverage.

Canada offers economic gains, Zuleeg says, in areas like financial markets and technologies CETA does not fully cover. "The more important argument is political, and it's geopolitical."

The existing EU-Canada partnership is CETA, provisionally applied since 2017. It removed 98% of tariff lines immediately, rising to 99% by 2024. Trade in goods and services reached €130 billion in 2025, up 80% from €72.1 billion in 2016, according to Commission figures.

But that model has run its course. Erik van de Merel, chief economist at the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) and associate professor at the Université Libre de Bruxelles, notes that "tariffs among developed countries and between Canada and the European Union are fairly low."

The next gains lie elsewhere, "in the area of services, technology collaboration, all these sort of intangible activities that are important for future growth," he says. Negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement began in March 2026.

What each side wants

For the EU, the appeal is security of supply. Canada says it holds deposits of more than 34 critical minerals and is a leading producer of 10 considered essential to the energy transition. Europe needs them for batteries, grids and defence.

"We are very dependent, in particular on China, at the moment," Zuleeg says. Reducing that reliance, he argues, matters less for prices than for keeping European industry running during a dispute. Cheaper energy is possible too, he adds, but not overnight.

For Ottawa, the logic is diversification. The US takes roughly seven in ten Canadian exports, while the EU was Canada's second-largest goods-trade partner in 2024 with 7.9% of its global goods trade. Canada also wants easier access to European customers and investors for its clean-energy, mining, AI, and defence firms. Canadian pension funds could co-finance mineral-processing and infrastructure projects.

Defence is already a test case. In June 2026, Canada became the first non-European country included in the EU's €150 billion SAFE defence instrument, a possible template for sector-by-sector integration.

The rule-taker question

The hardest issue is regulation. Canada wants better access to European banking, insurance, and professional services such as law, accountancy, and architecture.

Van de Merel expects the EU to ask for something in return. "The new rules that we are going to develop, to some extent, you would have to take them over," he says. If Canada wanted to set its own banking and professional rules without European oversight or harmonisation, he argues, it would have to think again because deeper market integration is a core EU goal.

Alignment, he says, is the test of whether the project works. He adds that "one has to have regulatory alignment and I think that's going to be really key and a challenge whether this is going to be a success or not." It will not be quick. The EU's single market in services remains unfinished after decades, so a newcomer seeking the same benefits faces a long catch-up.

Zuleeg is less worried about Canada becoming a mere rule-taker. Iceland follows single-market rules because it sits in the European Economic Area, he notes, but Canada would not be joining the single market. In his view, it would keep a distinct voice, for example on foreign policy. He doubts the deal would require treaty change and considers "associate membership" a misnomer. A tailored association agreement under Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU looks the more likely legal route.

Practical steps are already under way. In March 2026, a joint EU-Canada committee agreed to pursue regulatory alignment on motor vehicles and conformity assessment and to widen mutual recognition in pharmaceuticals.

The politics could still bite. In Ottawa, the question is how much EU regulation Canada can accept without a vote in EU institutions. In Brussels, candidate countries undergoing lengthy reforms may ask why Canada should get privileged access. Van de Merel is also watching the UK, which could object if Canada obtains terms it never had after Brexit.

Limits and risks

The idea should not be oversold. Canada cannot replace China's role in manufacturing and mineral processing or the scale of the US economy. Mines, refineries, and ports take years to build, and the Atlantic is a logistical hurdle. Canada's exposure to Washington means a US–Canada crisis could spill into its production and investment.

Then there is CETA itself. As of mid-September 2026, ten member states, including France, Italy, Poland, Belgium and Ireland, had still not ratified it, so its investment-protection provisions are not in force. The EU is discussing an unprecedented new tier while its flagship trade deal with Canada remains only partly ratified.

Van de Merel warns that without institutions behind it, the initiative could fizzle. "Otherwise it's just an idea that is very symbolic and without any sort of political institutional consequences," he says.

World.title: Rutte responds to Moscow's nuclear threats, and the UK leader weighs re-joining the EU
World.content:
Nuclear tensions: In an interview with Euronews, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has told Russia to stop issuing nuclear threats, after Moscow sent a letter to the alliance saying it is prepared to deploy its nuclear arsenal if its territory – including the enclave of Kaliningrad – comes under attack.

 

‘Stop’: "We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threats. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful," Rutte exclusively told the Euronews Defence and Space Summit on Wednesday, at a moment of heightened tension between Russia and the West.

Rutte, however, dismissed the immediate threat to the alliance’s members, saying "we will defend every inch of NATO territory”.

“That threat is not there, and if anything happens, we are ready to counter it,” he explained.

Reuters first reported that Russia had warned NATO in a document that it could resort to nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to annex the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, while also threatening strikes on “decision-making centres” in NATO member states from the outset of a conflict.

‘Worst-case scenario’: Earlier on Wednesday, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev – also speaking at Euronews’ summit – called for European dialogue with Russia to avert a nuclear attack. While rejecting the Kremlin’s escalatory rhetoric, Radev reminded his European counterparts of the “nuclear card”, noting Russia would be prone to play it if weakened or cornered.

"We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation,” Radev said.

Making Putin feel that ‘war is coming’: The European Commissioner for Defence, Andrius Kubilius, rejectedRadev’s call for diplomatic engagement, warning it could embolden President Putin and undermine Ukraine.

"Russians are standing with their position very clear: Ukraine needs to surrender - that is their diplomacy position," Kubilius told Euronews, adding that Putin needs to “feel that war is coming to Russia itself”.

‘Made in Europe’ under fire: A push from Brussels to prioritise domestic European companies in defence contracts was also front and centre of the debate on Wednesday. NATO chief Rutte described the debate as a “luxury”, warning that the initiative ignores a basic problem: Europe's defence industry cannot produce enough.

Earlier on Wednesday, the US Ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, slammed the EU’s “Buy European” weapons push as “self-interest”, saying it could disrupt the transatlantic defence industrial base and benefit Europe’s "enemies".

"One attack by a powerful adversary on a member state, and we’ll all be glad that we focused on weapon superiority rather than regional economics," Puzder told the summit audience.

My colleagues and I have more takeaways from the summit for you inthis debrief.

Migration talks: Home Affairs Ministers are meeting in Luxembourg with migration top of the agenda. Ministers are expected to discuss proposed measures to tackle irregular arrivals under the European Emergency Response Framework, expected to be unveiled by the Commission next month.

EU sources tell my colleague Vincenzo Genovese that the proposal is expected to include a temporary suspension of asylum rights.

Italy extends border controls: The meeting comes as tensions between Italy and Spain escalate again, after Rome extended aerial and maritime border checks with Spain by another 15 days in response to the situation in the enclave of Ceuta, where 80,000 migrants entered in an unprecedented mass entry in July.

Meanwhile, a delegation of MEPs visited the Spanish exclave on Wednesday, denouncing the attacks and smear campaigns directed against activists and organisations working on the ground by far-right groups.

French and Spanish leaders welcome Andy Burnham’s suggestion UK could go ‘all the way’ and rejoin the EU

French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez have welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could look to rejoin the EU, with Macron saying “welcome back” when asked about the prospect during a press conference in Madrid.

“If the British want to come back and if the Prime Minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans,” Macron said, speaking alongside Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who also said the UK would be welcome back in the bloc.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday floated going “all the way” and rejoining the EU, as he vowed to scope out options for future EU-UK ties.

“We could stay as we are. We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said about the (EU) single market, or we could go all the way," Burnham said.

The UK leader also said that the EU-UK summit postponed in July amid Starmer’s resignation would be held in November.

Burnham has so far been perceived as much less focused on international and EU affairs than his predecessor Keir Starmer, leaving EU officials second-guessing his intentions for resetting relations with the bloc. But his statements now offer the clearest indication yet that his government is prepared to consider a much more ambitious overhaul of post-Brexit ties with Brussels. More.

World.title: Before the Iran war vs now: How much of a worker’s wage is needed to fill a 50-litre tank?
World.content:
The cost of filling a 50-litre diesel tank now takes 15.4% of Bulgaria’s gross monthly minimum wage, up from 9.9% before the Iran war began, highlighting the growing pressure on workers in Europe’s lowest-paid countries.

 

Fuel prices have risen significantly since the Israeli-US joint attack on Iran resulted in effectively blocking the Strait of Hormuz, an essential route for one-fifth of global oil to pass through.

In the EU, average consumer diesel prices rose by 40% between 23 February, before tensions in the Middle East escalated, and 21 September, according to the EU Weekly Oil Bulletin.

Rising fuel prices affect many people both directly and indirectly, particularly low-paid workers and those earning the minimum wage.

Asked why lower-income households are particularly affected, Torsten Müller, senior researcher at the European Trade Union Institute, told Euronews Business: “Because they spend a larger proportion of their income on essentials such as housing, food and transport than high-income households.”

So, how much of the monthly minimum wage is needed to fill a 50-litre tank across Europe? And how much has that share increased since the war began?

On 23 February 2026, the average price per litre in the EU was €1.637 for Euro 95 petrol and €1.594 for diesel. By 21 September, these had risen to €2.092 and €2.226 respectively. This represents increases of 27.8% for petrol and 39.6% for diesel.

The table above shows all the details, including minimum wages and fuel prices across 22 EU countries and Turkey, an EU candidate country, for these two periods.

The comparison uses gross monthly minimum wages, before tax and social security deductions.

Minimum wages remained unchanged in most countries over this period, while Estonia recorded the largest increase in the eurozone at 6.8%, between the first and second halves of 2026.

In some countries, the rise in petrol prices exceeded 30%, while diesel prices rose by 50%. Malta was the only country in the comparison where fuel prices remained unchanged.

As of 21 September, the percentage of the monthly minimum wage needed to fill a 50-litre petrol tank ranged from 3.3% in Luxembourg to 13.4% in Bulgaria.

It was also above 10% in Latvia (12.8%), Turkey (11.5%), Romania (11.5%), Greece (10.2%), Czechia (10.2%), Estonia (10.1%) and Slovakia (10.1%). The percentage was below 5% in Ireland (4.1%) and Belgium (4.4%).

Among the major economies, Germany had the lowest figure, as minimum wage earners needed to spend 5% of their monthly minimum wage to fill a 50-litre petrol tank.

Torsten Müller noted that the large differences between countries in these shares can largely be explained by the wide differences in minimum wages.

“One litre of diesel is only marginally cheaper in Bulgaria while the minimum wage is less than a fourth of the one in Luxembourg,” he said.

He underlined that the large differences are still reflected in the value of minimum wages in purchasing power standards (PPS), which take differences in price levels into account. In Luxembourg, the minimum wage in PPS is still twice as high as in Bulgaria.

Workers in countries with lower minimum wages face a heavier burden, as they now need to allocate a larger share of their salaries to fuel than before the conflict. In Bulgaria, for example, the share rose by 3.6 percentage points for petrol, followed by Turkey (3.1) and Latvia (3).

Filling a tank takes more than 10% of the monthly minimum wage

A 50-litre diesel tank takes a bigger share of the monthly minimum wage where diesel costs more per litre than petrol. The share of the monthly minimum wage needed to fill a 50-litre diesel tank ranged from 3.8% in Luxembourg to 15.4% in Bulgaria.

“When the average cost of rent is already more than a third of the minimum wage, spending another 15% of your entire wage on fuel is just not possible,” Esther Lynch, general secretary of the European Trade Union Confederation, told Euronews Business.

She warned that people would be forced to give up their jobs, particularly in areas where there are no reliable public transport links. She said this would be bad for both workers and companies already facing labour shortages.

The country rankings are broadly similar for diesel. Minimum wage earners needed to allocate more than 10% of their monthly minimum wage to fill a 50-litre tank in several countries. The share was 13.9% in Latvia, 13.8% in Turkey, 12.7% in Romania, 11.2% in Czechia and Estonia, 10.8% in Hungary, 10.4% in Greece and 10.3% in Portugal.

Workers in Ireland (4.3%), Germany (5.2%), Belgium (5.3%) and the Netherlands (5.5%) needed to spend among the lowest shares of the minimum wage to afford a tank.

Where does the minimum wage buy more fuel?

The two charts above for petrol and diesel also show how much fuel a monthly minimum wage can buy in each country. A smaller share needed to fill a 50-litre tank means the minimum wage buys more fuel, while a larger share means it buys less.

For example, as of 21 September, a minimum wage earner could buy 324 litres of diesel in Bulgaria, compared with 1,311 litres in Luxembourg.

Fuel costs hit Central and Eastern European countries hardest

Compared with February, the shares needed for a diesel tank rose sharply in Bulgaria (5.5 percentage points) and Turkey (5.3 percentage points). Workers in Latvia, Czechia and Estonia were also hit hard by fuel inflation, as the share of their minimum wage needed for a tank rose by more than 3 percentage points.

Pointing to the gap in minimum wages between Western European countries and Central and Eastern European (CEE) countries, Müller said it is mainly in CEE countries that minimum wage earners have to spend the largest share of their salaries on petrol.
