World.title: EU court rejects Poland’s request to suspend implementation of Mercosur trade deal
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Court of Justice of the European Union has rejected a request from Poland to suspend the implementation of the EU’s recently launched free trade agreement with the Mercosur bloc of South American countries. The CJEU found that the Polish government had failed to prove its claims that the trade deal would cause serious harm to European farmers, consumers or the environment. #ECJ: Order in Case C-460/26 R Poland v Council: should the implementation of the Council’s decision authorising the provisional application of the EU-Mercosur interim trade agreement be suspended pending the Court’s ruling?#CJEU #Mercosur pic.twitter.com/ocb4I4PsE8 — EU Court of Justice (@EUCourtPress) September 29, 2026 Poland has long been critical of the agreement, in particular over the potential negative impact that imports of agricultural products from Mercosur, which includes Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, could have on Polish farmers, who have repeatedly protested against the deal. In January, Poland failed in a bid to block the agreement at the European Council, where 21 of the EU’s 27 member states voted in favour of the deal. Although the agreement has not yet received final ratification – still requiring approval from the European Parliament and national parliaments – it nevertheless went into provisional force on 1 May. Shortly afterwards, Poland submitted a complaint to the CJEU, calling for implementation of the agreement to be suspended. It argued, first of all, that the process through which the deal had been provisionally implemented violated the EU’s treaties. Second, it claimed that liberalising trade in agricultural products without imposing the same production standards in both the EU and Mercosur created a risk of harm to human and animal health, the environment, the income of farmers, and the functioning of the market in the EU. Poland has filed a complaint to the European Court of Justice against the EU's free-trade deal with the South American Mercosur bloc that recently went into provisional force. It wants the agreement to be suspended until the court issues a ruling https://t.co/wE7DIbDazU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 However, on Tuesday, the CJEU announced that it had dismissed the application to suspend the agreement, finding that “Poland has not provided any concrete evidence to establish the likelihood and imminence of serious and irreparable damage”. The court pointed out that agricultural products from Mercosur could already be imported to the EU before the free-trade deal, and that they were and continue to be subject to food safety and health regulations similar to those for products manufactured in the EU. It also noted that the new trade deal includes tools allowing the EU to bar products that do not meet standards, including emergency measures in the case of a serious threat to human, animal or plant life. Finally, the CJEU said that Poland’s “general and abstract claims” regarding potential harm to farmers and markets did not include “any evidence capable of establishing, with a sufficient degree of probability, that the implementation [of the agreement]…will cause disruption”. In response to the court’s decision, the Polish government’s spokesman, Adam Szłapka, immediately blamed the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) administration, which was in power in Poland from 2015 to 2023. Szłapka said that the details of the Mercosur deal had been agreed during that period and that PiS had “failed to secure Polish interests in any way”. He argued that it was the current government which secured the addition of last-minute safeguards intended to protect farmers. The spokesman also noted that Polish agricultural exports to the Mercosur bloc have actually increased under the new agreement while imports from there have fallen, showing that “Polish farmers are profiting from this”. Rząd i Premier Tusk najpierw mówili, że umowa UE-Mercosur będzie „bezpieczna dla polskich rolników”. Potem nie potrafili zbudować koalicji blokującej w Radzie Europejskiej – choć polityka europejska jest domeną rządu. Politycy KO, PSL i Lewicy nie potrafili nikogo przekonać.… https://t.co/EqOJr4sneP — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) September 29, 2026 However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the foreign policy office of President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the CJEU’s decision showed the impotence of the current pro-EU government. “The government and Prime Minister Tusk first said that the EU-Mercosur agreement would be ‘safe for Polish farmers’. Then they failed to build a blocking coalition in the European Council,” wrote Przydacz. “In the end, under pressure from public opinion in Poland, they filed a complaint with the ECJ. [It was] so weak that they lost the request for interim relief,” he added. “Ineffective policy and ineffective government.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland recovers looted painting that once hung in SS officers’ club in occupied Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish painting looted by Nazi Germany during World War Two, and which once hung in an SS officers’ club, has been returned by its owner, who donated it to the National Museum in Warsaw. “History is coming home,” said culture minister Marta Cienkowska, celebrating the return of Alfred Wierusz-Kowalski’s Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow, which she described as “one of the most significant wartime losses in Polish painting”. Her ministry is responsible for seeking the return of tens of thousands of artworks and other cultural items that were looted during the war and remain missing. Kolejny sukces restytucyjny! Odzyskaliśmy jedną z cenniejszych i najbardziej znanych strat wojennych malarstwa polskiego. Obraz „Zima – Odwrót Napoleona spod Moskwy” Alfreda Wierusza-Kowalskiego trafił dziś do zbiorów Muzeum Narodowego w Warszawie. To efekt naszej współpracy z… pic.twitter.com/Y0wDIBgIGG — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) September 28, 2026 Wierusz-Kowalski, who was active in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, was a renowned realist painter whose work often featured animals alongside people. His Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow had, by the 1930s, become part of the collection of Andrzej Rotwand, a wealthy banker and industrialist. In June 1939, it was featured in an exhibition organised by the Society for the Encouragement of Fine Arts in Warsaw, which occupied the building that is now the famous Zachęta National Gallery of Art. However, the exhibition was brought to an abrupt end when Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. The works on display, along with other items from the gallery, were seized by the occupiers, with many used to decorate the offices and apartments of German officials. Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow was displayed in a club for high-ranking SS and police officers located in Warsaw’s Blanka Palace. The same building also housed Warsaw’s German-installed commissioner, Helmut Otto, and mayor, Ludwig Leist. No information has been released as to the fate of the painting in the immediate aftermath of the war. However, it eventually came into the possession of Ewa Tsonis, who has now handed it back. Speaking at a ceremony in the National Museum in Warsaw, Tsonis said that her late father, Michał Stefan Koryzna, had purchased the painting in the 1960s from Desa, a major gallery and auction house, in the city of Kraków. “I grew up with this painting. It was greatly appreciated and loved in our family,” she said. However, after recently conducting research into the painting’s history, she became aware of its provenance and notified the culture ministry. Experts from the National Museum in Warsaw confirmed the identity of the painting, which remains in good condition and in its original frame. Tsonis then donated the work to the museum. “Restitution is not possible without the cooperation of many people and institutions – both on the side of the state and on the part of the owners of the works,” said Cienkowska, who thanked Tsonis for her “incredibly responsible and civic-minded attitude”. “Such attitudes are still rare but, because we constantly talk about restitution – we search for lost works and strive to recover them – we are increasingly approached by people who own lost objects and feel a sense of responsibility for cultural heritage.” Cienkowska noted that the culture ministry has so far secured the return of over 920 works, with around 200 more restitution cases currently underway in 18 countries. Germany has agreed to return to Poland a collection of 73 medieval documents that were looted during WWII. The culture minister has hailed it as "the most important and valuable return of stolen cultural heritage in modern Polish history" https://t.co/GxHQ8A0jyr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 1, 2025 However, that is still just a small fraction of the over 60,000 missing items listed in the ministry’s database of missing works, which includes seven further paintings by Wierusz-Kowalski. Two other works from Rotwand’s collection – Italian Woman by Anna Bilińska and Mother with Children by Kazimierz Alchimowicz – were also hung in the SS officers’ club during the war and today remain missing. Poland has in recent years stepped up efforts to secure the return of historical and cultural items looted during the German and Soviet occupations. In 2022, it appealed to UNESCO for help in securing the return of cultural items that remain missing after being looted by Nazi Germany. It also launched a campaign seeking the return of thousands of items that ended up in Russia after the war. World.title: Poland changes rules of engagement for firing on foreign aircraft amid growing Russia threat
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the “growing threat from Russia”. Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead. The move follows a series of violations of Polish airspace over the last year by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter, as well as Russia’s increasing use of jet-powered drones to attack targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border. Polska zmienia procedury użycia uzbrojenia dla lotnictwa w przypadku zwalczania obcych statków powietrznych. To wnioski Dowódcy Operacyjnego generała Ireneusza Nowaka z ostatnich tygodni. To także odpowiedź na rosnące zagrożenie ze strony Rosji, doświadczenia wojny w Ukrainie… — Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) September 28, 2026 “In the coming days, the defence minister will change the procedures for firing by Polish planes and helicopters at objects flying to us from the direction of Russia,” announced deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk on Monday, quoted by news service Defence24. The change, as Tomczyk explained in a statement later issued on social media, will shift requirements away from requiring visual identification of foreign aerial objects and towards so-called “positive identification”. The latter involves identifying an object based on a combination of several other, non-visual sources of information, such as using radar and other sensors to determine its speed, altitude, trajectory and flight parameters, as well as a lack of IFF (identification friend or foe) from an object. Tomczyk said that the change was being made based on the “conclusions from recent weeks” made by the operational commander of Poland’s armed forces, General Ireneusz Nowak. It is a “response to the growing threat from Russia, experiences from the war in Ukraine, and the emergence of new air attack means – primarily fast jet drones and cruise missiles in the case of which the time for reaction is very brief”, added Tomczyk. The minister said that positive identification would only be issued when there is a “sufficiently high degree of certainty in determining what we are dealing with”. He noted that accurate target identification is particularly crucial in peacetime, when there are civilian aircraft in Polish airspace. The change will mean “not less identification, but a different way of conducting it: faster and based on data from multiple sources”. Poland's government has issued public guidance on how to act in the case of airborne attacks, amid growing concerns over the threat from Russia. It is also preparing evacuation plans and clearer markings for 85,000 shelters across the countryhttps://t.co/vMEMU6mlRx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026 Defence24 reports that the government, military and many experts have found current rules of engagement to be overly restrictive and not suited to meeting the scale and type of threat facing Poland today. It points to last week’s violation of Polish airspace by a Russian helicopter, which crossed the border from Kaliningrad and spent around 42 seconds in Poland before returning. The website also notes that Russia’s growing use of jet-powered drones, which are able to travel much faster than traditional unmanned aerial vehicles, is a further threat. Such drones have recently been used to attack targets along the Ukrainian side of the border with Poland, including a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw. World.title: Halloween Trick-or-Treat for Charity to Return to Prague on October 22
World.content:
A Halloween charity event will bring children and families to several Prague neighbourhoods on October 22, combining trick-or-treating with fundraising for SOS Children’s Villages.

The Halloween Trick-or-Treat for Charity will take place from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. across Vinohrady, Vršovice, Žižkov, Prague 15, Holešovice and Barrandov.



The concept is simple. Children dressed in Halloween costumes and accompanied by their parents will visit participating host locations, which can include cafés, restaurants, shops, confectioneries, schools, children’s centres and other businesses or organisations.

The participating locations will remain a secret until children register for the event and receive a special map showing where they can go trick-or-treating.

At each location, children will make a contribution of at least CZK 10 to a sealed collection box supporting SOS Children’s Villages. In return, they will receive a sweet treat before continuing to the next location.

Last year’s event attracted more than 1,100 registered participants and raised CZK 296,157 despite rainy weather.

The entire amount was donated to SOS Children’s Villages, which has supported children, families, young people and foster carers in the Czech Republic for more than 50 years.

How to take part

Families who want to participate can register in advance and then use the secret map to find the participating locations on October 22.

Children are encouraged to come in costume and bring enough coins to make contributions at the individual stops.

Businesses and organisations can also join the event as hosts. Each host is asked to prepare sweets, add some Halloween decorations and wear at least part of a costume or Halloween accessory.

Hosts must be available for at least two hours between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m.

The organisers will provide the collection boxes, while hosts provide the sweets for visiting children.

World.title: Prague Study Reveals How Much Waste Tourists Leave in the City Center
World.content:
Specialists from Prague City Hall and the Institute of Circular Economy (INCIEN) have analyzed the contents of public waste bins in central Prague, finding that about one ton of rubbish is discarded on Wenceslas Square every day.

The latest analysis was carried out to examine how the composition of waste changes with the seasons and fluctuations in tourist traffic.

A similar measurement was conducted during the winter, providing a basis for comparison.



Beverage packaging made up roughly one-third of the waste collected from bins on Wenceslas Square. Cans and plastic bottles were among the most common items.

Another third consisted of disposable food-service items, particularly cups. The remaining third was made up of general household waste.

Researchers also found waste originating from businesses in the surrounding area, including cafes and shops. Some household rubbish appeared to have been left by tourists staying in apartments rented through short-term accommodation platforms.

Food waste was another recurring part of the findings. Partially eaten food was frequently found in the bins, with trdelník pastries among the more common examples.

The summer analysis gives Prague authorities a clearer picture of the waste generated in one of the city’s busiest public spaces during the peak tourist season and allows them to compare the results with the winter survey.

World.title: Prague Hospitals Warn of Critical Blood Shortages
World.content:
Several hospitals in Prague are reporting critically low blood supplies, prompting the Czech Ministry of Health to urge people to donate blood in the coming days.

The shortage is affecting more than individual blood groups. Hospitals and transfusion centers in several parts of the Czech Republic are reporting a broader decline in available supplies, with some facilities nearing the minimum levels needed to maintain safe operations.



The situation differs from one region to another. Some transfusion centers still have adequate reserves, while others are short of particular blood groups or are approaching critical levels.

The shortage also extends to individual blood components. In Prague, the Institute for Clinical and Experimental Medicine (IKEM) is currently seeking more platelet donors regardless of blood type.

People planning to donate are advised to check the latest information on the website or social media channels of their chosen transfusion center before visiting.

Why hospitals need more donors

Hospitals depend on regular blood donations not only during emergencies but also for planned medical treatment.

Blood is routinely needed for surgery, childbirth and the treatment of patients who require repeated transfusions. This includes some cancer patients whose treatment can interfere with the body’s production of blood cells.

Blood donations are also essential in cases of severe complications during childbirth. Heavy blood loss can become life-threatening within a short period, and an adequate supply of donated blood can be critical to saving the lives of mothers and newborns.

The demand for blood can increase during the summer and holiday period, when hospitals continue to perform scheduled procedures while also dealing with more injuries and traffic accidents. At the same time, the number of people coming to donate tends to fall as residents leave the country or travel elsewhere.

Number of donors continues to decline

Official figures indicate that the Czech donor base has been shrinking. Around 348,000 people donated blood last year, down from 362,000 the previous year.

Transfusion centers are also losing older regular donors as they reach the age limit, while the number of younger people replacing them has not been sufficient.

In the Czech Republic, adults can generally donate blood until the age of 65, provided they weigh more than 50 kilograms. Additional eligibility restrictions may apply, including for people who have recently travelled to countries where certain infectious diseases are present.

Donating blood in the Czech Republic is voluntary and free of charge. Donors are entitled to time off work on the day of their donation, while some health insurance companies provide additional benefits or rewards for regular donors.

World.title: Bangkok Gears Up for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
World.content:
All eyes are on Thailand as the country prepares to host the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) Annual Meetings, also known as the 2026 Annual Meetings or AM2026 Thailand.

Running from 12-18 October 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, the event will mark Thailand’s second time hosting the meetings, following its first in 1991. This will make Thailand one of only three nations to have hosted the IMF–WBG Annual Meetings twice.



The IMF–WBG Annual Meetings, held for two consecutive years in Washington D.C. and every third year in one of the 191 member countries, serve as a gathering of top economic figures from around the world. By covering a broad range of issues, the meetings aim to strengthen global financial stability, combat poverty, and ensure inclusive economic growth and job creation.

Thailand’s selection to host again in 2026 highlights how the country has advanced over the past three decades in terms of its institutional progress, economic resilience, and sustained engagement with international partners. As host, Thailand brings decades’ worth of experience in economic transformation and regional leadership to the table.

The “Olympics of Finance”

Often dubbed the “Olympics of Finance,” the meetings are set to attract more than 15,000 participants, including finance ministers, central bankers, economists, business leaders, civil society representatives, and journalists from the IMF and World Bank’s 191 member countries, including the Czech Republic.

The Annual Meetings will be held under the theme of “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”. Therefore, the meetings will focus on enhancing people’s potential and creating opportunities, with the goal of fostering a financial and economic system that is safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Under the theme, the government plans to showcase four policy priorities it believes are increasingly relevant in an era marked by geopolitical fragmentation, economic volatility, and demographic change. These are indeed the issues that warrant serious conversation and sincere collaboration among the global community and all stakeholders to address them in the most efficient way:

Digital Transformation : The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems.

The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems. Connected Economy : A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored.

A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored. Climate Finance : The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change.

The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change. Longevity Economy: The final priority seeks to turn the challenges of ageing populations into new sources of economic growth.

Alongside these focus areas, the Bank of Thailand plans to unveil the “Bangkok Blueprint,” an international framework developed jointly with the IMF and the World Bank aimed at combating digital financial fraud and strengthening trust in the digital economy.

Readiness in All Aspects

According to the Fiscal Policy Office, Thailand’s overall readiness has been assessed at “Grade A” following months of coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Thailand, and the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings Secretariat.

Preparations extend beyond the conference venue. Authorities have developed contingency plans for traffic management, emergency responses, and arrangements for high-level foreign officials. A working group has also been established to address cybersecurity matters.

Beyond Tourism: A Regional Economic Capital

Beyond its long-established reputation as a world-renowned tourist destination, the 2026 Annual Meetings offer Thailand an excellent opportunity to present another dimension of the Kingdom to the international community.

AM2026 reinforces Thailand’s standing as a trusted international partner while highlighting its growing role as a regional economic capital and a hub for finance, investment, policy innovation, and multilateral dialogue in Southeast Asia. Having said that, countries and companies vying for economic and business opportunities cannot overlook Thailand and its potential to become an important impetus for their long-term prosperity and growth.

(Source material and reporting courtesy of Thailand NOW)

World.title: British Pop Star Robbie Williams to Headline Colours of Ostrava 2027
World.content:
British pop star Robbie Williams will headline the opening day of Colours of Ostrava 2027, organisers have announced.

Williams will perform on Wednesday, July 21, at the Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex, marking his return to the Czech Republic after his recent concert at Prague’s O2 Arena.



The 2027 edition of Colours of Ostrava will run from July 21 to July 24. Williams is the first major act confirmed for the festival’s lineup.

“For me, Robbie Williams is, above all, a personality. He is someone you know, even if you aren’t necessarily a fan,” said Colours of Ostrava artistic director Filip Košťálek.

“Over more than three decades, he has managed to stay relevant, evolve and surprise audiences while remaining true to himself. And those are exactly the kind of personalities we want to bring to Colours.”

Košťálek said the festival is looking for artists with strong stories and songs who can create memorable moments for audiences.

Williams fits that profile after more than three decades at the centre of British pop. Since launching his solo career in the 1990s, following his departure from Take That, he has become one of the UK’s most successful solo artists.

His latest studio album, Britpop, was released in early 2025 after a delay. Williams had originally planned to release the record earlier but moved the date following the announcement of a new album by Taylor Swift.

The delay was also connected to Williams’ ambition to return to No. 1 on the UK album chart. The strategy paid off, with Britpop reaching the top of the chart and extending his record-setting run of No. 1 albums in the UK.

Williams has remained a major live attraction as well. His most recent Czech concert took place at Prague’s O2 Arena, where he combined songs from across his career with the humour and interaction that have become a defining part of his performances.

More artists for Colours of Ostrava 2027 are expected to be announced in the coming months.

World.title: Techno, Art and Live Performance Come Together at Strahov on October 10
World.content:
On October 10, the Prague electronic music collective EDEN will bring Rotten To The Core to Stadion Strahov for one of the collective’s largest and most ambitious events to date.

Running from 10pm until 7am, the night will bring together international and local DJs, dancers and visual artists for an event built around music, performance and visual art.



The lineup includes VLACE, SCHELLT, RiVid, 2NDRA and Mila (5), with the programme focused on techno and acid.

Among the artists, 2NDRA is a Prague-based schranz and techno producer and performer and one of the founders of EDEN Collective. RiVid, meanwhile, is a Czech-Japanese hard techno duo.

The event takes a broader approach to the club experience, combining the music programme with visual elements, art installations and live performances.

That approach comes at a time when electronic music events are becoming increasingly commercialised, while promoters and venues face rising production costs and growing regulatory pressures.

The event will take place beneath Strahov Stadium in Prague 6, continuing EDEN’s connection with unconventional venues and large-scale rave productions.

The collective previously hosted its 40-hour ALT BABYLON weekender in Prague in August, featuring dozens of local and international artists.

The event is for ages 18 and over, with tickets starting at CZK 300.

World.title: Václav Havel Would Be 90 This Year: From Playwright to President
World.content:
Václav Havel was one of the defining figures of modern Czech history.

Playwright, writer, dissident, political prisoner and, ultimately, the last president of Czechoslovakia and the first president of the Czech Republic, his life reflected some of the country’s most dramatic changes of the 20th century.

Born into a prominent Prague family, Havel experienced both privilege and political persecution. He became one of the leading voices of the opposition to communist rule and played a central role in the Velvet Revolution of 1989.



On October 5th, 2026, Havel would have turned 90. Here is a look at his life, political career and some of the places in Prague and beyond connected to him.

From a privileged Prague family to a banned writer

Havel was born in Prague on October 5, 1936, into a wealthy and well-connected family. His uncle, Miloš Havel, founded Barrandov Studios, while his grandfather was involved in construction and real estate.

His family’s position changed dramatically after the Communist Party took power in Czechoslovakia in 1948. Their property was confiscated, and Havel faced restrictions on his education and career because of his family background.

During the political liberalisation of the 1960s, Havel became increasingly involved in Prague’s theatre scene. He worked as a stagehand and later as a dramaturge, while also establishing himself as a playwright. His plays often explored power, bureaucracy and the absurdity of life under an authoritarian system.

The hopes of 1968

The Prague Spring of 1968 brought a period of political and cultural liberalisation to Czechoslovakia. Censorship was abolished, previously banned books began appearing in print and films that had been restricted were shown in cinemas again.

Havel embraced the new atmosphere and became increasingly active in public life. But the reforms ended abruptly when Warsaw Pact troops invaded Czechoslovakia on August 21, 1968.

Havel opposed the occupation and the return to political repression. He was subsequently banned from publishing and working in the theatre. For a period, he worked as a manual labourer at a brewery in Trutnov.

He later became one of the most prominent figures of the Czechoslovak dissident movement. He was a signatory of Charter 77, a civic initiative calling on the communist government to respect human rights, and was repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.

From dissident to president

The communist regime collapsed in November 1989 following mass demonstrations across Czechoslovakia. Havel was one of the leading figures of the Civic Forum, the opposition movement that helped negotiate the peaceful transfer of power.

On December 29, 1989, he was elected president of Czechoslovakia.

Havel remained in office after the country split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993, becoming the first president of the newly independent Czech Republic. During his political career, he supported the country’s integration into Western institutions, including NATO, and advocated closer ties with the European Union.

His presidency also left a visible mark on Prague Castle. Parts of the complex were opened to the public, while the South Gardens were restored following their pre-war design.

Life after Prague Castle

Havel left the presidency in 2003 but remained active as a writer and public figure. He continued to comment on political and social issues and maintained friendships with artists, intellectuals and international figures.

Among them was the Dalai Lama, who visited Havel in Prague on several occasions. Havel died on December 18, 2011, at his country house in Hrádeček, near the Krkonoše mountains.

Places connected to Václav Havel in Prague

Several Prague locations are closely connected to Havel and his family.

One is Lucerna Palace on Wenceslas Square, built by Havel’s grandfather. The complex includes the historic Lucerna Cinema, which has been operating for more than a century, as well as the famous Lucerna Café.

Prague Castle is another essential stop. Havel lived and worked there during his years as president and initiated several changes that made parts of the complex more accessible to the public.

Outside Prague, Havel was also closely associated with Lány Chateau, the traditional summer residence of Czech presidents. During his time there, he was known to visit the local pub and meet residents without the formality normally associated with a head of state.

World.title: Prague’s Kramář Villa to Open for Free Visits on October 3
World.content:
Prague’s Kramář Villa will open to the public on October 3, giving visitors a chance to see inside one of the Czech government’s official residences.

Admission will be free.

The villa, located on Gogolova Street in Prague’s Letná district, is the official residence of the Czech prime minister. It was also the home of Karel Kramář, Czechoslovakia’s first prime minister, and his wife, Nadezhda.



Visitors during the open house will be able to take guided tours of the building and learn about its history, architecture and former residents. The tour will include parts of the villa that are normally closed to the public, including its living quarters and ceremonial rooms.

Built with a combination of Neo-Baroque and Art Nouveau influences, Kramář Villa has been one of Prague’s government residences since the early 20th century.

Its history is closely linked to Karel Kramář, who became the first prime minister of Czechoslovakia following the country’s establishment in 1918.

The open house will also include access to the villa’s garden. Located above the city, the grounds provide views across Prague and will remain open for longer than the villa itself.

The villa will welcome visitors from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on October 3. The garden will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

World.title: Hungary’s first smart supermarket opens: say goodbye to closing time
World.content:
Hungary’s smart retail revolution has reached supermarket scale, with Szeged opening what is being presented as the country’s first staffless supermarket. The new Coop Szeged store on Temesvári Boulevard operates as a conventional shop during staffed hours before switching to an automated mode, allowing registered customers to shop without cashiers or sales assistants.

A supermarket that stays open

The 470-square-metre store stocks more than 6,000 products, meaning customers can do a full grocery shop rather than simply pick up a handful of items from vending machines. Outside normal opening hours, customers registered with the 247 Shop app can enter using a QR code. They select their goods from the shelves and pay by bank card at a self-service checkout, writes 24.hu.

To leave, they scan a code displayed on their receipt or available in the app. A remote dispatcher is available if customers need assistance. The system combines traditional retail with technology rather than eliminating staffed shopping altogether. During regular opening hours, the store operates normally, while the automated system extends its availability into the evening and overnight.

AI keeps watch

Although no employees are physically present during the automated period, the supermarket is not left completely unattended. Its camera surveillance system is supported by artificial intelligence, which can detect and flag suspicious incidents. A remote dispatcher monitors the store and can intervene when necessary or assist customers.

Coop Szeged chief executive János Kelemen said the company’s first hybrid smart shop, which opened at Szeged’s Szent István Square in May 2025, had provided encouraging results. During its first year, the smaller 150-square-metre shop recorded more than 27,000 purchases during staffless periods. The average basket value was around 22% higher than during conventional opening hours, while 24-hour operation generated 23.61% additional revenue, according to the company.

In case you missed it: Can farming survive Hungary’s growing drought crisis? New documentary reveals the stakes

Could the model spread?

Coop Szeged studied similar hybrid shops in the Czech Republic before introducing the concept. Kelemen said the experience had shown that customers were willing to change their shopping habits, with some deliberately choosing staffless hours.

The model could also have applications beyond larger cities. Kelemen suggested that smaller settlements could benefit from shops operating with limited staffing, particularly where maintaining a conventional grocery store is difficult. Such a system could allow residents to shop locally rather than travelling 20 or 30 kilometres to the nearest supermarket.

Kelemen does not expect every Hungarian shop to become staffless within a few years. However, the company hopes the hybrid model will spread beyond Szeged and eventually become a more familiar feature of Hungarian retail.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar named among TIME100 Next 2026’s rising stars
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has been included in TIME’s TIME100 Next 2026 list, which highlights rising figures the magazine considers to be shaping the future.

Péter Magyar, who became Hungary’s prime minister after the Tisza Party’s April election victory, has been named among TIME’s TIME100 Next 2026, a list recognising what the magazine describes as the world’s most influential rising stars.

In its profile of the Hungarian prime minister, TIME highlights the political significance of Magyar’s victory over Viktor Orbán and the 16-year period of Fidesz government that preceded it.

TIME highlights Magyar’s election victory

TIME describes the April election result as a major political change in Hungary, noting that Magyar’s Tisza Party ended 16 uninterrupted years of Orbán’s rule.

The magazine says the result represented a strongly pro-European political shift at a time when Eurosceptic populism has gained ground in several parts of Europe.

TIME also points to Magyar’s political background. Before founding Tisza, he was associated with Orbán’s Fidesz party and served in several government-related positions. The magazine describes him as a conservative who remains sceptical of immigration and has referred to Hungary’s Austro-Hungarian heritage.

At the same time, TIME contrasts Magyar’s approach with that of the former prime minister, highlighting his promises to tackle corruption and rebuild state institutions.

Living, working or doing business in Hungary?

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

A different direction for Hungary

According to TIME, Magyar’s political programme has focused in part on strengthening institutions and the rule of law after years of controversy over Hungary’s democratic institutions and its relationship with the European Union.

The magazine characterises his election as an opportunity for Hungary to move beyond what it calls an “illiberal period” and argues that the result demonstrated the continuing influence of voters and institutions in shaping the country’s political direction.

Magyar’s inclusion places him among a group of emerging political, business, cultural, scientific and other figures selected by TIME for the 2026 edition of TIME100 Next. The recognition comes less than six months after his party’s election victory and as Magyar’s government continues its first year in office.

TIME’s full profile of Péter Magyar is part of its TIME100 Next 2026 special issue.

World.title: Legendary Orient Express passes through Hungary and enters Türkiye – Videos
World.content:
The historic Venice Simplon-Orient-Express entered Türkiye on its second trip to Istanbul this year after departing from Paris on 25 September.

The luxury train, operated by British-based Belmond, travelled through Germany, Austria, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria before entering Türkiye through Kapikule with more than 70 passengers.

Due to renovation work at Kapikule railway station, the train continued to Edirne station, where passengers and crew underwent passport procedures before continuing toward Istanbul.

Train official Francesco Bonotto said the journey included overnight stays in Budapest, Bucharest and Varna, adding that many passengers planned to spend several days in Türkiye.

The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is known for recreating the historic luxury rail experience associated with the famous Orient Express route, which also inspired Agatha Christie’s novel “Murder on the Orient Express.”

Here’s how the train passes through Békéscsaba, Hungary:

Passenger Janan Benabud said returning to Türkiye felt like coming home because of memories from the period when her father served as Morocco’s ambassador to Ankara. She said she planned to visit several landmarks in Istanbul.

Another passenger, Tansel Dogan, who lives in Germany, said the journey was a birthday gift from her husband and described travelling through seven countries and seeing four capitals aboard the historic train as a special experience.

After passport procedures in Edirne, the train continued toward Istanbul. It is scheduled to begin its return journey and arrive back in Paris on 2 October.

World.title: Vingardium in the City: When Hungary’s wine regions come to Budapest for one evening
World.content:
On 10 October, Bálna Budapest will once again be filled with wine, gastronomy and vibrant city life as Vingardium in the City returns for a special walk-around wine tasting experience.

What if you could explore Hungary’s diverse wine regions without leaving Budapest? On 10 October, the answer can be found at Bálna Budapest.

Vingardium in the City is a relaxed, walk-around wine tasting where guests can explore the stands at their own pace, taste a wide variety of Hungarian wines and meet the wineries and their representatives. The event is not only for experienced wine lovers – it is also an exciting opportunity for anyone who is curious about Hungarian wines or simply looking for a unique Saturday evening experience in Budapest.

Photo: Vingardium in the City

Discover Hungary’s wine regions in one evening

One of the greatest attractions of Vingardium in the City is its diversity. In one evening, visitors can discover wines from several Hungarian wine regions and compare different grape varieties, wine styles and terroirs side by side.

There is no fixed tasting order. Guests can decide which wineries to visit, which wines they would like to discover and where they would like to spend more time. The aim is to make wine accessible and enjoyable – not something reserved for experts, but an experience that everyone can share.

Photo: Vingardium in the City

More than just wine

The event is also an ideal choice for couples, groups of friends and international visitors who want to experience Hungarian wine culture in an easy and enjoyable way. Instead of travelling from winery to winery, guests can discover a wide range of Hungarian wines in one evening, right in the heart of Budapest.

World.title: Hungary’s controversial Chad mission cost nearly EUR 11 million, defence minister claims
World.content:
Hungarian Minister of Defence, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, shared a few details in a social media post regarding the Hungarian Defence Forces’ mission to Chad, which was approved by former prime minister Viktor Orbán, while raising questions about the role of his son, Gáspár Orbán.

Almost EUR 11 million to a military peace mission in the middle of Africa

Nearly HUF 4 billion (more than EUR 10.9 million) in public funds was spent preparing Hungary’s planned military mission to Chad, Ruszin-Szendi has claimed. He disclosed the figure after briefing the Hungarian Parliament’s Defence and Law Enforcement Committee in a closed session on Wednesday. He said classified information prevented him from publicly detailing how the money had been spent.

“When I explained what had happened and what the money had been spent on, the committee members looked utterly stunned.”

Minister raises questions over Gáspár Orbán’s role in the mission in Chad

In a Facebook post, Ruszin-Szendi said the committee had been informed about the preparation of the Chad mission and Gáspár Orbán’s involvement in the programme. “Nearly HUF 4 billion in public money was spent in connection with the mission,” the minister wrote, adding that he knew how the funds had been used but could not disclose the details because some of the information was classified on national security grounds.

Based on what he had heard during the closed briefing, Ruszin-Szendi said he believed Orbán’s family background had provided him with opportunities and state support without which the programme “would hardly have been realised in this form”. He also said:

“We can only thank our luck that this did not turn into a catastrophe.”

The minister did not provide publicly available evidence detailing what he meant by the statement or specify what potential danger he was referring to.

Parliament had approved the mission

Ruszin-Szendi also stressed that Parliament had formally approved the establishment of the mission and authorised the use of several billion forints in related expenditure. As a result, he said, the legal authorisation provided by Parliament meant that he currently had no legal basis for filing a criminal complaint over the circumstances he had learned about.

The planned Chad mission had previously attracted attention because of Gáspár Orbán’s involvement. Official documents obtained by Hungarian media outlet 444.hu reportedly indicated that his role went beyond that of a simple liaison, with his approval reportedly required for certain decisions. The former defence minister, Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky, had previously described Orbán as a “liaison” involved in the preparations.

If you missed it: Orbán-era ministers arrested as National Asset Recovery and Protection Office and prosecution order detention

Classified details remain undisclosed

The government has not publicly disclosed a complete breakdown of the nearly HUF 4 billion expenditure, and Ruszin-Szendi said some details could not be released because of their security classification. The Chad mission was intended to strengthen Hungary’s military and security presence in the African country, although the plans have subsequently become a subject of political and public scrutiny.

During Wednesday’s committee session, Ruszin-Szendi also briefed lawmakers on developments surrounding a separate hand-grenade accident at the Újdörögd military training area.

World.title: Budapest antifa attack case: Maja T. prison verdict becomes final
World.content:
Metropolitan Court has reduced the prison sentence of German national Maja T., who was convicted over a series of antifa attacks on people perceived to be far-right supporters in Budapest in February 2023.

Maja T.’s sentence was cut from eight years to seven years by the Metropolitan Court on Wednesday. The court also reduced the sentence of fellow defendant Gabriele M. from seven to six years, while upholding a two-year prison sentence for German national Anna Christina M. The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

Antifa attacks targeted people seen as far-right

The defendants were accused of taking part in antifa group attacks between 9 and 11 February 2023, targeting people they believed were far-right based primarily on their clothing. The victims were allegedly identified as people attending events associated with the so-called “Day of Honour” and the Breakout Memorial Tour, gatherings connected with commemorations of a 1945 attempt by Nazi and Hungarian forces to break out of encircled Budapest.

Five antifa attacks were recorded during the period, leaving nine people injured, six of them seriously, according to reports cited in the case. Prosecutors accused Maja T. of attempted aggravated bodily harm causing life-threatening injuries and attempted serious bodily harm committed with a base motive, both allegedly carried out as part of a criminal organisation.

Defence challenged first-instance ruling

The case reached the appeals stage after both prosecutors and defence lawyers challenged the original verdicts. Maja T.’s lawyer had disputed the classification of the group as a criminal organisation and argued that video footage did not show his client actively participating in some of the attacks. The defence also questioned aspects of the medical expert evidence.

Their lawyer had additionally raised concerns about Maja T.’s ability to defend themselves while they were on hunger strike during the proceedings. Judge Géza Szalai said defendants have a right to effective legal defence, but argued that the state cannot compel a defendant to exercise that right. He said Maja T. had effectively chosen to exercise their right to express their views through the hunger strike rather than their right to participate fully in their defence.

In case you missed it: Orbán-era ministers arrested as asset recovery office and prosecution order detention

Antifa supporters gather outside court

The verdict attracted significant attention, with supporters of Maja T. gathering outside the court before the hearing. Media and antifa supporters formed a queue to enter the courtroom, while a representative of the German embassy was also present. Maja T. entered the courtroom accompanied by officers before hearing their final sentence, writes Telex.

Another defendant, Italian national Ilaria Salis, is currently covered by a separate legal situation after being elected to the European Parliament in 2024. Proceedings against their have been suspended. The appeals court’s ruling in the present case is final.

World.title: EPPO chief Kövesi reveals what could be achieved in Hungary by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office
World.content:
European Chief Prosecutor Laura Codruța Kövesi says the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) could begin operating in Hungary as early as next year, potentially giving European prosecutors powers to investigate EU-fund fraud, corruption and money laundering in the country.

European Chief Prosecutor gives interview to the Hungarian press

Speaking to Telex during a visit to Budapest, Kövesi said she had met Hungary’s justice, finance and interior ministers, whom she described as strongly committed to making the initiative work. She said the sides had agreed that ten European delegated prosecutors would work in Hungary, alongside police officers, financial investigators and customs officials specifically assigned to EPPO cases.

Hungary did not originally join the EPPO, which began operating in June 2021. However, the EU has now confirmed Hungary’s participation, with the office set to become operational after the appointment of the country’s European Prosecutor.

What could the EPPO investigate?

The chief prosecutor said the office would be able to investigate fraud involving EU funds, as well as related corruption, embezzlement and money laundering. The EPPO’s existing mandate covers fraud affecting the EU budget involving more than EUR 10,000, while cross-border VAT fraud falls within its remit when the damage reaches at least EUR 10 million.

She said the office would examine matters falling within its jurisdiction from 2021 onwards once its Hungarian operation is fully functional. Kövesi also warned that Hungary could become a particular target for Chinese criminal networks, although she did not identify specific cases that could be investigated. The European chief prosecutor said the first investigations could start next year, following the establishment of the Hungarian office and necessary legislative changes.

Living, working or doing business in Hungary?

Raids, arrests and asset seizures

Kövesi said European delegated prosecutors would have the same investigative powers as domestic prosecutors, including ordering investigative measures, conducting searches, requesting arrests, bringing charges and freezing or seizing assets. The EPPO’s cross-border structure could be particularly significant when allegedly misappropriated money or assets are moved abroad.

The chief prosecutor cited property purchases elsewhere in Europe as an example, arguing that a national authority can face difficulties tracing and securing assets outside its jurisdiction. The EPPO already operates as an independent European prosecution service, conducting investigations and bringing cases before national courts in participating countries.

Stay up-to-date: Orbán-era ministers arrested as National Asset Recovery and Protection Office and prosecution order detention

‘It is time for them to take back their country’

Kövesi believes some investigations could produce results within a year or two, depending partly on Hungary’s legislative framework and the independence and quality of the prosecutors appointed. She also offered a broader assessment of Hungary’s recent political history, saying: “It is time for them to take back their country,” and arguing that police, prosecutors and judges must be able to perform their duties independently.

Asked about cooperation with Viktor Orbán’s governments, Kövesi said there had been cooperation in some VAT cases, but claimed cooperation became more difficult when investigations involved people close to politicians. The EPPO already has a cooperation agreement with Hungary’s prosecution service dating from 2021, but until now Hungary has remained outside the office’s full operational structure.

World.title: BudapestGO receives useful new update to make metro journeys easier
World.content:
Should you board at the front, in the middle or towards the end of the train? The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) has added a new feature to BudapestGO that will now help passengers make this choice.

When planning a metro journey, the app shows passengers exactly which carriage they should board to reach the exit at their destination as quickly as possible, or to make a simpler transfer to another metro line. The new feature will be rolled out gradually and will be available to all users within a few days.

BudapestGO gains another useful feature

BKK is continuously developing BudapestGO to ensure that the app can provide assistance with more and more aspects of everyday travel. One of the key new features in the update released on 29 September – which will become available to all users within a few days – is that, when planning a journey, the app now also shows passengers which part of the metro train they should board.

The new feature can be particularly useful on journeys where passengers have little time to make a connection or are less familiar with the metro station concerned. At the same time, it can also help regular passengers travelling along the same route to reach their exit more directly, avoiding a few unnecessary minutes or detours.

The new feature also plans step-free routes without any additional settings

The new feature works automatically, without requiring any additional settings. If a route recommended by BudapestGO includes a metro journey, the app indicates which carriage passengers should board to reach their destination exit more quickly or make a faster transfer between metro lines.

The app also takes accessibility into account when planning a journey. In such cases, it recommends the carriage closest to the exit with a lift and will only plan routes that are accessible without steps.

BudapestGO continues to evolve

The latest update is another milestone in the continuous development of BudapestGO. When planning new features, BKK takes customers’ needs and feedback into account, and requests for recommendations on which metro carriage to board have been raised in feedback from several customers.

The aim is for BudapestGO to provide travellers with an increasing amount of information to help them choose the most suitable route, making public transport faster, more predictable and more convenient as a result.

World.title: With Jansa’s Return, Slovenia’s Media Landscape Is Being Reshaped
World.content:
Chokehold could tighten even without Orban

Milosavljevic says it would only be “a wild guess what could happen next”. He points to other important actors on the Slovenian and wider regional market, which recently included United Group deals with the Czech investment group PPF, resulting in the pushing down of N1 and Nova S outlets in the Serbian cable line-ups after PPF sold these to state-owned Telekom Srbija.

Moreover, in 2024, the United Arab Emirates technology and investment group e& acquired a controlling stake in PPF’s telecom assets in Bulgaria, Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia, paving the way for the UAE’s historic entry into EU and EU candidate markets. With his close ties to the UAE, there is speculation that Vucic himself could be “behind the UAE links”.

PPF also received negative publicity for scaling down critical news reporting on Markiza, the largest commercial TV channel in Slovakia, shortly after the populist Robert Fico rebranded himself as a pro-Kremlin nationalist and Orban ally, and then made an improbable return to power in 2023.

“PPF Group might be interested in taking over Telemach, one of Slovenia’s four internet providers,” Ribac says, repeating speculation reported in the Slovenian media in September. At the same time, he says, the group “might be ready to relinquish its ownership of production company Pro Plus in exchange for control of Telemach.”

One of the richest Slovenes, Dari Juzna, is reported to be interested in buying Pro Plus, the largest media house in Slovenia. Pro Plus is part of Central European Media Enterprises, which PPF acquired in 2020 from Time Warner. At the time, the IPI and other press associations raised concerns with PPF’s owner, the late Petr Kellner, regarding media ownership and editorial independence.

“A group of wealthy individuals close to current Prime Minister Jansa might conversely be interested in taking over Pro Plus, as it produces the most popular commercial television channel POPTV and the most visited news website in the country 24.com,” Ribac explains.

This fits with Jansa’s desire to keep a primary focus on Slovenia while maintaining ties with like-minded politicians and businessmen abroad. “Jansa alone has no designs to influence Croatia or other countries near abroad,” Pengov Bitenc tells BIRN, but adds that even if Jansa’s main focus remains domestic, it won’t stop him continuing to make use of the existing network of nationalist leaders abroad to boost his credibility.

Jansa is “now indebted to Netanyahu”, Pengov Bitenc tells BIRN, referring to the involvement of the Israeli Mossad-linked company Black Cube in Slovenia’s election campaign. He argues that Jansa is much more likely to return favours to the sitting Israeli prime minister than to Orban, “who is out of power and the money flows have been turned off”.

Indeed, Israeli Minister of Foreign Affairs Gideon Saar visited Slovenia in September, when he opened Israel’s permanent embassy in Ljubljana and heralded the country’s shift from being one of the most outspoken critics of Israel’s campaign in Gaza and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank to one of its staunchest backers.

World.title: Pro-Russian Voters May Hold Key in Bulgaria’s Presidential Election
World.content:
On October 25, Bulgarians will vote for a new president in an election that highlights old-school East-West divisions in the country.

The election will likely produce a second round run-off between current acting President Iliana Iotova, the frontrunner, who is supported by President Rumen Radev’s ruling Progressive Bulgaria, the pro-Kremlin Bulgarian Socialist Party and the smaller nationalist far-right party VMRO-BND.

On the other geopolitical side of the race is former interim prime minister Andrey Gyurov - a pro-EU, Western-oriented candidate supported by the centre-right opposition parties We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria.

Apart from Gyurov and one other candidate, former agriculture minister Ivan Hristanov, almost all the contenders are fronting Eurosceptic, nationalist campaigns, which often border on Russia-sympathetic sentiment.

Experts say voters who support such stances might back various rivals to Iotova in the initial round, but switch to her if she faces a pro-EU candidate like Gyurov in the second round, in early November.

World.title: Bosnian Parties’ Election Gender Quotas Mask Failure to Empower Women
World.content:
On paper, Bosnia and Herzegovina boasts some of the most progressive gender representation mandates in the Western Balkans. Ahead of the current election, political parties have met the state’s legal requirement: that at least 40 per cent of candidates on their electoral lists belong to the less represented gender. Officially, women make up 42.2 per cent of all political hopefuls across the country.

But beneath this formal display of civilizational progress lies a bleaker administrative reality. Recent metrics released by the United Nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina through its ongoing "Izvan Fokusa" (Out of Focus) monitoring campaign show women head just 15.5 per cent of all electoral lists. This is significant, as candidates topping lists are more likely to get elected than those lower down. Crucially, the share of female-led lists has plummeted by 6.1 percentage points compared to the 2022 general elections.

World.title: Romania’s Crisis Spirals as Parliament Rejects PM-Designate’s Govt
World.content:
Romania’s parliament on Wednesday rejected the programme and proposed cabinet of Siegfried Muresan, a Member of the European Parliament, adding to the country’s political crisis.

The Prime Minister-designate needed 233 votes for his government to be approved. He received only 182.

“The parties that triggered the political crisis have voted to prolong it … We are now waiting to see what position the President … will take,” Muresan said after the result was announced.

His proposed cabinet was backed by the centre-right National Liberals, PNL, and two smaller former coalition partners, but the Social Democrats, PSD, the biggest party in parliament, rejected it.

The far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians, AUR, the second-largest party in parliament, also declined to endorse Mureșan. Party leader George Simion said the AUR would not vote for any government until the far-right politician Calin Georgescu “is freed from prison”.

A court on Tuesday ordered 30 days’ detention for former presidential candidate Georgescu, who is accused of defrauding a businessman of more than 1 million euros.

President Nicusor Dan must now nominate another Prime Minister-designate, who will have ten days to put together a cabinet and seek parliament’s approval.

Under the law, the President may dissolve parliament and call an early election if two prime ministers-designate fail to secure parliamentary backing within 60 days. However, Dan has ruled out an early election, arguing that it would likely fail to produce a strong parliamentary majority.

Since May 5, Romania has been operating under an interim government, following the collapse of the previous cabinet. During this period, Dan has made two previous nominations for prime minister, both of whom failed to secure parliamentary support.

In June, independent Eugen Tomac, the first of them, withdrew before even facing a parliamentary vote. Three weeks later, parliament rejected the proposed programme and cabinet of liberal politician Adrian Vestea.

Romania’s political crisis stems from deep tensions among the parties that previously formed the pro-European governing coalition.

The coalition, formed in June 2025, brought together the centre-left PSD, the centre-right National Liberal Party, PNL, and two smaller centre-right parties. One of its main objectives was to curb the rise of the far-right AUR.

Its mandate included stabilising the economy, which is burdened by the largest budget deficit in the European Union, securing access to 11 billion euros in EU recovery funds and safeguarding Romania’s investment-grade credit rating.

But unpopular austerity measures introduced to cut the budget deficit placed growing strain on the coalition, particularly with the Social Democrats, who withdrew support in May.

World.title: In Serbia, ‘Fictitious’ Corruption Campaign Becomes Tool of Distraction
World.content:
Over the same period, Serbia has slid 11 places on Transparency International’s annual Corruption Perception Index, published in February. It now stands in 116th place out of 182 countries, the worst ranking of any country in the Western Balkans.

Last year, Transparency Serbia published a report showing that for the first time since the fall of Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosevic in October 2000, the Serbian public considers corruption the biggest issue in the country.

“Vucic came to power in 2012 on, among other things, a campaign of ‘zero tolerance for corruption’,” said Draskovic. “That zero tolerance has turned into absolute tolerance of corruption.”

Nemanja Nenadic, programme director of Transparency, questioned the very notion of an ‘anti-corruption campaign’, given fighting corruption is the day-to-day remit of special corruption departments within the public prosecution service.

“Based on what has been announced, it can be concluded that a large number of arrests presented as part of this campaign essentially have nothing to do with corruption, but with other criminal offences,” Nenadic told BIRN.

“For example, cases in which owners of private companies engage in schemes to avoid paying taxes, not in collusion with tax officials, but with other private business owners.”

“In 2025, the number of reported corruption cases and indictments did increase compared with the previous year. For four major criminal offences, the number of indictments was 52 per cent higher than a year earlier, but there were only nine per cent more first-instance judgments.”

Arrests are the least important indicators of success, Nenadic said.

“More important indicators include how quickly reports submitted by citizens are examined, which can encourage more people to report cases; the amount of benefit obtained through corruption offences or the level of damage caused to public property or the public interest; the number and seniority of those indicted; the speed of court decisions; and, finally, the value of unlawfully obtained assets that are confiscated.”

Draskovic said that long-running proceedings without final judgments risk weakening public confidence.

“It sends a signal that it is not worth fighting corruption,” he told BIRN.

World.title: Three Kosovo Serbs Plead Not Guilty Over 2022 Unrest in North
World.content:
Barricades set up by Kosovo Serbs on a road in Rudare leading to the Jarinje border crossing with Serbia, December 2022. Photo: Adelina Ahmeti/BIRN.

Three Kosovo Serbs, Dusan Maksimovic, Nemanja Jolovic and Srdjan Vucinic, pleaded not guilty at the Pristina Basic Court on Wednesday to violating the constitutional order by participating in setting up roadblocks in the north of the country in December 2022.

A fourth defendant, Nenad Orlovic, was not present in court. Judge Rrahman Beqiri said that “every effort has been made to secure his presence in the criminal proceedings but it appears that he is not in Kosovo”.

The charges relate to unrest in December 2022, when Serbs in northern Kosovo set up barricades at the two border crossings with Serbia, parking trucks, ambulances, diggers and other vehicles across access roads in what was cast as a spontaneous outpouring of popular anger after the arrest of a Kosovo Serb on suspicion of attacking election facilities.

Two Kosovo Serbs have already been convicted over the case. Dusan Dobrac and Milos Radosavlevic were given prison sentences of one year and nine months respectively on August 31, 2026, after pleading guilty to charges.

Dobrac was convicted of acts breaching the constitutional order and obstruction of an official in the performance of their duties, and Radosavlevic of violating the constitutional order.

The indictment charged six people – Maksimovic, Drobac, Radosavljevic, Jolovic, Orlovic and Vucinic – with staging violent activity to subvert the constitutional order by blocking roads to two border crossings with Serbia: Jarinje and Bernjak.

The prosecution file, seen by BIRN, claims the unrest endangered the lives of police and customs officers. Those involved also allegedly participated in creating “a tense security situation through the opening of fortified positions and the presence of uniformed and armed persons”, according to the prosecution.

The police discovered a Viber group named “Barricades December 2022” on Maksimovic’s phone, suggesting the incidents were organised and coordinated.

They obtained the phone in September 2023 after Maksimovic was arrested over the armed attack on police in the northern village of Banjska, in which one Kosovo Albanian police officer was killed and a cache of military-grade weaponry was seized. He was sentenced in the first instance to 30 years in prison over the Banjska incident.

The contents of his phone helped prosecutors investigating the unrest in Serb-majority municipalities and the setting up of the barricades of December 2022. The messages it contained included: “Today we’ll all receive ammunition” and, “In the afternoon we could try the weapons in Suvi Dol [local village] with two or three bullets each.”

Prosecutors said the phone evidence undermined claims that local Serbs spontaneously set up the barricades.

World.title: Kosovo’s Kurti Pushes for Deal on President to Avoid Elections
World.content:
Photos of Kosovo’s presidents. Photo: BIRN/Denis Sllovinja

With a court deadline to elect a new President approaching, Prime Minister Albin Kurti on Wednesday called on opposition leaders to take urgent steps to address the issue, which risks triggering another legislative election only five months after the last one.

Last week, the Constitutional Court ordered MPs to elect a new head of state by October 6 to avoid new snap elections – the fourth parliamentary polls in two years.

“The Constitutional Court verdict … has put us in an urgent situation,” Kurti said. “The election of a new President is possible, and subsequently new repeat, unnecessary and costly elections, with heavy consequences, are [then] avoidable,” he added.

Kurti, who was re-elected Prime Minister less than three weeks ago, wants an agreement to be implemented that has already been reached with the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK. This would see Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and diplomat, take the post of president.

But Sejdiu withdrew from consideration on September 14, following disagreements within the LDK parliamentary group over his candidacy.

“We have Bekim Sejdiu as a candidate who withdrew because six LDK MPs did not agree with the deal. But from Vetevendosje’s point of view, we have a political agreement and we respect it. We don’t have a new name,” Kurti said on Wednesday when pressed on a possible new agreement with the opposition on a fresh candidate.

For a vote electing a President to be valid, at least 80 out of 120 MPs must be present in the chamber. If the first two rounds of voting fail, the third round requires only a simple majority of MPs to elect a President – but at least 80 of them still need to be in the chamber.

Kosovo has been without a President since April 4, when Vjosa Osmani’s five-year term ended. Parliament speaker Albulena Haxhiu from Kurti’s Vetevendosje party is serving as Acting President.

While the deal with the LDK hangs in the balance, the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK is meanwhile urging parliament to support amendments to the law on the Specialist Chambers, approved in 2015, which would limit the scope of this court before considering any discussion on a President. This comes after the Hague-based court found four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, guilty of war crimes.

On Wednesday, PDK MPs boycotted the work of parliamentary committees in order to press Vetevendosje to proceed with the law change. “Six laws have been brought to the committee today but the Law on the Specialist Chambers is being dragged out because they say it needs expertise. We won’t participate in the committees without proceeding with this law,” Blerta Deliu Kodra, a PDK MP, warned.

World.title: Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević: We Won’t Pay Workers for Their Strike
World.content:
October the 1st, 2026 – Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević has stated that the workers who went on strike from both ZET and Zagreb Holding won’t be paid.

After three days, the strike by ZET and Zagreb Holding workers has ended. Trams and buses are running again, and Čistoća has resumed regular waste collection. The County Court in Zagreb today declared the strikes at ZET and Holding illegal and ordered them to stop.

The unions then suspended the strike and announced they would appeal the rulings. Index reports that ZET has announced that from today onwards, all tram and bus traffic will again run according to the regular timetable.

what you need to know…

A ZET union lawyer has stated that he received two drastically different rulings. Municipal workers and ZET workers have now formally ended the strike after the court banned the ZET workers’ strike and the municipal workers’ strike.

After three days, the strike of ZET and Zagreb Holding workers has ended. Trams and buses are running again, and Čistoća has continued regular waste collection. The County Court in Zagreb today declared the strikes at ZET and Holding illegal and ordered their termination. The unions then suspended the strike and announced appeals against the rulings. Mayor Tomislav Tomašević stated that workers will not be paid for the days spent on strike. ZET published that from tomorrow all tram and bus traffic will again operate according to the regular schedule.

The strike had caused significant disruption in Zagreb for three days, with no trams, buses or regular waste collection.
