E-bike injuries in children quadruple

According to new data from the Sydney Children's Hospital Network, the number of children presenting with injuries from e-bikes or scooters has more than quadrupled since 2023.

So far this year, 183 children have presented to Westmead and Randwick hospitals with e-bike or e-scooter injuries.

A spokesperson for the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network said injuries from electric vehicles were now the third most common reason for admission.

"Children's injuries range from minor soft tissue injuries and bone fractures through to deep tissue wounds, friction burns and severe head injuries," the spokesperson said.

" Around one in five presentations have involved major trauma, requiring intensive care, surgery and extended recovery. "

There were 40 presentations for injuries related to e-bike and e-scooters in 2023, compared to 166 in 2025 and 78 in 2024.

Mr Graham said the government had received the final report into a review of minimum age limits for e-bike riders, which was due in June this year.

The expert review, led by Transport for NSW, had recommended a legal age limit between 12 and 16 years.

"I want to be clear I don't think it's sensible to have primary school kids on these heavy e-bikes," he said.

"I think the idea there's no age limit...makes common sense, but we need to strike the right balance."

The report will be released to the public at a later date following government consultation.

World.title: Darwin childcare centre guilty of supervision breach before child's death
World.content:
The Humpty Doo Community & Child Care Centre (HDCCCC) and its supervisor Casandra Harris have pleaded guilty in the Darwin Local Court to charges laid after the death of a toddler in 2023.

Warning: This article contains content some readers may find distressing.

Northern Territory Coroner Elisabeth Armitage last year found that on the morning of August 31 that year, Ebony Thompson had gone unsupervised at the childcare centre for about 10 minutes, before she was discovered unconscious and trapped by her neck in a low, loop-topped fence in a blind spot in the centre's playground.

In November, HDCCCC and three of its staff, including Ms Harris, were charged with inadequately supervising children and inadequately protecting children from harm and hazards.

Judge Stephen Geary said Ebony's death was "an absolute tragedy" and warned the sentence might seem "totally inadequate". (Supplied)

One of the workers on duty the day of Ebony's death, Gurmeet Kaur, today had her charges withdrawn, and the inadequate supervision charge against Ms Harris was also dropped.

The court heard Ms Harris had been the nominated supervisor for Ebony's class that day, but was not rostered to work or present at the time of her death. Today she pleaded guilty to inadequately protecting children from harm.

At a Darwin Local Court hearing in May, the childcare centre's director, Rachel Marsh, indicated she would contest similar charges against her. She is expected to return to court next month.

Nadia Brooker fronted court today, where she entered guilty pleas on behalf of the childcare centre. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Today, HDCCCC community management committee vice president Nadia Brooker pleaded guilty on behalf of the centre to both charges.

The court heard it was the first time such charges had been prosecuted in the Northern Territory.

Lawyers for HDCCCC and Ms Harris argued fines in line with similar, non-fatal incidents in Queensland would be appropriate.

But Judge Stephen Geary said those fines — of up to $15,000 — were imposed in "a different context".

Casandra Harris (back) pleaded guilty to inadequately protecting children from harm and hazards after another charge was dropped. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

"A child has passed on," he said.

" Ebony was a beautiful, intelligent little girl; it's an absolute tragedy. "

Around a dozen members of Ebony's family, including her parents Floyd and Jade Thompson, were present in the public gallery, dressed in her favourite colour, purple.

No yard checks conducted

The court heard HDCCCC had been deemed to be "meeting" all of its seven national quality and safety standards at the time of Ebony's death and had undergone inspections by the regulator twice in the preceding twelve months.

But prosecutor Nicholas Goodfellow said there had been four instances of non-supervision at HDCCCC found to be in breach of the regulator's code in the years between 2019 and 2023.

Nicholas Goodfellow said there was no written policy in place at the centre requiring a walk-through of its yard at the time. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Mr Goodfellow told the court HDCCCC had failed to notify the regulator of changes to the playground that created the "blind spot" behind the shed where Ebony was found unconscious.

"Ebony was not accounted for from 11:32am till she was found at 11:41am," he said.

"From around 11:28am to 11:37am, when children were transitioning from the outdoor play area, no educator was in a position to see if children were in the blind spot behind the island shed.

"No walk-through or checks of the yard were conducted when transitioning children from the outdoor play area.

The Humpty Doo childcare centre staff will return to court later this year. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

"No written policy required a walk-through of the yard, or a checking of the blind-spot behind the island shed."

Likely sentence 'a fine'

Defence lawyer Adam Mason told the court HDCCCC now updated and reviewed its site plans every six months, with more regular headcounts and room-to-room hazard inspections.

But he said families had withdrawn from the centre in the wake of Ebony's death and the Department of Home Affairs had revoked an application by HDCCCC to sponsor the visas of its international workers.

"Possibly they'll never recover, in terms of their reputation," he said.

Adam Mason argued for convictions not to be recorded against the centre or Casandra Harris. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Mr Mason argued that no conviction should be recorded against either the centre or Ms Harris.

The maximum penalty for each offence under the Education and Care Services National Law is $34,200 for an individual and $172,200 for a childcare centre.

"The sentence that I will impose is a fine," Judge Geary said.

"I can understand that it may come across as, to many people, totally inadequate."

HDCCCC and Ms Harris are expected to return to court for sentencing next month.

World.title: Australia records first detections of 'devastating' plant disease
World.content:
An exotic plant pest species capable of quickly "devastating" crops has been detected in Australia for the first time.

Monosporascus cannonballus is a soil-borne fungus that causes root rot, according to Northern Territory Chief Plant Health Officer Sally Heaton.

The disease was detected in a cucumber plant in the Darwin region and in honeydew and rock melon crops in the Katherine region, about 300 kilometres south.

Ms Heaton said the fungus had been found overseas in cucurbit plants such as pumpkins, squash, melons, cucumbers and gourds.

"If it's been left unmanaged … what they've seen is whole crops, mature crops, just suddenly die off," she said.

" Once you've got it into your crop, you really can't do much to save it. "

A rockmelon crop that has been severely damaged by the disease. (Supplied: Gerald Holmes, California Polytechnic State University)

Farmers reported disease

Ms Heaton said the NT Department of Agriculture and Fisheries was not sure how the disease arrived in Australia, but it could have been here for a long time.

It was identified in August after two separate farmers noticed something wrong with their crops.

Ms Heaton said the fungus could not be eradicated.

"We were looking at them [the plants] and looking at the fine roots, that's where we detected this fungal pathogen," she said.

The pest has spread in multiple countries including the US, India, Taiwan, Japan and in parts of Europe and the Middle East.

Ms Heaton said the disease caused plants to look as though cannonballs were erupting out of their roots.

Melons Australia chief executive Johnathon Davey said the discovery was concerning and that it was causing "significant loss" for affected NT growers.

"We now need to really work with out growers to understand what the spread of this fungus is and start working with them on how to manage it," he said.

Melons are grown in the NT near Darwin, as well in the Katherine and Mataranka areas. (ABC Rural: Lucie Bell)

Mr Davey said growers were under pressure as they grappled with other challenges, including varroa mite, and that the incursion would likely lead to an increase in production costs.

"Providing fresh melons for Australian consumers is only [going to] become harder," he said.

"This is going to see increased management costs.

"We need to have a discussion about what does it look like for the general community in terms of pricing.

"If it becomes clearer how it got into the country or what that pathway was, we'd expect that there'd be a fairly substantial investigation."

No restrictions planned

NT authorities are not planning to impose biosecurity restrictions in response to the detections, but Ms Heaton said it was important farmers had their own measures in place.

She said the department would work with industry groups to assist growers, who already took biosecurity seriously.

"They've got good biosecurity practices in place that manage these diseases very well," Ms Heaton said.

"A lot of those practices can be carried over to help deal with this."

World.title: Pilot's prophetic words one year before stabbing
World.content:
During a podcast interview uploaded just 11 months ago, Captain Smit Machchhar reflected on what would be needed "when things are going wrong" on a flight.

Warning: This article contains graphic images.

He said in an emergency, you would be "lucky" to have a doctor onboard but crew members "could save your life".

" When we are up there, if something happens, who's going to save you? "

"When things are going wrong, you need them [the cabin crew]."

He told the host of the Bona-Fide Banter podcast that he had not had any emergency landings so far, saying "touch wood".

But less than a year later, these words became eerily prophetic.

Pilot fights off attack in the air

Captain Smit Machchhar was operating the Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday when his co-pilot allegedly attacked him and "apparently tried to crash the plane", according to Israel's prime minister.

The plane reportedly entered a "tailspin", but according to passengers onboard and Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Captain Machchhar "fought back" and "resisted", despite his injuries.

He also managed to open the door to the cockpit, allowing a passenger and crew member to enter and subdue the co-pilot.

A second pair of off-duty flydubai pilots then landed the plane in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

Loading...

India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi has since hailed the Indian captain a "hero" and said India is "proud".

"In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others," he said in a social media post.

Mr Netanyahu has also given a "salute" to the Indian pilot on social media site X, for his "extraordinary bravery".

"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals," he said.

Leading news outlets in India have praised the pilot for his bravery, with The Times of India calling him a "hero".

Flydubai said in a statement that the underlying reasons for the event remained unknown. It has warned against "premature speculation".

Bit by the 'aviation bug'

Captain Smit Machchhar spoke about his aviation career and mentoring young pilots in a vodcast in 2025. (YouTube: )

Captain Machchhar is from Gujarat but his parents live in Mumbai, India's largest city, and its financial centre.

Local newspaper, the Mumbai Mirror, said his parents had left their home in the Tilak Nagar neighbourhood to travel to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday afternoon to be with their son.

Captain CS Randhawa from the Federation of Indian Pilots, a professional welfare organisation representing pilots, told the ABC he was waiting for an investigation report into what happened, but if media reports were correct and the co-pilot was trying to "take down the plane", then Captain Machchhar did a "miraculous job".

According to his LinkedIn, Captain Machchhar flew for SpiceJet Limited in Mumbai for more than 11 years, before joining flydubai four years ago.

In a statement the budget airline said his "SpiceJet family" joined "millions across the country and around the world" in wishing him a swift recovery.

"You are a hero to us all, Captain," the company wrote.

Loading...

In his podcast interview, Captain Machchhar spoke about discovering an interest in flying during a management course at 19, saying the "aviation bug bit him".

He said his mum was initially "scared" of him flying.

Captain Machchhar completed his early flight training in New Zealand.

Indian newspaper, The Times of India, has reported multiple friends and colleagues referred to Captain Machchhar as a "great guy" with one senior pilot who trained him, describing him as "very decent".

Childhood friend and former neighbour Prateek Gandhi told Press Trust of India that Captain Machchhar was "very calm and composed" and the "least trouble-making kid in our society".

But like other friends and family, he is concerned about his recovery.

"We heard that he is doing good, operation done but other than this we have not seen news from the family," he said.

'The pilot was in real bad shape'

Passengers gather around an injured man on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. (Reuters/Social media)

Vision filmed in the aftermath of the attack on Wednesday showed Captain Machchhar on the ground bleeding, wearing an oxygen mask.

An Israeli dentist who was onboard the flight rendered first aid, according to Israeli media.

"When I came into the cockpit, the pilot was in real bad shape, with heavy bleeding, particularly from his head," Dr Shota Musayev told the Times of Israel.

" I was the only doctor on the plane, and eventually I managed to stop the bleeding and stabilise his blood pressure. "

Dr Musayev told CNN the pilot had suffered "massive blood loss" and was "severely wounded".

"He was covered in cuts — his head, his hands — they were practically sliced open, almost severed in two," he said.

The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Captain Machchhar had been taken to hospital and was now in a stable condition.

In an online statement, it said it was following the condition of the "brave pilot" with a "full update" on his health was to come.

"We hope that he recovers from his injuries at the earliest."

World.title: Warning bus service cuts could leave Aboriginal people stranded in Alice
World.content:
Aboriginal people will be stranded in Alice Springs and forced to stay off country in overcrowded housing unless funding for a remote bus service is reinstated by the NT Government, according to local organisations.

Centre Bush Bus has been transporting people, critical medical supplies and goods to remote Indigenous communities from Alice Springs for three decades.

Earlier this week the organisation's owners said a funding cut at the end of February had forced the reduction of services on five routes across Central Australia, from two trips a week to just one.

Centre Bush Bus user Marlene Nampijinpa Spencer, who is from Kintore — a 10.5 hour drive from Alice Springs — said while her route had not been cut, a reduction in the service for any remote community would be devastating.

Marlene Spencer says people "want and need that bus" so they're not stuck in town. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Ms Spencer is the chair of remote dialysis service Purple House and said she witnesses the necessity of remote transport on a daily basis.

"Old people with renal [needs]… people want to go to funerals in communities, they don't want to get stuck here, lonely," she said.

"We want and need that bus, so people can jump in, and go to their community."

The Centre Bush Bus is so well-known features in art from across the desert. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

The affected routes include Santa Teresa, Atitjere-Engawala, Willowra, Hermannsberg-Areyonga and Titjikala-Finke, and Centre Bush Bus owner Tahnee Passmore-Barns said all of those routes were at risk of being cancelled altogether unless they received support.

Ms Passmore-Barns said since their funding stopped, they had been operating at a loss and had been trying to work behind the scenes to get it reinstated before going to the media this week.

"We just can't run at a loss … It's something that is quite heartbreaking for us because we have close relationships with all our communities and all our passengers," she said.

Tahnee Passmore-Barns says the service has been operating at a loss on five routes since the end of February. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Recipe for 'absolute catastrophe'

Local Aboriginal organisations and politicians have united in their calls for the service's funding to continue, citing health, safety and overcrowding concerns.

The chief executive of remote Aboriginal dialysis provider Purple House Sarah Brown said it made "no sense" to cut services.

"It would be an absolute catastrophe if the Northern Territory government lets down Bush Bus," she said.

Sarah Brown says the closure Centre Bush Bus routes could have a catastrophic effect on health and wellbeing. (ABC News: Sarah Brown)

"If there's only one Bush Bus a week, it means they're stuck in Alice Springs.

"We know that for a lot of people, they've already got more family members than the house can maintain.

" People being stuck in town in inadequate housing puts a severe pressure on that family group and their relationships. "

Central Land Council chief executive Les Turner said the government had a duty to ensure people in remote places had transport options and described any funding cut as "short sighted".

"Our concern is that this is a vital arterial route for people in remote areas to access services and the service is important, which should be available to all citizens in the Northern Territory," he said.

Les Turner describes the funding cuts as "short-sighted". (Supplied)

Too expensive to run

Infrastructure Minister Bill Yan, whose electorate of Namatjira covers many of the impacted bus routes, said the service missed out on funding in 2025-26 because "they didn't meet the criteria" and "costs were not comparative with services provided in other regions" in the NT.

"The total budget for the Remote Transport Program in 2026-27 is $3.132 million, increased by $67,000 from the 2025-26 budget of $3.065 million to offset fuel and wages increases," Mr Yan said in a statement.

"We did provide a one-off time limited grant of $667,000 between October 1 and February 28 to Centre Bush Bus on five specific runs with twice weekly services for support over the summer period.

Bill Yan says extending the grant would take up "around half the budget". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Based on these figures, if a decision was made to extend the grant funding to 12 months, it would have cost $1.6m to service nine communities.

"This would leave around half the budget to service the other 50 communities across the Territory."

He said the funding was not designed as ongoing and the service could reapply for the grant program.

However, Centre Bush Bus is the only scheduled transport and freight service running on regular timetables to some communities.

The government has not confirmed whether any other bus companies were successful in securing a grant to cover these routes.

Labor member for the remote electorate of Gwoja Chansey Paech said this was "an absolutely pathetic excuse".

Chansey Paech says the government should subsidise public transport in remote communities. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"The government heavily subsidises public transport in Darwin and Alice Springs, so why should people living in remote communities be treated any differently," he said.

Ms Passmore-Barns said increased diesel prices, long travel distances and staffing were all part of the cost of the service.

No communication

Ms Passmore-Barns said information in Mr Yan's statement about the service's cost effectiveness and having not met the criteria was new to her.

"The criteria over the last 10 or 20 years was pretty much the same, we've done dozens of applications and they've all been successful so I was actually very surprised … to be told it was not accepted was quite a shock," she said.

"Then to try and get feedback and not get any doesn't help."

Centre Bush Bus has been operating for three decades. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

She said the service was providing value for money.

"The only reason you would need funding is for those smaller communities who don't have the population to make the services sustainable," she said.

"The government even call our services essential services on their list of services in the Territory, but it doesn't look like they're essential services so much anymore."

Amid the back and forth, Marlene Spencer just hopes the services remain the same, so people can get to and from community for their health.

"Why are they talking about Bush Bus stopping? We want and need that important Bush Bus," she said.

World.title: Man who sourced gun used in fatal Ipswich brawl given longer sentence than shooter
World.content:
A Supreme Court judge has ruled a man who sourced the gun used to kill another man in an Ipswich brawl should spend more time in jail than the man who pulled the trigger.

In July 2021, Tye Bickle, Brayden Wilson-Knight and a teenage boy were charged with the murder of Carlo Stewart.

Mr Stewart died in hospital after suffering three gunshot wounds during a brawl between two groups outside a North Booval home.

Earlier this month the three men, now aged between 22 and 33, pleaded guilty to several charges, including a downgraded offence of manslaughter, and faced a sentencing hearing last week.

Due to how much time has passed since their arrest, the then-16-year-old boy involved was sentenced as an adult and can now be identified as Wilson-Knight's younger brother, Kobi Wilkins.

Kobi Wilkins (left) was handed a five-year suspended sentence and allowed to leave the court on parole. (ABC News: Talissa Siganto)

On Thursday Wilkins and Bickle were handed wholly suspended 5-year prison terms, while Wilson-Knight was jailed for nine years.

Fatal brawl sparked by stolen motorbikes

The court previously heard the fatal brawl stemmed from Mr Stewart wanting to help his friend retrieve stolen motorbikes, which had been sold to Wilson-Knight unknowingly.

Wilson-Knight planned to meet Mr Stewart in a public car park to exchange the motorbikes for cash, and he asked his brother and friend to go with him.

Instead of meeting at the arranged location, Mr Stewart decided to go to Wilson-Knight's home, and he brought several men with him, including some wearing gloves, masks and hoods.

The court previously heard the fatal brawl stemmed from Mr Stewart wanting to help his friend retrieve stolen motorbikes. (Facebook)

When Wilson-Knight, who had been armed with an unregistered .22 calibre handgun, was told the group had gone there instead, where his wife and children were alone, he returned to his house with Bickle and Wilkins.

When they arrived, CCTV captured Mr Stewart saying "you boys have our bikes", before Wilson-Knight pulls the gun from his pants.

A fight broke out between the two men, and Mr Stewart told Wilson-Knight to shoot him, which he attempted to do, but the weapon did not fire.

Mr Stewart then punched Wilson-Knight in the face and armed himself with a baseball bat.

During this time, Bickle gained possession of the gun, but was immediately struck in the head with the bat by Mr Stewart which caused a serious head injury.

The court heard Wilson-Knight brought the unregistered firearm to the scene, and Bickle fired it. (ABC News: Michael Rennie)

Bickle then fired 10 shots indiscriminately in about seven seconds, and three of the bullets connected with Mr Stewart.

Victim's mother describes him as 'lovable larrikin'

Several people provided victim impact statements to the court including Mr Stewart's mother Kay Stewart, who described her son as her "lovable larrikin".

"How can something so tragic happen to such a good-hearted person," she said in her statement.

Ms Stewart penned that "Carlo was my first love" and she has "been in hell" since his death.

"I cannot describe the pain of losing your first born … he was my everything," she said.

Bonita Ruben told the court the pain she felt when Mr Stewart died was "unlike anything I'd ever experienced". (ABC News)

His partner Bonita Ruben said in her statement that Mr Stewart was a "devoted and deeply loving father figure" to her daughter, who worked hard for their family.

She wrote that Mr Stewart was "loud, energetic and larger than life" and the pain she felt when he died was "unlike anything I'd ever experienced".

Shooter was 'hurt, dazed and disoriented', judge finds

When handing down their sentences on Thursday, Justice Peter Callaghan told the court no punishment would change the "awful reality" faced by Mr Stewart's loved ones.

"The story of grief will continue to be told irrespective of anything that occurs here," he said.

Justice Callaghan acknowledged Mr Stewart and his group had been "hostile and menacing" when they deviated and went to Wilson-Knight's home and were "intent on their own brand of law enforcement".

"The momentum towards a violent encounter was gathering and became unstoppable once Mr Stewart's group changed the plan," he said.

" They must have known they had set themselves on a collision course. "

He accepted Wilson-Knight would have been "horrified and frightened" by the group descending on his family home but his decision to arm himself with a loaded gun, warranted a harsher penalty to "denounce and deter" others from similar offending.

Wilson-Knight was given a head sentence of nine years in prison.

When sentencing Bickle, Justice Callaghan told the court although he was the principal offender and had "voluntarily placed himself into a potentially violent situation", his case was unique.

"This offence of manslaughter is marked by a number of features which has not been present in any other case of manslaughter dealt with by this court," he said.

Rachid Kachour and Matthieu Rees pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court in Brisbane on Thursday. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

He accepted Bickle had no prior knowledge of the gun, was not "proactively aggressive" in the altercation before being handed it, was severely injured and "scared and in a state of panic" when he shot Mr Stewart.

"He was hurt, dazed and disoriented," he said.

Bickle was sentenced to five years in jail wholly suspended and given immediate parole for two grievous bodily harm charges.

The same sentence was handed to Wilkins, and both men were free to leave the dock.

Their pre-sentence custody was not declared as time served, however 270 days that Wilson-Knight served on remand, was.

He will be eligible to apply for parole in April, 2028.

World.title: Keogh says he can still work with veterans after health cap backdown
World.content:
Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh says he will keep working with veterans, rebuffing calls to resign as minister after the government backed down on its proposed cap on allied health services for veterans.

Fronting cameras for the first time since scrapping the limit on veteran supports two weeks ago, Mr Keogh said he had listened to veterans and could still "work collaboratively" with them.

"We engaged with the veteran community. We heard, and we responded. And I think that's what people actually want from good, effective government," he said.

"What's really important about how I do my job is the commitment to engage, to listen, to bring forward good ideas and to make sure that we're delivering good outcomes for our veteran community."

Veterans healthcare change sparks fury Jacqui Lambie's emotional moment in the Senate taps into veteran fury over a government change to healthcare access.

The proposed cap would have imposed a $5,000 annual limit on services such as physiotherapy and dentistry unless veterans could demonstrate "clinical need".

The policy announced in the May budget would have saved the federal government $750 million over three years. Still, critics argued it would create barriers for ex-servicemen and women, particularly those with complex, ongoing medical needs.

Senator Jacquie Lambie, who is a veteran, made an impassioned plea on the floor of the Senate not to restrict health services for veterans, describing her own health issues after service.

The backdown also came days after Mr Keogh conceded he had made a mistake when he initially refused to meet with a veterans group who had pleaded for the veteran cap to be axed.

Before the policy shift, frustrated veterans who had travelled to Canberra for the meeting said they had lost faith in the minister, urging he be sacked.

Angus Taylor called on Matt Keogh to be sacked over the government's treatment of Australian veterans. (ABC News)

Several opposition members, including Liberal leader Angus Taylor, also called for Mr Keogh's resignation, saying the veteran community had "lost faith" and it was untenable for him to remain in the position.

Today, Mr Keogh rebuffed calls for him to step down, arguing "there's still more to do".

Asked who made the call to scrap the cap, he said it was a government decision.

"That's how governments work. We listen and we responded," Mr Keogh said.

"We've worked collaboratively with the sector the whole way through, making once-in-a-century reform to improve the veteran entitlement system as well the legislative system."

Department figures suggest that only about 10 per cent of veteran cardholders spend more than $5,000 on allied health services each year.

Advocacy group Fair Care for Veterans spokesman John Armfield, a former Navy clearance diver, thanked Mr Keogh for ditching the health service cap.

"Nobody had to lose for this to happen. The minister made the right call, and he deserves credit for it," he said.

Mr Keogh said the government was "on track" to deliver two-thirds of the recommendations made by the Royal Commission into Defence and Veterans suicide.

That includes increasing fees paid to providers to encourage more to take on veterans as clients and removing requirements for referral.

"We've maintained the fee increase. We dropped the threshold proposal, and we'll continue to work closely with the sector on the further implementation of recommendations as we go forward," he said.

World.title: Parents of Australian brothers killed in Mexico to visit scene as they await verdict
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaCrime Parents of Australian brothers killed in Mexico to visit scene as they await verdict Lorena Lamas Michael Koziol and Updated October 1, 2026 — 5:01pm ,first published October 1, 2026 — 8:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ensenada, Mexico: The grief-stricken parents of Jake and Callum Robinson will return to the remote location on Mexico’s north-west coast where their sons died for a private memorial ceremony as they await a verdict next week in the murder trial of the three accused killers. Debra and Martin Robinson are expected to make the journey on Thursday (Mexican time) from Ensenada to the beachside spot where the Mexican nationals are accused of killing the Australian brothers and their American friend, Carter Rhoad, in April 2024. Debra and Martin Robinson speak to media outside court in Mexico. They have attended each day of the four-week trial. AFP On Wednesday, the judge overseeing the trial scheduled closing arguments for next Thursday, with a verdict to be delivered the following day – just hours before the Robinsons are due to return to Perth after spending the past four weeks in Mexico for the trial. Debra Robinson stood in court on Wednesday to thank the judge and ask for a verdict to be delivered before she and her husband head home. She told the court they had flights booked for next Friday night.



“If there is any possibility of the verdict being delivered before then – even if the sentencing occurs at a later date – we would be extraordinarily grateful,” she said as her voice quivered. “It would mean so much for us, as parents of Jake and Callum, to be here for the verdict. We have travelled such a long way to seek justice for our sons and Carter.” Jake and Callum Robinson were killed while on a surfing trip in Mexico. They are pictured with their parents, Martin and Debra Robinson. The judge scheduled the verdict for 10am next Friday, when the court would not ordinarily sit. Following the hearing, Debra Robinson said it had been “an incredibly difficult and emotional few weeks”.



“We are deeply grateful for all the support and kindness we have received since we have been here,” she said outside court. “To everybody back home in Australia and around the world, we feel your love and your arms around us. It is giving us strength during some difficult days. Loading “As you know, we don’t want to comment on the proceedings while the trial is ongoing out of respect for the court and its process. We will wait for the verdict before we speak any further. “Right now, our focus is on Callum, Jake and Carter – on honouring them, their memory and seeing the process through.”



The Robinsons have attended every day of the four-week trial, sitting within a few metres of the three men accused of murdering their sons, inside a small, beige courtroom under fluorescent white lights. Related Article Crime Agonising wait for justice for parents of Australian brothers killed in Mexico On Wednesday, the accused sat in bright orange prison jumpsuits with their ankles cuffed to each other, as two police stood behind them. It was initially thought a verdict could be delivered as soon as this week. At Wednesday’s hearing, which lasted less than an hour, the defence opted not to cross-examine two key witnesses: a former girlfriend of alleged ringleader Jesus Gerardo, also known as “El Kekas”, and her son. Both are in witness protection and cannot be identified. No further witnesses are due to appear.



The prosecution alleges the Robinson brothers and Rhoad, all in their early 30s, were killed in a robbery gone wrong in a remote beachside area of Baja California, where they were camping during a surfing holiday. The accused allegedly sought to steal the men’s ute. When the campers tried to defend themselves, the attackers pulled out a gun and shot them before throwing their bodies down a well, the prosecution alleged. Lawyers for the defendants argued there was not enough evidence to prove the three men were involved in the deaths of the Robinson brothers and Rhoad. The girlfriend of El Kekas was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery to steal the tyres off the men’s ute.



El Kekas and the two other accused men, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, have been charged with aggravated homicide, aggravated robbery committed at night, violent robbery and vehicle theft with violence. Prosecutors have asked for 200-year sentences for each of them. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘You’re going to end up like the gringos’: Witness tells court he was threatened to keep quiet after Australian brothers killed in Mexico There is no jury: the verdict will be delivered by a judge alone. He has presided over the trial since the original judge was involved in an accident the weekend before proceedings began. Australian consular staff are providing support to the Robinson family in Ensenada, and it is expected that Australia’s ambassador to Mexico, Crispin Conroy, will travel to the Pacific Coast city for the verdict. World.title: ‘He deserves to play’: Roosters sweat on Connor Watson concussion verdict
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘He deserves to play’: Roosters sweat on Connor Watson concussion verdict Christian Nicolussi October 1, 2026 — 4:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Connor Watson will know by Friday if an independent concussion consultant is prepared to allow him to play in the NRL grand final. Watson underwent testing with a specialist on Thursday morning and was due to have further examinations on Thursday night in the hope of being cleared to play against Newcastle in Sunday’s decider. Loading The representative utility had only been on the field for one minute last Friday against the Dolphins when he suffered a concussion. Watson was initially ruled to have displayed category-two symptoms, which was later upgraded to a category-one concussion. That meant Watson was automatically forced to stand down from training and playing for 11 days under the NRL’s concussion protocols, essentially ending his grand final dream.



The Roosters monitored Watson’s condition on Saturday and in the days that followed, and asked the NRL to review the category-one grading in the hope it would be re-classified as a category two, which removes the mandatory 11-day enforced rest. One of the country’s top neurologists, Mark Parsons, stressed the risks involved in rushing Watson back, telling this masthead at the start of the week: “I’d be very surprised if an independent neurologist would clear him.” Connor Watson will know by Friday if he is free to play in the grand final. Getty Images Roosters coach Trent Robinson stressed the decision was in the hands of professionals and said the club would have an answer by Friday at the latest, when the Roosters are due to hold their main training session. Should Watson be ruled out of what would be his final game at the club before he joins St George Illawarra, Robinson said Benaiah Ioelu loomed as the logical “plan B” to be the second dummy-half on the bench.



“He had an appointment this morning that went well, he has another one this afternoon,” Robinson said at the grand final press conference during a fan fest on Thursday in Martin Place. “It’s out of our hands. We’ll get a ruling on that tonight or tomorrow. He’ll either be in or out. It’s pretty simple from our end. Connor Watson gets knocked out on Friday night. Nine “Connor has played his key role in the balance of our team in the middle of a game. He’s really done that well. He’s fit, played multiple positions, and he’s in our 17 every week for a reason. “That’s a really important ‘in’ for us. If he’s out, I’ve got other players who will step in who have played many games and are really clear on their roles.



“Connor, we want him to play, he deserves to play – whether he’s fit to play will get decided by someone else, then we’ll adapt. “I don’t think it would take too much to work our what plan B is. We have some really good hookers. Benaiah Ioelu has played some really good footy for us this year, he brings a lot of energy, and he’ll come into consideration.” James Tedesco leads the Roosters out at Thursday’s Fan Fest in Martin Place. Jessica Hromas/SMH Newcastle skipper Kalyn Ponga is one of Watson’s best friends from their days playing together at the Knights, and said: “He’s one of the hardest-working blokes I know. The injuries he’s had to overcome over the years, the adversity, he’s one of the most deserving blokes to be in a grand final. “His [Roosters teammates] know just how hard he works, how committed and dedicated he is to rugby league.



“If he gets cleared, I’ll be stoked for him. Obviously if he doesn’t, he has to take care of his health first.” One player whose grand final hopes have already been dashed is Phoenix Crossland, the Newcastle hooker who was banned for four matches for a hip-drop tackle on Penrith’s Nathan Cleary last weekend. The Knights made sure Crossland joined the group in Sydney for the last of the media commitments, and coach Justin Holbrook said he would still be named in the No.9 on the team sheet. “It’s been his jersey all year,” Holbrook said. “We love the job he’s done ... I didn’t want to replace that jersey for the last game of the year.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘There is no precedent’: Tennessee fails to execute woman after two doses of lethal injection
World.content:
Graphic content WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty ‘There is no precedent’: Tennessee fails to execute woman after two doses of lethal injection Emily Cochrane and Ann E. Marimow Updated October 1, 2026 — 4:53pm ,first published 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains graphic content Nashville: A Tennessee woman convicted of murder survived two doses of lethal injection on Wednesday night (US time) before state officials suspended the execution and had her taken to a hospital for medical care, her lawyers said. It was the second botched execution in the state this year. This photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction shows Christa Pike in 2023. Tennessee Department of Correction via AP The apparent failure came after duelling court rulings delayed the execution of the woman, Christa Pike, by about nine hours. The state had raced to go ahead with the execution before the day ended and to avoid having to reschedule.



In a pair of emergency legal filings, Pike’s lawyers said while two syringes of pentobarbital, the lethal drug, had been administered, Pike had not lost consciousness. She still had a heartbeat, they said, and was audibly snoring. It was not immediately clear what went wrong with the administration of the drugs, or what Pike’s medical condition was. In a statement late on Wednesday, her lawyers said she was at a nearby hospital but they did not know her condition. Tennessee officials confirmed to a federal judge late on Wednesday that Pike was receiving medical care. Emergency vehicles arrived at the prison shortly after witnesses were escorted out and left about 15 minutes later. AP Photo/George Walker IV “This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre. “There is no precedent.” At a news conference after the execution attempt, members of the media who served as witnesses described Pike as somewhat alert, at one point singing with her spiritual adviser. They were brought into the witness room outside the execution chamber just before 6.30pm. Shortly after, the curtains separating the execution chamber from the witnesses were opened to show Pike, strapped to a gurney, they said.



“I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life,” she said. “And that is with love.” At one point, they said, she described a burning spot in her arm that felt like it was going to burst. She asked if that was normal. The curtains briefly closed, then reopened. ‘This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era.’ Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre The curtains were then closed again for nearly an hour, reporters said, adding that they could hear breathing and steady snoring. Just before 9pm, reporters were told to leave for the news conference. Emergency vehicles arrived at the prison as the witnesses were addressing the news conference and left about 15 minutes later.



Officials at the prison, the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, did not address reporters afterwards. In a statement, the Tennessee Department of Correction said it “had followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general’s office”. “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective,” the department said. Media witnesses leave Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted. AP Photo/George Walker IV It was the second time this year that Tennessee had failed to administer the lethal drugs. In May, the state called off one of four planned executions because medical staff could not find a vein while administering a lethal drug. Pike’s lawyers had argued the procedure could be torturous for her because she has small veins, a history of sexual trauma and other medical conditions.



“We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy,” they said in a joint statement after the execution attempt. Pike, 50, who was convicted of murdering her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, in 1995, would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in more than 200 years. The attempted execution came hours after the US Supreme Court allowed the state to proceed, overturning a pause imposed by a lower court earlier in the day. The lower court briefly paused the execution, saying more time was needed to consider the case. Her lawyers had argued that Pike’s initial legal defence did not adequately present her history of child sexual abuse and neglect. The three liberal justices on the Supreme Court dissented from the order allowing the execution to proceed, with Justice Sonia Sotomayor writing that the majority “unnecessarily prevents” the appeals court from fully considering Pike’s argument. “I see no reason to short-circuit the ordinary process of appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision,” Sotomayor wrote. She was joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.



Sotomayor added that “Tennessee’s desire to expedite Pike’s execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh” Pike’s interest in protecting her own life. In January 1995, Pike, her boyfriend at the time and a friend lured Slemmer into the woods on the University of Tennessee campus, taunting and torturing her. They beat her with asphalt rocks and slashed her with a box carver. Pike, who was 18 then, took a piece of Slemmer’s skull with her, which she showed to at least one other person. Tadaryl Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend at the time, testified to carving a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest, a gesture that sparked fears of Satan worship. Because Tennessee law applies the death penalty only to people 18 and older at the time of the crime, Shipp, at 17, was sentenced to life in prison. He was denied parole last year. Slemmer’s family remained firmly in support of Pike’s execution and raised funds to cover the drive from their home outside of Jacksonville, Florida, to Nashville to witness the execution. May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, was adamant that Pike could not atone for the death of her daughter and should be executed. The lone woman on Tennessee’s death row, Pike has expressed remorse for her crime. She was diagnosed and treated while in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, something which her lawyers said had contributed to her violence. Women who were incarcerated alongside Pike said she was a supportive and kind presence.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Pilot arrested after midair ‘stabbing and crash attempt’, heroes praised for thwarting disaster
World.content:
London: A commercial aircraft flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after issuing an alert that sparked fears of a disaster when one of the two pilots stabbed the other in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the evidence suggested that crew members and passengers prevented a disaster by entering the cockpit and stopping the attacker, in an “extremely serious” security incident. Loading The midair crisis began when flydubai flight FZ1073, carrying 174 people including prominent Sydney businesspeople Steven and Carol Moss, suddenly lost altitude and issued an emergency alert more than two hours into its journey, leading the Israeli government to scramble fighter jets in response. Steven is the son of the late Sam Moss, a Czechosolovakian-born Holocaust survivor who went on to co-found the Katies fashion empire. Carol is the descendant of a famous Rabbi. The couple are major financial supporters of Jewish schools, aged care homes and charities and live in Sydney’s eastern suburbs.



Contacted for comment, Steven Moss said he was struggling after the ordeal and did not wish to speak with the media. Related Article Aviation ‘I grabbed the terrorist’: How hero passengers helped save flight FZ1073 Netanyahu made his televised remarks on Wednesday afternoon in Israel (shortly after 11.30pm AEST) in the first official statement on the attacks by the Israeli government after hours of speculation about whether the incident was a hijacking, an altercation between pilots or a brutal attempt to kill all on board. “I salute the heroes who demonstrated resourcefulness and extraordinary courage,” Netanyahu said. “They saved many lives and averted a terrible disaster. The pilot who committed the stabbing has been arrested and is currently being interrogated by Saudi authorities.”



More details emerged after the passengers arrived safely in Tel Aviv on Wednesday night (about 1.45am Thursday AEST) on a second flydubai flight, which carried them from the emergency landing site in Saudi Arabia. The plane’s captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, unlocked the cockpit door to let passengers in. Netanyahu spoke to a passenger and officials who told him one of the pilots stabbed the other and apparently tried to crash the aircraft. At least one passenger joined a crew member in breaking into the cockpit to stop the pilot attempting to damage the plane. Another crew member then joined them and managed to stabilise the aircraft, he said. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said the attempted attack “was thwarted solely thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers who stormed the cockpit, subdued the terrorist, and – with their own hands – restored control of the aircraft to an additional flight crew present on board”.



“According to our preliminary information, the terrorist had a single objective: to crash the plane,” Katz said in a statement. Public flight radar sites showed that the Boeing 737 MAX was diverted to Saudi Arabia and landed about 90 minutes after a shocking plunge in altitude, with passengers describing “blood in the cockpit” after the fight on board. Israeli media cited unnamed officials who said there was a “growing assessment” that the emergency had been intended as an act of terror. Other options were also being looked into, including the possibility of a mental health episode. Passenger Almog Italie told Reuters it felt like the plane was passing through “massive turbulence” before he realised a life-or-death struggle had unfolded in the cockpit.



View post on X “It was dropping like for 20, 30 seconds, and then balanced, and then started dropping again, and balanced again, and then we saw that [there] are people in the front, directly [in front of] the cockpit,” he said. Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister’s office, said the wounded captain – identified as Captain Smit Machchhar – had drawn on “the last moments of his energy” as he lay bloodied on the floor to click open the release on the cockpit door. “At that moment, some of the passengers that realised something was happening raced forward [and] entered the pilot’s cabin. They saw the injured pilot on the ground, and the other … the attacking pilot was standing over the control panel, bashing the control panel,” he said. A photo purportedly showing one of the passengers on flydubai FZ1073 with blood on his shirt. Amichai Stein/Twitter



Netanyahu said on X that, “despite being stabbed and seriously injured, [Machchhar] fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster … He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.” One passenger, in a text message to Israeli media network Channel 12 that was reported by The Times of Israel and other outlets, said: “We heard screams on the plane.” “Then they opened the cockpit and we saw blood, and someone had stabbed the pilot with a pocketknife.” In a video shared by one person on the flight, the captain is covered in blood as some passengers support him and praise him for saving the aircraft from disaster. A second member of the crew, possibly the other pilot, is seen tied up nearby and apparently unconscious. The aircraft departed Dubai at 7.05am local time on Wednesday (1.05pm AEST) and initially flew over the southern part of the Persian Gulf before crossing over Saudi Arabia and heading towards Israel.



Loading Fluctuations in its altitude began about two hours into the trip, according to Flightradar24. The plane then dropped 14,000 feet (4300 metres) in less than 30 seconds. Authorities first became aware of the unfolding crisis when the aircraft issued a 7700 “squawk” code to signal an international emergency about 2½ hours into the flight, before changing this to a 7500 code to signal a hijacking or unlawful interference. Netanyahu called urgent meetings to monitor the emergency. The emergency lasted for the next 90 minutes before it turned out of Jordanian airspace and landed at Tabuk, a city in the far west of Saudi Arabia. A replacement plane carrying passengers from the earlier flight left Saudi Arabia and landed at Ben Gurion International Airport in Israel on Wednesday night to cheers and a crowd waving Israeli flags.



Passengers arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit Israeli journalist Amichai Stein reported an account of the emergency from those on board and posted images of one passenger with a blood-stained shirt. “We heard screams and saw blood,” one passenger said, according to Stein. “The pilot was stabbed. There were moments when we thought we weren’t going to make it out alive.” The Israeli media said authorities were planning to question the crew and inspect the aircraft as part of an investigation. People celebrate the arrival of the replacement aircraft in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit



A passenger called Yaniv met Netanyahu after the passengers made it to Tel Aviv, and he told the prime minister how he had forced his way into the cockpit to stop the attack. In a discussion posted on social media, Yaniv described how he had “pulled the yoke up” on the aircraft’s controls to bring the plane out of its steep dive. The pilot who suffered the knife attack was able to open the cockpit door even though he was wounded, allowing passengers and crew to come to his aid and prevent a disaster. A passenger called Daniel told Israeli media outlet Channel 12, in remarks reported by The Times of Israel, that he had seen a struggle in the cockpit and an attempt to push someone out. View post on X



“Then three Israelis who were sitting behind me came to see what was happening, and the plane suddenly went into a very steep dive, nose down, with a very intense spin,” he said. “The spinning stopped. It took some — I don’t know, it felt like an eternity, but I think it was two minutes, at least two or three minutes, during which the plane was simply diving and spinning like crazy. “It felt like, that’s it. It’s over. September 11 is happening again.” Israeli airspace was briefly closed during the emergency. Budget airline flydubai is owned by Dubai. iStock



After the passengers made it to Tel Aviv on the second aircraft, Israeli authorities said one 51-year-old male passenger with a mild upper body wound was transported to a hospital. Of the 174 passengers on Flight FZ1073, the media said 166 were Israelis. Flydubai says flights to and from Israel will be suspended while an investigation continues into the pilot attack. World.title: Critica adds global commodities clout to board
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Critica adds global commodities clout to board Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 1, 2026 — 4:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Critica has appointed seasoned global commodities executive Hannah Badenach to its board in a move that looks to be less about finding minerals and more about selling them. The appointment comes as the company pushes both of its key critical minerals projects towards commercial reality. The Hong Kong-based specialist brings more than 20 years of experience in commodity trading, marketing, offtake and financing, particularly in tin, tungsten and rare earths, exactly the suite of commodities in Critica’s portfolio. Critica has appointed global commodities executive Hannah Badenach to its board. Ms Badenach’s resume seems tailor-made for the challenge. She previously spent 13 years at global commodity trader Noble Resources, where her most recent role was executive director, Metals & Mongolia. In that position, she managed international trading activities and negotiated marketing, offtake, financing and prepayment arrangements. Her board experience also spans several listed and private resources companies, including Peak Rare Earths, Materra Metals and Xanadu Mines.



‘As we advance Mt Lindsay and Jupiter, her commercial expertise and experience building commodity supply chains will be invaluable.’ Critica Limited chairman Tim Lindley In a strong show of alignment, Ms Badenach intends to receive her non-executive director fees in equity, subject to shareholder approval. The appointment is effective from October 1st, with current director Jamie Byrde set to resign from the board on October 26th. Critica chairman Tim Lindley said: “We are delighted to welcome a Director of Hannah’s calibre to the Critica Board. Hannah has traded the commodities we intend to produce. She has a deep understanding of the tungsten, tin and rare earths markets and, importantly, the commercial mechanisms that protect and enhance shareholder value, from offtake structuring and pricing to prepayment, project financing and supply chain development.” Her appointment looks particularly timely given the company’s recent run of form. Just last week, a new scoping study for its Mt Lindsay tin-tungsten project in Tasmania delivered in spades, modelling a whopping pre-tax net present value of $1.42 billion and featuring an eye-catching 64.9 per cent internal rate of return. The study forecasts pre-production capital at a modest $244.5 million. Mt Lindsay isn’t Critica’s only project rounding the corner towards commercialisation. The company recently produced its first high-purity mixed rare earth oxide sample from its Jupiter project in WA, grading a stellar 98.2 per cent total rare earth oxides. Critica says the sample, which contains a high concentration of valuable magnet rare earths, will now be put in front of strategic partners to kick off offtake discussions.



The market backdrop for Critica’s key commodities adds another layer of intrigue. Western tungsten markets remain tight, with an S&P Global report pointing to a sizeable ex-China supply gap. At the same time, China’s export controls and US defence procurement restrictions are expected to impact the supply of rare earths, making tungsten and rare earths commercial expertise particularly relevant as Western customers seek secure sources. With a billion-dollar study now on the table for Mt Lindsay and its first saleable product samples emerging from Jupiter, Critica seems to be firing on both cylinders. Appointing a commercial heavyweight such as Badenach, whose remuneration is tied directly to share price growth, looks like a calculated move to turn impressive study numbers and high-grade samples into binding offtake deals. World.title: A terrifying plunge, loud screams, blood everywhere: How flight FZ1073 unfolded, moment by moment
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was a routine daily flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. But on Wednesday, two hours into the short journey, flight FZ1073 rapidly turned to chaos. Screams filled the cabin as 174 passengers plunged 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds. Crew members called for help. A distress signal was sent. Passengers stormed the cockpit – usually locked, if not for some quick thinking by a pilot close to losing consciousness after apparently being stabbed by his co-pilot – to find blood everywhere. Here is what we know about how the flight unfolded. September 30, 7.05am (Dubai time) After a 20-minute delay, flydubai flight FZ1073 departs Dubai International Airport, bound for Tel Aviv, Israel. The three-year-old Boeing 737 MAX 8 climbs to a cruising altitude of 34,000 feet. 9.21am: A terrifying rapid plunge



Two hours and 16 minutes into the flight, which typically takes about 3½ hours, FZ1073 plummets. According to data captured by flightradar24, it plunges more than 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds. “Suddenly, the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down like a massive G-force,” passenger Almog Itali told BBC’s Newsnight. Loading A sharp ascent follows, but the plane abruptly drops again. It’s at this point that people rush to the cockpit, according to Itali. About three or four passengers subdue the co-pilot, acquiring minor injuries in the process. An Israeli passenger said the crew asked passengers for help, and passengers helped tie down the co-pilot after tackling him. “They are very brave. They literally saved our lives,” Itali said. According to Yasmin Abukasis, whose daughter Miriam was on the flight, a man holding a knife had forced one of the pilots onto the floor. Blood was everywhere, and loud screams could be heard.



‘Thrown around the cabin’ In total, the aircraft falls 17,350 feet, going from 34,000 feet to 16,650 feet in two minutes. The safest passengers during this erratic change in altitude would have been those seated with their seatbelts securely fastened, says Dr Salim Hijazeen, a lecturer in aviation at Swinburne University of Technology. When Singapore Airlines flight SQ321 dropped 178 feet in 4.6 seconds and a total 6000 feet in three minutes, in May 2024, British passenger Geoff Kitchen, 73, suffered a cardiac arrest and died. His wife, Linda, sustained a head wound and spinal fractures in the incident. “Those rapid changes in movement are what could cause passengers to be lifted from their seats or thrown around the cabin,” Hijazeen said. “It would have been absolutely terrifying.”



9.28am: First emergency alert issued The aircraft issues an emergency alert signal, known as a “squawk 7700”, as it flies along the Jordan-Saudi Arabia border. Related Article Updated

Aviation Pilot arrested after midair ‘stabbing and crash attempt’, heroes praised for thwarting disaster A squawk 7700 is an internationally standardised code that indicates a “general emergency”, which could be anything from engine failure to a severe medical crisis. It automatically highlights the aircraft on air traffic control’s radar, making it priority. If needed, air traffic control will clear surrounding airspace to get the aircraft to the nearest runway. The code is discrete – no verbal radio call is necessary as it’s transmitted directly through the aircraft transponder when the pilot types in the four digits directly. Passengers take control



After the altitude stabilises at about 15,000 feet, a second emergency alert – a squawk 7500, meaning “unlawful interference” – is sent, sparking fears of a hijacking. The aircraft turns west and briefly enters Jordanian airspace, then turns 180 degrees back towards Saudi Arabia, flying south-west in the direction of Tabuk. Passenger Yaniv Hayoun, with blood on his shirt after subduing the attacker. X/@AmichaiStein1 An unnamed passenger later tells the Jerusalem Post that two other passengers seated at the back of the plane were off-duty pilots. “I shouted at them to run and take control of the plane,” the passenger said. The injured pilot – identified as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar – received life-saving care from a dentist on board, the passenger said. 9.44am: Plans for emergency landing

World.title: Teacher allegedly raped Newington student during Great Barrier Reef trip
World.content:
A Newington College teacher allegedly raped a student during an interstate trip and sexually assaulted him during school hours on or near the inner west campus, court documents reveal. Deandra Kontou, 32, was last week charged with nine child abuse offences, including aggravated sexual assault, four counts of sexual assault, and using an electronic device to groom her victim. Deandra Kontou allegedly raped the student during a school trip to the Great Barrier Reef. She went by her maiden name, Haralambidis, while teaching at the prestigious private school. The alleged abuse spanned six months and began with Kontou allegedly showing the boy indecent material, intending to make it easier to “procure the child for unlawful sexual activity”, according to court documents.



Over the next month, Kontou allegedly began grooming the boy through messages, twice coerced him to sexually touch and carry out a sex act on her without his consent and twice sexually touched him. Each of these offences occurred in Stanmore, where the school is located, and during school hours. Teacher Deandra Kontou in a staff school photo taken this year. A few months later, the abuse allegedly continued on a senior boys’ camp at Fitzroy Island, on the Great Barrier Reef. There, Kontou is accused of twice sexually touching the child during the day before sexually assaulting him between 10pm and 11pm at night. Most of the sexual offences are categorised as aggravated as Kontou was the child’s teacher. Research trips to the Great Barrier Reef, where students are exposed to the reef’s unique marine life and ecosystems, are not uncommon among Sydney’s private schools.



Kontou was moved on by Newington shortly after the Fitzroy Island camp, once the allegation was conveyed to college staff. She was arrested last Monday and appeared before Sutherland Local Court that day. She was granted bail on the condition she reported to police daily, surrender her passport and not contact the alleged victim or witnesses. The court also barred her from entering any school grounds, teaching children and being in the company of a child without the child’s parent or guardian. Kontou taught for two years at Newington and led a year 7 mentorship group. Parents in Kontou’s mentorship class were told she was on an “approved leave of absence”, days after the allegation was made to college staff.



The leave announcement followed days of confusion from parents, who contacted Newington’s head of year 7 after Kontou failed to return to campus after the school trip. “Mrs Haralambidis [Kontou] will not be responding to emails and will appreciate respect for her privacy,” Newington’s head of year 7 told parents enquiring about her prolonged absence, in an email soon after the trip. “Please do not hesitate to communicate with me any issues or concerns regarding the boys … the boys will continue to be supported in the Newington way.” Kontou began permanent work at Georges River College Senior Campus in Oatley in 2024 after a string of casual jobs, where she taught society and culture, history and geography until she was arrested in her Sutherland home last week. Deputy Premier and Education Minister Prue Car has ordered an urgent review into the Education Department’s hiring of Kontou at the Oatley school in 2024. The review is expected to examine any correspondence between the police and the Education Department before Kontou was hired, and any issues raised about her character in the recruitment process.



The review was ongoing as of Thursday afternoon, and may involve interviews with staff from the Oatley campus, who are on school holidays until the end of next week. The NSW Education Standards Authority has revoked her accreditation while she is banned from teaching children and entering schools. She remained on the public payroll until Wednesday morning, when Education Department officials suspended her without pay after accessing her charge sheet and bail conditions. The charges Kontou faces don’t relate to her time at the Oatley school, and she is not accused of any criminal wrongdoing while employed by the Department of Education over the past two years. Georges River College Senior Campus principal Anna Girginis encouraged students to seek counselling and contact professional hotlines while their former teacher confronts the offences. She called pupil care wellbeing the school’s “highest priorities” in a letter to parents on Wednesday afternoon. Girginis didn’t address in the letter whether the school was aware of the police investigation when Kontou was hired or over the course of her employment.



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Parents of Australian brothers killed in Mexico to visit scene as they await verdict
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaCrime Parents of Australian brothers killed in Mexico to visit scene as they await verdict Lorena Lamas Michael Koziol and Updated October 1, 2026 — 5:01pm ,first published October 1, 2026 — 8:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ensenada, Mexico: The grief-stricken parents of Jake and Callum Robinson will return to the remote location on Mexico’s north-west coast where their sons died for a private memorial ceremony as they await a verdict next week in the murder trial of the three accused killers. Debra and Martin Robinson are expected to make the journey on Thursday (Mexican time) from Ensenada to the beachside spot where the Mexican nationals are accused of killing the Australian brothers and their American friend, Carter Rhoad, in April 2024. Debra and Martin Robinson speak to media outside court in Mexico. They have attended each day of the four-week trial. AFP On Wednesday, the judge overseeing the trial scheduled closing arguments for next Thursday, with a verdict to be delivered the following day – just hours before the Robinsons are due to return to Perth after spending the past four weeks in Mexico for the trial. Debra Robinson stood in court on Wednesday to thank the judge and ask for a verdict to be delivered before she and her husband head home. She told the court they had flights booked for next Friday night.



“If there is any possibility of the verdict being delivered before then – even if the sentencing occurs at a later date – we would be extraordinarily grateful,” she said as her voice quivered. “It would mean so much for us, as parents of Jake and Callum, to be here for the verdict. We have travelled such a long way to seek justice for our sons and Carter.” Jake and Callum Robinson were killed while on a surfing trip in Mexico. They are pictured with their parents, Martin and Debra Robinson. The judge scheduled the verdict for 10am next Friday, when the court would not ordinarily sit. Following the hearing, Debra Robinson said it had been “an incredibly difficult and emotional few weeks”.



“We are deeply grateful for all the support and kindness we have received since we have been here,” she said outside court. “To everybody back home in Australia and around the world, we feel your love and your arms around us. It is giving us strength during some difficult days. Loading “As you know, we don’t want to comment on the proceedings while the trial is ongoing out of respect for the court and its process. We will wait for the verdict before we speak any further. “Right now, our focus is on Callum, Jake and Carter – on honouring them, their memory and seeing the process through.”



The Robinsons have attended every day of the four-week trial, sitting within a few metres of the three men accused of murdering their sons, inside a small, beige courtroom under fluorescent white lights. Related Article Crime Agonising wait for justice for parents of Australian brothers killed in Mexico On Wednesday, the accused sat in bright orange prison jumpsuits with their ankles cuffed to each other, as two police stood behind them. It was initially thought a verdict could be delivered as soon as this week. At Wednesday’s hearing, which lasted less than an hour, the defence opted not to cross-examine two key witnesses: a former girlfriend of alleged ringleader Jesus Gerardo, also known as “El Kekas”, and her son. Both are in witness protection and cannot be identified. No further witnesses are due to appear.



The prosecution alleges the Robinson brothers and Rhoad, all in their early 30s, were killed in a robbery gone wrong in a remote beachside area of Baja California, where they were camping during a surfing holiday. The accused allegedly sought to steal the men’s ute. When the campers tried to defend themselves, the attackers pulled out a gun and shot them before throwing their bodies down a well, the prosecution alleged. Lawyers for the defendants argued there was not enough evidence to prove the three men were involved in the deaths of the Robinson brothers and Rhoad. The girlfriend of El Kekas was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery to steal the tyres off the men’s ute.



El Kekas and the two other accused men, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, have been charged with aggravated homicide, aggravated robbery committed at night, violent robbery and vehicle theft with violence. Prosecutors have asked for 200-year sentences for each of them. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘You’re going to end up like the gringos’: Witness tells court he was threatened to keep quiet after Australian brothers killed in Mexico There is no jury: the verdict will be delivered by a judge alone. He has presided over the trial since the original judge was involved in an accident the weekend before proceedings began. Australian consular staff are providing support to the Robinson family in Ensenada, and it is expected that Australia’s ambassador to Mexico, Crispin Conroy, will travel to the Pacific Coast city for the verdict.
