World.title: ‘He deserves to play’: Roosters sweat on Connor Watson concussion verdict
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘He deserves to play’: Roosters sweat on Connor Watson concussion verdict Christian Nicolussi October 1, 2026 — 4:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Connor Watson will know by Friday if an independent concussion consultant is prepared to allow him to play in the NRL grand final. Watson underwent testing with a specialist on Thursday morning and was due to have further examinations on Thursday night in the hope of being cleared to play against Newcastle in Sunday’s decider. Loading The representative utility had only been on the field for one minute last Friday against the Dolphins when he suffered a concussion. Watson was initially ruled to have displayed category-two symptoms, which was later upgraded to a category-one concussion. That meant Watson was automatically forced to stand down from training and playing for 11 days under the NRL’s concussion protocols, essentially ending his grand final dream.



The Roosters monitored Watson’s condition on Saturday and in the days that followed, and asked the NRL to review the category-one grading in the hope it would be re-classified as a category two, which removes the mandatory 11-day enforced rest. One of the country’s top neurologists, Mark Parsons, stressed the risks involved in rushing Watson back, telling this masthead at the start of the week: “I’d be very surprised if an independent neurologist would clear him.” Connor Watson will know by Friday if he is free to play in the grand final. Getty Images Roosters coach Trent Robinson stressed the decision was in the hands of professionals and said the club would have an answer by Friday at the latest, when the Roosters are due to hold their main training session. Should Watson be ruled out of what would be his final game at the club before he joins St George Illawarra, Robinson said Benaiah Ioelu loomed as the logical “plan B” to be the second dummy-half on the bench.



“He had an appointment this morning that went well, he has another one this afternoon,” Robinson said at the grand final press conference during a fan fest on Thursday in Martin Place. “It’s out of our hands. We’ll get a ruling on that tonight or tomorrow. He’ll either be in or out. It’s pretty simple from our end. Connor Watson gets knocked out on Friday night. Nine “Connor has played his key role in the balance of our team in the middle of a game. He’s really done that well. He’s fit, played multiple positions, and he’s in our 17 every week for a reason. “That’s a really important ‘in’ for us. If he’s out, I’ve got other players who will step in who have played many games and are really clear on their roles.



“Connor, we want him to play, he deserves to play – whether he’s fit to play will get decided by someone else, then we’ll adapt. “I don’t think it would take too much to work our what plan B is. We have some really good hookers. Benaiah Ioelu has played some really good footy for us this year, he brings a lot of energy, and he’ll come into consideration.” James Tedesco leads the Roosters out at Thursday’s Fan Fest in Martin Place. Jessica Hromas/SMH Newcastle skipper Kalyn Ponga is one of Watson’s best friends from their days playing together at the Knights, and said: “He’s one of the hardest-working blokes I know. The injuries he’s had to overcome over the years, the adversity, he’s one of the most deserving blokes to be in a grand final. “His [Roosters teammates] know just how hard he works, how committed and dedicated he is to rugby league.



“If he gets cleared, I’ll be stoked for him. Obviously if he doesn’t, he has to take care of his health first.” One player whose grand final hopes have already been dashed is Phoenix Crossland, the Newcastle hooker who was banned for four matches for a hip-drop tackle on Penrith’s Nathan Cleary last weekend. The Knights made sure Crossland joined the group in Sydney for the last of the media commitments, and coach Justin Holbrook said he would still be named in the No.9 on the team sheet. “It’s been his jersey all year,” Holbrook said. “We love the job he’s done ... I didn’t want to replace that jersey for the last game of the year.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘There is no precedent’: Tennessee fails to execute woman after two doses of lethal injection
World.content:
Graphic content WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty ‘There is no precedent’: Tennessee fails to execute woman after two doses of lethal injection Emily Cochrane and Ann E. Marimow Updated October 1, 2026 — 4:53pm ,first published 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains graphic content Nashville: A Tennessee woman convicted of murder survived two doses of lethal injection on Wednesday night (US time) before state officials suspended the execution and had her taken to a hospital for medical care, her lawyers said. It was the second botched execution in the state this year. This photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction shows Christa Pike in 2023. Tennessee Department of Correction via AP The apparent failure came after duelling court rulings delayed the execution of the woman, Christa Pike, by about nine hours. The state had raced to go ahead with the execution before the day ended and to avoid having to reschedule.



In a pair of emergency legal filings, Pike’s lawyers said while two syringes of pentobarbital, the lethal drug, had been administered, Pike had not lost consciousness. She still had a heartbeat, they said, and was audibly snoring. It was not immediately clear what went wrong with the administration of the drugs, or what Pike’s medical condition was. In a statement late on Wednesday, her lawyers said she was at a nearby hospital but they did not know her condition. Tennessee officials confirmed to a federal judge late on Wednesday that Pike was receiving medical care. Emergency vehicles arrived at the prison shortly after witnesses were escorted out and left about 15 minutes later. AP Photo/George Walker IV “This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre. “There is no precedent.” At a news conference after the execution attempt, members of the media who served as witnesses described Pike as somewhat alert, at one point singing with her spiritual adviser. They were brought into the witness room outside the execution chamber just before 6.30pm. Shortly after, the curtains separating the execution chamber from the witnesses were opened to show Pike, strapped to a gurney, they said.



“I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life,” she said. “And that is with love.” At one point, they said, she described a burning spot in her arm that felt like it was going to burst. She asked if that was normal. The curtains briefly closed, then reopened. ‘This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era.’ Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre The curtains were then closed again for nearly an hour, reporters said, adding that they could hear breathing and steady snoring. Just before 9pm, reporters were told to leave for the news conference. Emergency vehicles arrived at the prison as the witnesses were addressing the news conference and left about 15 minutes later.



Officials at the prison, the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, did not address reporters afterwards. In a statement, the Tennessee Department of Correction said it “had followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general’s office”. “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective,” the department said. Media witnesses leave Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted. AP Photo/George Walker IV It was the second time this year that Tennessee had failed to administer the lethal drugs. In May, the state called off one of four planned executions because medical staff could not find a vein while administering a lethal drug. Pike’s lawyers had argued the procedure could be torturous for her because she has small veins, a history of sexual trauma and other medical conditions.



“We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy,” they said in a joint statement after the execution attempt. Pike, 50, who was convicted of murdering her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, in 1995, would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in more than 200 years. The attempted execution came hours after the US Supreme Court allowed the state to proceed, overturning a pause imposed by a lower court earlier in the day. The lower court briefly paused the execution, saying more time was needed to consider the case. Her lawyers had argued that Pike’s initial legal defence did not adequately present her history of child sexual abuse and neglect. The three liberal justices on the Supreme Court dissented from the order allowing the execution to proceed, with Justice Sonia Sotomayor writing that the majority “unnecessarily prevents” the appeals court from fully considering Pike’s argument. “I see no reason to short-circuit the ordinary process of appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision,” Sotomayor wrote. She was joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.



Sotomayor added that “Tennessee’s desire to expedite Pike’s execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh” Pike’s interest in protecting her own life. In January 1995, Pike, her boyfriend at the time and a friend lured Slemmer into the woods on the University of Tennessee campus, taunting and torturing her. They beat her with asphalt rocks and slashed her with a box carver. Pike, who was 18 then, took a piece of Slemmer’s skull with her, which she showed to at least one other person. Tadaryl Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend at the time, testified to carving a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest, a gesture that sparked fears of Satan worship. Because Tennessee law applies the death penalty only to people 18 and older at the time of the crime, Shipp, at 17, was sentenced to life in prison. He was denied parole last year. Slemmer’s family remained firmly in support of Pike’s execution and raised funds to cover the drive from their home outside of Jacksonville, Florida, to Nashville to witness the execution. May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, was adamant that Pike could not atone for the death of her daughter and should be executed. The lone woman on Tennessee’s death row, Pike has expressed remorse for her crime. She was diagnosed and treated while in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, something which her lawyers said had contributed to her violence. Women who were incarcerated alongside Pike said she was a supportive and kind presence.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Pilot arrested after midair ‘stabbing and crash attempt’, heroes praised for thwarting disaster
World.content:
London: A commercial aircraft flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after issuing an alert that sparked fears of a disaster when one of the two pilots stabbed the other in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the evidence suggested that crew members and passengers prevented a disaster by entering the cockpit and stopping the attacker, in an “extremely serious” security incident. Loading The midair crisis began when flydubai flight FZ1073, carrying 174 people including prominent Sydney businesspeople Steven and Carol Moss, suddenly lost altitude and issued an emergency alert more than two hours into its journey, leading the Israeli government to scramble fighter jets in response. Steven is the son of the late Sam Moss, a Czechosolovakian-born Holocaust survivor who went on to co-found the Katies fashion empire. Carol is the descendant of a famous Rabbi. The couple are major financial supporters of Jewish schools, aged care homes and charities and live in Sydney’s eastern suburbs.



Contacted for comment, Steven Moss said he was struggling after the ordeal and did not wish to speak with the media. Related Article Aviation ‘I grabbed the terrorist’: How hero passengers helped save flight FZ1073 Netanyahu made his televised remarks on Wednesday afternoon in Israel (shortly after 11.30pm AEST) in the first official statement on the attacks by the Israeli government after hours of speculation about whether the incident was a hijacking, an altercation between pilots or a brutal attempt to kill all on board. “I salute the heroes who demonstrated resourcefulness and extraordinary courage,” Netanyahu said. “They saved many lives and averted a terrible disaster. The pilot who committed the stabbing has been arrested and is currently being interrogated by Saudi authorities.”



More details emerged after the passengers arrived safely in Tel Aviv on Wednesday night (about 1.45am Thursday AEST) on a second flydubai flight, which carried them from the emergency landing site in Saudi Arabia. The plane’s captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, unlocked the cockpit door to let passengers in. Netanyahu spoke to a passenger and officials who told him one of the pilots stabbed the other and apparently tried to crash the aircraft. At least one passenger joined a crew member in breaking into the cockpit to stop the pilot attempting to damage the plane. Another crew member then joined them and managed to stabilise the aircraft, he said. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said the attempted attack “was thwarted solely thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers who stormed the cockpit, subdued the terrorist, and – with their own hands – restored control of the aircraft to an additional flight crew present on board”.



“According to our preliminary information, the terrorist had a single objective: to crash the plane,” Katz said in a statement. Public flight radar sites showed that the Boeing 737 MAX was diverted to Saudi Arabia and landed about 90 minutes after a shocking plunge in altitude, with passengers describing “blood in the cockpit” after the fight on board. Israeli media cited unnamed officials who said there was a “growing assessment” that the emergency had been intended as an act of terror. Other options were also being looked into, including the possibility of a mental health episode. Passenger Almog Italie told Reuters it felt like the plane was passing through “massive turbulence” before he realised a life-or-death struggle had unfolded in the cockpit.



View post on X “It was dropping like for 20, 30 seconds, and then balanced, and then started dropping again, and balanced again, and then we saw that [there] are people in the front, directly [in front of] the cockpit,” he said. Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister’s office, said the wounded captain – identified as Captain Smit Machchhar – had drawn on “the last moments of his energy” as he lay bloodied on the floor to click open the release on the cockpit door. “At that moment, some of the passengers that realised something was happening raced forward [and] entered the pilot’s cabin. They saw the injured pilot on the ground, and the other … the attacking pilot was standing over the control panel, bashing the control panel,” he said. A photo purportedly showing one of the passengers on flydubai FZ1073 with blood on his shirt. Amichai Stein/Twitter



Netanyahu said on X that, “despite being stabbed and seriously injured, [Machchhar] fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster … He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.” One passenger, in a text message to Israeli media network Channel 12 that was reported by The Times of Israel and other outlets, said: “We heard screams on the plane.” “Then they opened the cockpit and we saw blood, and someone had stabbed the pilot with a pocketknife.” In a video shared by one person on the flight, the captain is covered in blood as some passengers support him and praise him for saving the aircraft from disaster. A second member of the crew, possibly the other pilot, is seen tied up nearby and apparently unconscious. The aircraft departed Dubai at 7.05am local time on Wednesday (1.05pm AEST) and initially flew over the southern part of the Persian Gulf before crossing over Saudi Arabia and heading towards Israel.



Loading Fluctuations in its altitude began about two hours into the trip, according to Flightradar24. The plane then dropped 14,000 feet (4300 metres) in less than 30 seconds. Authorities first became aware of the unfolding crisis when the aircraft issued a 7700 “squawk” code to signal an international emergency about 2½ hours into the flight, before changing this to a 7500 code to signal a hijacking or unlawful interference. Netanyahu called urgent meetings to monitor the emergency. The emergency lasted for the next 90 minutes before it turned out of Jordanian airspace and landed at Tabuk, a city in the far west of Saudi Arabia. A replacement plane carrying passengers from the earlier flight left Saudi Arabia and landed at Ben Gurion International Airport in Israel on Wednesday night to cheers and a crowd waving Israeli flags.



Passengers arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit Israeli journalist Amichai Stein reported an account of the emergency from those on board and posted images of one passenger with a blood-stained shirt. “We heard screams and saw blood,” one passenger said, according to Stein. “The pilot was stabbed. There were moments when we thought we weren’t going to make it out alive.” The Israeli media said authorities were planning to question the crew and inspect the aircraft as part of an investigation. People celebrate the arrival of the replacement aircraft in Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit



A passenger called Yaniv met Netanyahu after the passengers made it to Tel Aviv, and he told the prime minister how he had forced his way into the cockpit to stop the attack. In a discussion posted on social media, Yaniv described how he had “pulled the yoke up” on the aircraft’s controls to bring the plane out of its steep dive. The pilot who suffered the knife attack was able to open the cockpit door even though he was wounded, allowing passengers and crew to come to his aid and prevent a disaster. A passenger called Daniel told Israeli media outlet Channel 12, in remarks reported by The Times of Israel, that he had seen a struggle in the cockpit and an attempt to push someone out. View post on X



“Then three Israelis who were sitting behind me came to see what was happening, and the plane suddenly went into a very steep dive, nose down, with a very intense spin,” he said. “The spinning stopped. It took some — I don’t know, it felt like an eternity, but I think it was two minutes, at least two or three minutes, during which the plane was simply diving and spinning like crazy. “It felt like, that’s it. It’s over. September 11 is happening again.” Israeli airspace was briefly closed during the emergency. Budget airline flydubai is owned by Dubai. iStock



After the passengers made it to Tel Aviv on the second aircraft, Israeli authorities said one 51-year-old male passenger with a mild upper body wound was transported to a hospital. Of the 174 passengers on Flight FZ1073, the media said 166 were Israelis. Flydubai says flights to and from Israel will be suspended while an investigation continues into the pilot attack. World.title: Critica adds global commodities clout to board
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Critica adds global commodities clout to board Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 1, 2026 — 4:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Critica has appointed seasoned global commodities executive Hannah Badenach to its board in a move that looks to be less about finding minerals and more about selling them. The appointment comes as the company pushes both of its key critical minerals projects towards commercial reality. The Hong Kong-based specialist brings more than 20 years of experience in commodity trading, marketing, offtake and financing, particularly in tin, tungsten and rare earths, exactly the suite of commodities in Critica’s portfolio. Critica has appointed global commodities executive Hannah Badenach to its board. Ms Badenach’s resume seems tailor-made for the challenge. She previously spent 13 years at global commodity trader Noble Resources, where her most recent role was executive director, Metals & Mongolia. In that position, she managed international trading activities and negotiated marketing, offtake, financing and prepayment arrangements. Her board experience also spans several listed and private resources companies, including Peak Rare Earths, Materra Metals and Xanadu Mines.



‘As we advance Mt Lindsay and Jupiter, her commercial expertise and experience building commodity supply chains will be invaluable.’ Critica Limited chairman Tim Lindley In a strong show of alignment, Ms Badenach intends to receive her non-executive director fees in equity, subject to shareholder approval. The appointment is effective from October 1st, with current director Jamie Byrde set to resign from the board on October 26th. Critica chairman Tim Lindley said: “We are delighted to welcome a Director of Hannah’s calibre to the Critica Board. Hannah has traded the commodities we intend to produce. She has a deep understanding of the tungsten, tin and rare earths markets and, importantly, the commercial mechanisms that protect and enhance shareholder value, from offtake structuring and pricing to prepayment, project financing and supply chain development.” Her appointment looks particularly timely given the company’s recent run of form. Just last week, a new scoping study for its Mt Lindsay tin-tungsten project in Tasmania delivered in spades, modelling a whopping pre-tax net present value of $1.42 billion and featuring an eye-catching 64.9 per cent internal rate of return. The study forecasts pre-production capital at a modest $244.5 million. Mt Lindsay isn’t Critica’s only project rounding the corner towards commercialisation. The company recently produced its first high-purity mixed rare earth oxide sample from its Jupiter project in WA, grading a stellar 98.2 per cent total rare earth oxides. Critica says the sample, which contains a high concentration of valuable magnet rare earths, will now be put in front of strategic partners to kick off offtake discussions.



The market backdrop for Critica’s key commodities adds another layer of intrigue. Western tungsten markets remain tight, with an S&P Global report pointing to a sizeable ex-China supply gap. At the same time, China’s export controls and US defence procurement restrictions are expected to impact the supply of rare earths, making tungsten and rare earths commercial expertise particularly relevant as Western customers seek secure sources. With a billion-dollar study now on the table for Mt Lindsay and its first saleable product samples emerging from Jupiter, Critica seems to be firing on both cylinders. Appointing a commercial heavyweight such as Badenach, whose remuneration is tied directly to share price growth, looks like a calculated move to turn impressive study numbers and high-grade samples into binding offtake deals. World.title: A terrifying plunge, loud screams, blood everywhere: How flight FZ1073 unfolded, moment by moment
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was a routine daily flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. But on Wednesday, two hours into the short journey, flight FZ1073 rapidly turned to chaos. Screams filled the cabin as 174 passengers plunged 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds. Crew members called for help. A distress signal was sent. Passengers stormed the cockpit – usually locked, if not for some quick thinking by a pilot close to losing consciousness after apparently being stabbed by his co-pilot – to find blood everywhere. Here is what we know about how the flight unfolded. September 30, 7.05am (Dubai time) After a 20-minute delay, flydubai flight FZ1073 departs Dubai International Airport, bound for Tel Aviv, Israel. The three-year-old Boeing 737 MAX 8 climbs to a cruising altitude of 34,000 feet. 9.21am: A terrifying rapid plunge



Two hours and 16 minutes into the flight, which typically takes about 3½ hours, FZ1073 plummets. According to data captured by flightradar24, it plunges more than 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds. “Suddenly, the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down like a massive G-force,” passenger Almog Itali told BBC’s Newsnight. Loading A sharp ascent follows, but the plane abruptly drops again. It’s at this point that people rush to the cockpit, according to Itali. About three or four passengers subdue the co-pilot, acquiring minor injuries in the process. An Israeli passenger said the crew asked passengers for help, and passengers helped tie down the co-pilot after tackling him. “They are very brave. They literally saved our lives,” Itali said. According to Yasmin Abukasis, whose daughter Miriam was on the flight, a man holding a knife had forced one of the pilots onto the floor. Blood was everywhere, and loud screams could be heard.



‘Thrown around the cabin’ In total, the aircraft falls 17,350 feet, going from 34,000 feet to 16,650 feet in two minutes. The safest passengers during this erratic change in altitude would have been those seated with their seatbelts securely fastened, says Dr Salim Hijazeen, a lecturer in aviation at Swinburne University of Technology. When Singapore Airlines flight SQ321 dropped 178 feet in 4.6 seconds and a total 6000 feet in three minutes, in May 2024, British passenger Geoff Kitchen, 73, suffered a cardiac arrest and died. His wife, Linda, sustained a head wound and spinal fractures in the incident. “Those rapid changes in movement are what could cause passengers to be lifted from their seats or thrown around the cabin,” Hijazeen said. “It would have been absolutely terrifying.”



9.28am: First emergency alert issued The aircraft issues an emergency alert signal, known as a “squawk 7700”, as it flies along the Jordan-Saudi Arabia border. Related Article Updated

Aviation Pilot arrested after midair ‘stabbing and crash attempt’, heroes praised for thwarting disaster A squawk 7700 is an internationally standardised code that indicates a “general emergency”, which could be anything from engine failure to a severe medical crisis. It automatically highlights the aircraft on air traffic control’s radar, making it priority. If needed, air traffic control will clear surrounding airspace to get the aircraft to the nearest runway. The code is discrete – no verbal radio call is necessary as it’s transmitted directly through the aircraft transponder when the pilot types in the four digits directly. Passengers take control



After the altitude stabilises at about 15,000 feet, a second emergency alert – a squawk 7500, meaning “unlawful interference” – is sent, sparking fears of a hijacking. The aircraft turns west and briefly enters Jordanian airspace, then turns 180 degrees back towards Saudi Arabia, flying south-west in the direction of Tabuk. Passenger Yaniv Hayoun, with blood on his shirt after subduing the attacker. X/@AmichaiStein1 An unnamed passenger later tells the Jerusalem Post that two other passengers seated at the back of the plane were off-duty pilots. “I shouted at them to run and take control of the plane,” the passenger said. The injured pilot – identified as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar – received life-saving care from a dentist on board, the passenger said. 9.44am: Plans for emergency landing

World.title: Teacher allegedly raped Newington student during Great Barrier Reef trip
World.content:
A Newington College teacher allegedly raped a student during an interstate trip and sexually assaulted him during school hours on or near the inner west campus, court documents reveal. Deandra Kontou, 32, was last week charged with nine child abuse offences, including aggravated sexual assault, four counts of sexual assault, and using an electronic device to groom her victim. Deandra Kontou allegedly raped the student during a school trip to the Great Barrier Reef. She went by her maiden name, Haralambidis, while teaching at the prestigious private school. The alleged abuse spanned six months and began with Kontou allegedly showing the boy indecent material, intending to make it easier to “procure the child for unlawful sexual activity”, according to court documents.



Over the next month, Kontou allegedly began grooming the boy through messages, twice coerced him to sexually touch and carry out a sex act on her without his consent and twice sexually touched him. Each of these offences occurred in Stanmore, where the school is located, and during school hours. Teacher Deandra Kontou in a staff school photo taken this year. A few months later, the abuse allegedly continued on a senior boys’ camp at Fitzroy Island, on the Great Barrier Reef. There, Kontou is accused of twice sexually touching the child during the day before sexually assaulting him between 10pm and 11pm at night. Most of the sexual offences are categorised as aggravated as Kontou was the child’s teacher. Research trips to the Great Barrier Reef, where students are exposed to the reef’s unique marine life and ecosystems, are not uncommon among Sydney’s private schools.



Kontou was moved on by Newington shortly after the Fitzroy Island camp, once the allegation was conveyed to college staff. She was arrested last Monday and appeared before Sutherland Local Court that day. She was granted bail on the condition she reported to police daily, surrender her passport and not contact the alleged victim or witnesses. The court also barred her from entering any school grounds, teaching children and being in the company of a child without the child’s parent or guardian. Kontou taught for two years at Newington and led a year 7 mentorship group. Parents in Kontou’s mentorship class were told she was on an “approved leave of absence”, days after the allegation was made to college staff.



The leave announcement followed days of confusion from parents, who contacted Newington’s head of year 7 after Kontou failed to return to campus after the school trip. “Mrs Haralambidis [Kontou] will not be responding to emails and will appreciate respect for her privacy,” Newington’s head of year 7 told parents enquiring about her prolonged absence, in an email soon after the trip. “Please do not hesitate to communicate with me any issues or concerns regarding the boys … the boys will continue to be supported in the Newington way.” Kontou began permanent work at Georges River College Senior Campus in Oatley in 2024 after a string of casual jobs, where she taught society and culture, history and geography until she was arrested in her Sutherland home last week. Deputy Premier and Education Minister Prue Car has ordered an urgent review into the Education Department’s hiring of Kontou at the Oatley school in 2024. The review is expected to examine any correspondence between the police and the Education Department before Kontou was hired, and any issues raised about her character in the recruitment process.



The review was ongoing as of Thursday afternoon, and may involve interviews with staff from the Oatley campus, who are on school holidays until the end of next week. The NSW Education Standards Authority has revoked her accreditation while she is banned from teaching children and entering schools. She remained on the public payroll until Wednesday morning, when Education Department officials suspended her without pay after accessing her charge sheet and bail conditions. The charges Kontou faces don’t relate to her time at the Oatley school, and she is not accused of any criminal wrongdoing while employed by the Department of Education over the past two years. Georges River College Senior Campus principal Anna Girginis encouraged students to seek counselling and contact professional hotlines while their former teacher confronts the offences. She called pupil care wellbeing the school’s “highest priorities” in a letter to parents on Wednesday afternoon. Girginis didn’t address in the letter whether the school was aware of the police investigation when Kontou was hired or over the course of her employment.



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Massage therapist jailed for more than 11 years on sexual offence charges
World.content:
A Christchurch massage therapist convicted of sexually offending against 15 women has been jailed for more than 11 years.

Neil Yardeni was sentenced in the Christchurch District Court on Thursday on 21 charges including rape, sexual violation and indecent assault, as well as two charges of making an intimate visual recording.

The offending happened between 2015 and 2022 at the 55-year-old's therapeutic massage practice at his home.

The women, who were all clients, described the offending as horrific, disgusting and violating, and told the court of the ongoing impact it had had on them.

In a victim impact statement, one woman said the assault had affected her relationships, her ability to trust, and her ability to feel comfortable alone in a room with a professional.

She said she had lived with shame, anger, guilt and trauma.

"This man was physically and mentally assaulting people in a small suburb of Christchurch out of his home advertising his business, as if it was completely normal to rape and sexually assault others," she said.

"He filmed his unknowing clients, planned to perform indecent acts in a calculating and revolting manner."

Another woman said she remembered lying on the massage bed feeling completely terrified and paralysed.

"I felt stripped of my humanity and dignity... the whole massage I was trying to convince myself to get up and leave but I was too frightened to move in case he got violent," she said.

"I came to this massage looking for a reprieve during a very stressful period of my life. Instead I left with more trauma to carry. I experienced feelings of shame, embarrassment and confusion after."

Judge Jane Farish told Yardeni his offending was a gross abuse of trust.

"You repeatedly exploited women who attended your practice seeking treatment, relief from pain and professional assistance, using your position to sexually offend against them for your own gratification," she said.

The impact on the victims was and continued to be significant, Farish said.

"All of the victims were courageous to have not only come forward but to persevere with dignity and composure whilst giving their evidence in what was and is an extremely stressful environment."

Yardeni's trial commenced in June 2026 and he was found guilty by a jury on 21 charges.

He was found not guilty on three other charges of indecent assault.

"The jury in reaching their guilty verdicts rejected your various defences of accidental touching, consent or a belief in consent on your behalf and in one point the suggestion the complainant had fantasized," Farish said.

Crown prosecutor Penny Brown said Yardeni continued to deny the offending.

"He has demonstrated no insight, and demonstrated no acknowledgement of the harm he has caused, that's despite sitting through a lengthy trial where we heard from 15 victims," she said.

Defence lawyer Josh Lucas said Yardeni had no previous convictions and would benefit from rehabilitation.

"He's going to address what led him down this path," Lucas said.

World.title: NZ fishing guides call for cap on number of seasonal Australian guides
World.content:
Audio player for " Concern FIFO Aussie fishing guides taking business from locals " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/environment/1673685%2Fnz-fishing-guides-call-for-cap-on-number-of-seasonal-australian-guides

Concern FIFO Aussie fishing guides taking business from locals Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Australian fishing guides are crowding out locals, says the New Zealand Professional Guides Association, and a new license is needed.

Association president Dean Bell told Checkpoint Australian guides were coming to stay for about three to four months in the summer, and operate through a social license with New Zealand recreational anglers.

He said it was a "numbers game" and New Zealand's resources were finite.

"There's a limited number of fishable rivers and in that a limited number of trout. These trout are only catchable for certain periods and they'll stop feeding."

That's led the association to call for an "effective guides license" and a serious look at capping the number of guides in the country.

"We would make it that you would have to pay tax in New Zealand to start with, the Australian guides coming in through a tax arrangement do not have to pay any GST or tax in New Zealand."

Bell said Minister for Hunting and Fishing James Meager has said the closer economic relations agreement with Australia means the guides can work in New Zealand.

"Currently he's correct on that but that's also not reciprocated for New Zealanders wanting to go and guide in Australia," Bell said.

He said regulations for fishing in Australia varied state by state which made it difficult in some regions for New Zealanders to "just rock up" and start guiding.

In a statement to Checkpoint, Meager said he was not considering a guide's license because not enough evidence had been given to show one was needed.

He encouraged interested parties to develop the case, including Fish and Game, though said he was yet to see any material for it.

Meager also said New Zealand and Australia have a long-standing trade agreement and that means citizens of both countries can work as nationals in either one.

World.title: Liquidators start court proceedings against SolarZero directors
World.content:
The liquidators of collapsed solar power company solarZero have launched High Court proceedings against four former directors, alleging decisions made before the company's collapse left creditors facing significant losses.

Liquidators Adele Hicks and Malcolm Moore, of Grant Thornton New Zealand, said proceedings had been filed against four former directors of Lunar Infinity Limited, formerly known as solarZero.

The liquidators allege the directors breached duties under sections 135, 136 and 137 of the Companies Act, covering reckless trading, incurring obligations a company cannot meet, and directors' duties of care, diligence and skill.

The liquidators say the claims relate to decisions made before the company was placed into liquidation in November 2024.

"The company benefited from significant public and private investment and left creditors with substantial losses, so it's important to pursue those claims and maximise any potential recovery available," Hicks said.

The liquidators said they had undertaken an extensive investigation of the company's financial position, governance records, financing arrangements and related transactions before deciding to commence proceedings.

The allegations have not been tested in court and the defendants are entitled to respond.

The liquidators have not identified the four former directors named in the proceedings.

When the company went into liquidation, Companies Office records show the directors of Lunar Infinity Limited, formerly solarZero, were Andrew Booth, Simon McIver, Charles Rid and Valerie Speth.

SolarZero was one of New Zealand's largest residential solar businesses, providing rooftop solar and battery systems under long-term subscription-style contracts. The company collapsed in late 2024.

The liquidators' most recent report identified BlackRock Inc, the world's largest asset manager, as the ultimate parent of the group at the time of the collapse.

It said investigations into the collapse included reviewing the group's trading performance, solvency, the actions of directors and management, and transactions that might produce recoveries for creditors.

The report said a number of potential claims had been identified.

The liquidators said creditors yet to be adjudicated are owed an estimated $476 million. Any money recovered through the proceedings would be distributed in accordance with the Companies Act.

Companies Office records show the company was known as Lunar Infinity Limited at the time the proceedings were filed.

"Following an extensive investigation into the company's financial position, governance records, financing arrangements and related transactions, we have concluded it is appropriate to commence proceedings.

World.title: NZ First gets $161,000 boost from anonymous donors, latest Electoral Commission disclosure shows
World.content:
NZ First has received $161,000 in large anonymous donations within the last three months.

The money was given to the party through the "protected from disclosure" scheme, which shrouds donors' identities in secrecy.

The donations are within the rules and were revealed by the Electoral Commission in a new disclosure on Thursday afternoon.

While NZ First got the biggest boost from large secret donors, bringing its annual total to $173,162, National still has by far the most from this source with $346,160.

The latest update shows National received another $30,000 and ACT $15,000 since the last update by the commission.

With one quarter still to be reported, 'protected from disclosure' donations of $629,322 this year have exceeded 2023's total by more than a quarter of a million dollars.

The scheme allows donors to give up to $61,425 per party during this election cycle through the protected from disclosure scheme without public scrutiny. The donations are funnelled to political parties by the Electoral Commission to keep the donor's identity secret.

Donors need to confirm they are based in New Zealand but don't have to explain why they want to donate in secrecy.

They are banned by law from telling anybody - including the recipient - that they have donated, or even that they intend to. Breaching this rule can result in a $10,000 penalty.

Other methods of donating require the public disclosure of donors who have given more than $6000. If a donor wants to remain hidden from the party as well as the public the most they can donate is $1500, unless they use the "protected from disclosure" channel.

Prior to 2026, donations to NZ First through this mechanism were smaller. In 2023, the party received just $5000, however it did receive $88,628 in 2017 and $61,822 in 2020.

The latest donation boost came via three donations of $51,160, $50,000 and $15,000.

Since the scheme was introduced in 2008 Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori have not received any donations of this type.

A recommendation to abolish the scheme was put forward by an Independent Electoral Review in 2023.

In August, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith told RNZ numerous recommendations were made in the review's final report, which the government considered.

"Abolishing protected disclosure donations is not a priority, just as it wasn't for the previous Labour Government either."

Professor Andrew Geddis, from the University of Otago law faculty and Transparency International New Zealand executive director Julie Haggie have previously told RNZ they believe the recommendation should be revisited.

"I do think that the current way we're funding our political parties is very problematic. I think that it is undermining a certain degree of trust and confidence in the way our political processes work."

Opportunity party, which has received $70,000 in protected from disclosure donations this year, is campaigning on a policy to "clean up politics". It aims to ban "pass-though arrangements" and says this policy is a bottom line for a coalition agreement.

World.title: Homicide investigation launched after man dies in Glen Innes incident
World.content:
A homicide investigation has been launched after the death of a man in Glen Innes on Thursday afternoon.

Acting Detective Inspector Craig Bolton said Police were called to Sunnymead Road at around 2.45pm with reports that a person had been critically injured.

"Police quickly attended and sadly, despite best efforts by emergency services, a man was pronounced deceased at the scene.

"One person was swiftly taken into custody and is assisting Police with enquiries."

The Tamaki Regeneration Company confirmed the incident occurred at a Tamaki Housing property.

The company said it was working with police and whānau.

St Johns responded with one ambulance, one rapid response vehicle and one operations manager.

A scene guard was established and cordons were put in place.

Jessica Hopkins/RNZ

Police said there is not believed to be any risk to the wider public.

"Police recognise the impact an incident of this nature has on the community, and we want to reassure residents that support is being provided to the family of the deceased and those in the wider community.

"Staff will also be conducting reassurance patrols in the coming days," Bolton says.

A nearby liquor store owner says he saw about a dozen police cars in the vicinity of Sunnymeas Road, Fenchurch Street and Taniwha Street.

He says it's not great for the community, as just last year, a man who came off a bus outside his shop on Fenchurch Street had been stabbed, and later died.

World.title: Bikepackers to take on 'ridiculous looking ride' to the six corners of Golden Bay
World.content:
Bikepacking enthusiasts will gather in Golden Bay this weekend to take on a gruelling challenge that takes riders to remote coastlines and through national parks on a mix of sealed and gravel roads.

Participants have to connect six points - the northern tip of the South Island at Cape Farewell, Brown Hut at the start of the Heaphy Track, the Anatori River on the West Coast, Tōtaranui Beach in the Abel Tasman, the Rameka Track at the top of the Tākaka Hill & Trilobite Hut in the Cobb Valley - in 36 hours.

Brian Alder was living in Golden Bay when he came up with the idea for the Six Corners Challenge. Inspired by a similar road race that traversed the corners of the bay by road, he mapped out what it would look like to ride on unpaved roads, to the far reaches of the region.

The course covers roughly 450 kilometres, with around 6500 metres of elevation gain.

Map showing the points on the Six Corners Cycling Challenge. Supplied

Alder and a handful of other riders first set out to give it a go in 2017.

It was like, 'oh, yeah, this works, it's about the right distance, it's quite challenging, but it's doable'," he said.

Almost 10 years on, the challenge is still going strong. Riders aren't allowed any assistance and must be fully self sufficient. There's no registration, no entry fee and no official tracking unless a rider chooses to submit proof they've fully completed it.

Alder said it took riders into remote, scenic places that many people wouldn't otherwise visit.

"I think some of the rides, especially down the West Coast to Anatori and up the Cobb Road into the head of the Tākaka River are particularly amazing pieces of road through National Parks and some of the best riding in the country I would argue."

With no set order for the points to be completed in, he said the magic of the event was in seeing different people cycling in all different directions and not knowing how much of it they had completed.

"One of the nice things about it is you can turn up and be invisible and completely do your own thing and go home again. Some people love that, they just have their own personal challenge and it's not for anyone else to know about."

Totaranui Beach in the Abel Tasman National Park. AFP

In recent years, the number of people taking part has grown to around 80. Around 20 percent each year make it to all six corners.

Wellingtonian Jim Ashley didn't know about the challenge until he saw it pop up on Strava.

"I saw a friend of mine had ridden this ridiculous looking ride, about 450 kilometres and it took him 24 hours and I didn't realise it was an event, I thought he was just a bit nuts and had gone out and ridden this ridiculous looking course by himself."

When Ashley noticed some of Brian's other adventures, like Tour Te Waipounamu, a bikepacking race the length of New Zealand, he realised Six Corners was an organised event and he said he was "absolutely keen to give it a go".

Ashley currently holds the record for the fastest time on Six Corners, completing it in 20 hours and 21 minutes in 2024.

"It got pretty hard, towards the tail end I was starting to get quite hungry, it was 2 or 3 o'clock in the morning and there were very few resupply points and I was running out of food and I was ready to finish."

Riders will have to tackle the Tākaka Hill to get to the Rameka Track. RNZ/ Tracy Neal

He said because each of the corners required cycling out and back on the same road, you often saw other riders.

"You can see the people you're riding with and you get a wave from your competitors as you're going past. There's quite a lot of solidarity there, which is a really nice aspect of the race and it's not something you experience when you're doing the big, long point-to-point rides."

Karen Le Sueur was living in Wellington when her husband suggested they give the Six Corners Challenge a go.

Her first attempt, back in 2020, was in terrible weather.

"I had a really good first half but in the second half, the rain hit and it was biblical, torrential, West Coast Golden Bay kinda rain and my jacket leaked like a sieve and I was having some knee problems so I ended up pulling out after four corners."

It didn't put her off, she went on to complete it in 2021, and then again when she set the record in 2023 as the fastest woman to complete the challenge in 27 hours and 39 minutes.

"The beauty of the event is it's about the challenge, but it's also about the camaraderie and the social side of things... it's free, you do as many or as little corners as you like, it's completely a personal challenge."

Tākaka Hill. RNZ / Tracy Neal

The event will be Dave Schaper's first attempt at bikepacking after he heard about it from a friend.

"I've been to all six corners, but definitely not on a bike and it's a little bit daunting, driving to some of those six corners is a really long drive so I'm not sure what it will be like to do it under my own steam."

He's expecting it to be type two fun, enjoyable in retrospect.

"It's not like closed roads, you register and here's your bib number, it's people who are interested and want to have a go and that's part of the appeal as well.

"There's a little bit less pressure. It's not a race, it's an adventure and to see how far you can personally go."

World.title: World War I medals of Far North soldier uncovered in Christchurch
World.content:
Police are trying to track down relatives of a Far North soldier after his World War I medals were discovered during a search in Christchurch.

Detective Sergeant Jason Hunuki said officers found Private Victor Powell's medals while they were executing a search warrant on an unrelated matter.

With the help of the organisation Medals Reunited New Zealand, police learned Powell was born in 1892 in the Far North and enlisted in 1916.

He was sent to Egypt with the 12th Reinforcements as part of the 1st Battalion, Auckland Infantry Regiment, and later killed in action in France.

He was just 25 years old.

Private Victor Powell was born in the Far North in 1892 and died in action during World War I. SUPPLIED/POLICE

Powell's name is inscribed on the Herekino War Memorial, in a remote part of the Far North's west coast.

He was also remembered in the Hall of Memories at the Auckland War Memorial Museum.

Hunuki said police wanted to return the medals to Powell's relatives.

Private Victor Powell is thought to have been born in Herekino, a remote Far North settlement next to a harbour of the same name. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

He said the medals were an important part of New Zealand history - but they would mean even more to Powell's family.

If his family could not be found the medals would be sent to the National Army Museum in Waiouru.

It was not clear how the medals ended up in Christchurch, almost at the other end of the country.

World.title: Federal Court rules against challenge to SA government's golf course plans
World.content:
Two South Australians have failed in a bid to stop the felling of trees as part of the North Adelaide golf course redevelopment.

Public servant Edwin Kemp Attrill and Kaurna Arabana woman Janette Milera brought the action against the State Government in the Federal Court earlier this year arguing the redevelopment was in breach of federal conservation laws.

The Federal Court trial heard last month that 400 trees had been cut down to date, with the government previously saying 585 would ultimately go.

In reading out a summary of her judgement, Justice Natalie Charlesworth said there was evidence brought before the court during the trial that “more than 70,000 trees will remain” in the Adelaide Parklands.

“The evidence showed that there remained a very large number of trees in the project site and in the parklands,” she said.

“I’m not satisfied that the depletion, or proposed future depletion, is such that it has had, will have or is likely to have significant impact on species.”

Justice Charlesworth added that during the proceedings the government did not diminish the importance of the parklands for the Kaurna people, and that the court's findings shouldn’t be viewed that way.

"Nothing in the findings should be understood as diminishing the significance of the parklands for the Kaurna people – that … was not disputed by the respondent," she said.

Justice Charlesworth ordered that lawyers for the government inform the court by October 22 if they wished to file an order for costs against Mr Kemp Attril and Ms Milera.

Mr Kemp Attrill and Ms Milera have 28 days to file an appeal against the decision.

Justice Charlesworth ordered that the injunction on the works at the North Adelaide golf course lift immediately despite the 28-day appeal period.

World.title: From tattoos to blue sausages, Newcastle has gone 'Knights crazy'
World.content:
It's been 25 years since the Newcastle Knights last played in an NRL grand final, and Newcastle has not forgotten how to celebrate.

From fresh tattoos to blue sausages, the city is going all out ahead of the decider against the Sydney Roosters on Sunday.

Tattoo artist Dave Ross cancelled all his appointments this week to make space for footy fans itching to get one of his limited-edition Knights tattoos.

"It's just been insane, like nothing I could ever imagine," he said.

Local tattoo artist Dave Ross says he is fully booked out with Newcastle Knights fans lining up to get commemorative tattoos. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

"I get to spend the week tattooing Knights designs on all these diehard fans … it's been incredible."

Fifteen more tattoos have been booked in for later this week, with Mr Ross staying back until 9pm to get them done.

Lifelong supporter Sam Mawer decided to get a tattoo after the team made it to the grand final.

Sam Mawer got a tattoo with the Knights' slogan: "Defend the kingdom." (ABC Newcastle: Keely Johnson)

"I'm a Knights tragic … I didn't think we would happen again in my lifetime," he said.

"I'm getting it on the back of my calf so I can look down every now and then and hopefully have fond memories of the grand final."

On the cusp of their first premiership in 25 years, local tattoo shops have jumped on the Newcastle Knights bandwagon. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

Armidale man Dave Battese got inked live on the radio to win tickets to the Knights' last grand final match against the Parramatta Eels in 2001.

"People were cringing because you could literally hear the tattoo gun bouncing on my skull," he said.

"I was making jokes about how this is nothing [compared] to the pain that Newcastle are going to put on Parramatta."

Dave Battese says he's proudly worn his Knights tattoos for 25 years. (Supplied: Dave Battese)

Mr Battese said he's proudly displayed his tattoos for 25 years, including through five wooden spoon seasons, and hopes he can add a fresh tattoo this year to celebrate a third premiership.

Blue and red food

Other Newcastle businesses have jumped on the bandwagon, including a butcher creating a blue sausage.

"It's a pork sausage and just added a little bit of food dye," manager Johnny Emeny said.

"We just wanted to get behind our mighty boys as they get to this grand final and no better way than throwing a few blue sausages on the barbecue," he said.

Johnny Emeny says he enjoys getting creative by making blue sausages. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

" The whole town has just gone Knights crazy. "

Since Monday, homes and businesses across the Hunter have been painted red and blue in support of the team.

Other Knights-themed foods like blue burgers in pubs and blue-and-red ice cream have also popped up around town.

A Newcastle pub is selling a blue burger with red sauce to support the Knights. (ABC Newcastle: Keely Johnson)

The original Knight

Like many Novocastrians, Cliff Parker remembers exactly where he was when the Knights won their first grand final in 1997.

Dressed in a suit of shining armour, Mr Parker and his trusty horse Rocky led the Knights team bus back through the city after their win against Manly.

Loading...

"It was absolutely mad … I could not believe the amount of people lining the streets," Mr Parker said.

"I was riding up and down in the crowd, and they were going nuts."

For 25 years, Cliff Parker was the Newcastle Knights' mascot on horseback at the team's home games. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

For 25 years, Mr Parker and Rocky were the team's mascot, the Newcastle Knight, riding along the sidelines at home games to hype up the crowd before kick-off.

But no-one ever knew the identity of the mysterious armoured crusader.

"No-one ever knew me as Cliff by name," said Mr Parker.

"Rocky was definitely the more famous one."

Sammy Pistolas wears the original suit that his dad, Chris Kelly, wore as the Newcastle Knights' mascot, Sir Rusty. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

Another iconic mascot at Knights home games was Sir Rusty, portrayed by Chris Kelly.

"Dad would ride around the ground on a quad bike as Sir Rusty and have fun with the crowd … just goofing off," Mr Kelly's son, Sammy Pistolas, said.

For this final, Mr Pistolas is supporting the team by tattooing Knights fans in the original Sir Rusty costume.

"I think my Mum made it … the body piece is from the 1997 grand final, and the head piece is from the 2001 grand final," he said.

World.title: Chris Fagan steps down from Brisbane Lions
World.content:
Chris Fagan has told the Brisbane Lions he is stepping down as coach following the club's third-straight AFL premiership success.

The 65-year-old led Brisbane to a stunning 14.12 (96) to 12.17 (89) victory against Fremantle on Saturday, a win that he hailed as the best moment he experienced in his time at the club.

However, he told the club he wanted to step away from the final year of his contract to be closer to his family.

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. Chris Fagan took a weary Brisbane Lions side from the bottom right to the very top of the AFL Before we leave you, don't forget to check out this piece from the ABC Brisbane team on the legacy of Chris Fagan at the Lions. Chris Fagan headed the ultimate Lions reawakening And that's the end of the press conference Thanks very much for joining us there, folks. And congratulations to Chris Fagan on a stunning career as Lions coach. I daresay there will be plenty of Melbourne-based clubs interested in seeing what he has to say when he gets down there about how he turned such a struggling club around. 'We'll be backing whoever is taking over' Andrews admits that he was one of the players who didn't know Fagan's name before he came in. But he says that he was very impressed that he tried to get a sense of "the lay of the land" before he started, asking the individually players three questions in a Gabba meeting before he took charge. That being said, the players are fully committed to the next coach when he comes in. "We'll be backing whoever is taking over," Andrews says. Show more

"I've been thinking about this for some time and I'm comfortable that now is the right time for [my wife] Ursula and I to return to Melbourne," Fagan said in a statement.

"Telling the players and football staff today was one of the hardest things I've done in my life.

"Together, we have been on a mission to make the Lions the most entertaining and competitive team in the competition, and we have done that.

"I was grateful to be given the role to coach the club, and it has been an incredible ride.

"This job is all-encompassing; I've given it my absolute all and I'm so proud of what we've achieved, but now is the right time to go."

Fagan coached the Lions to the second premiership three-peat in the club's history. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

Fagan took charge of the Lions in 2017, and leaves having coached 243 games with a winning record of 61.32 per cent.

This year, he passed legendary Lions coach Leigh Matthews as having coached the most games for the club.

The former school teacher was also part of the Hawthorn coaching staff as the club also won a three-peat of flags from 2013–2015 as well playing a role in their 2008 triumph.

In total, Fagan led the Lions in eight-straight finals series after claiming the wooden spoon in his opening season, winning just five games in each of his first two seasons.

Saturday's stunning come-from-behind triumph was the Lions' third-successive victory in a decider after beating Sydney and Geelong over the past two years.

He also led the Lions to the 2023 grand final, falling four points short of Collingwood.

Fagan speaking to his Lions players during his first season in charge. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Brisbane Lions chair Andrew Wellington hailed Fagan for his "unwavering commitment" to helping others achieve their goals.

"Chris arrived at our club with a clear view of what good people, strong relationships and shared belief could achieve," Wellington said.

"His influence has reached far beyond the Brisbane Lions. Chris has helped strengthen football across Queensland, inspired a new generation of players and supporters, and earned the respect of the wider football public for the way he has carried himself through success and adversity."

Chief executive Sam Graham said the club respected Fagan's decision and that steps would be taken to appoint a new coach "in due course".

"Chris has played a massive role in the transformation of this club both on and off the field," he said.

"While we would have loved nothing more for him to continue on, he has earned the right to call time when he was ready, and we're pleased he's going out on top.

"Chris's achievements speak for themselves, but his greatest legacy is the environment he created, the people he developed and how he has nurtured this playing group."

Leigh Mathews (left) congratulates Chris Fagan after Saturday's grand final. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Darrian Traynor)

His departure means the Lions will have to look for a new coach to help a stacked playing list attempt to win the first AFL/VFL four-peat since the Collingwood team of 1927–30.

Possible internal candidates include Brisbane's football boss Danny Daly, senior assistant coach Cameron Bruce or backline coach Dale Morris.

Former league head coaches Nathan Buckley, Adam Simpson and Simon Goodwin have also been proposed as possible replacements.

"This club has never been in greater shape, and the list profile would suggest this," Fagan said.

"The boys will continue to contend, and I'll be their number-one fan, but a fresh face at the helm will be a key pillar for the players to come back to next season as they work hard to achieve more success.

"I'll miss the club and it will feel strange not to be involved, but for the last 10 years I've thought about nothing other than how we can improve, get better and be successful.

"To see the club develop on field from cellar dwellers to three-time premiers has been amazing.

"The Lions are the sum of our parts and everyone across the club has played their role."

World.title: Forrester breaks 17yo record at short course titles
World.content:
Jenna Forrester's outstanding 2026 has continued at the Australian Short Course Championships in Sydney, lowering the Australian women's 400m individual medley record on her way to gold.

The 23-year-old beat Ellen Fullerton's 17-year-old mark with a time of 4:28.39, taking 0.33 seconds off the record.

The time was comfortably under the qualifying standard for the upcoming world championships in Beijing.

Remarkably, Forrester had only just competed in the 200 backstroke, finishing second to Iona Anderson, also swimming under the qualification time for Beijing.

Iona Anderson held on to beat a fast-finishing Forrester in the 200m backstroke. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"That was a shock. I came here with no expectations, just to jump in and have a bit of fun," Forrester said after the race.

"I haven't done a lot of short course and that hurt doubling up [with the 200m backstroke] but I've done a lot of double-ups, especially internationally."

Forrester has already had a year to remember in 2026, claiming three individual gold medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow in the 200m backstroke, 200m IM and 400m IM, as well as winning bronze in the 400m freestyle.

She also won silver in the 400m IM at the Pan Pacs in California behind Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh.

Just 24 athletes will be selected for the team that will head to China and the famous Water Cube from December 1-6 — and Forrester has put her hand up to be one of them.

"I've always wanted to represent Australia at [the World] short course," Forrester said.

"Hopefully this year is my year."

Anderson, who also claimed four medals at the Commonwealth Games, including gold in the 100m backstroke and silver in the 50m, did her chances of selection no harm by claiming her second title of the meet.

Southam delivers statement win

In the men's 100m freestyle, Commonwealth Games champ Flynn Southam cruised to victory with a rapid 45.61.

"It's good to back up after Comm Games and be consistent but it's been pretty hard to stay motivated," Southam said.

"I'm pretty stoked with that time, to be honest … bring on the World Champs."

The 21-year-old Bond swimmer was a scratching from the 200m freestyle on the opening night to focus on the four-length dash, and he duly delivered, beating Ed Sommerville into silver by 0.45 seconds.

Flynn Southam is eyeing up the world championships in Beijing. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Southam, who won gold in the 4x50m freestyle relay at the 2022 short course worlds in Melbourne, as well as picking up three relay silvers and a bronze, said is ready to make the jump to claim an individual medal in Beijing.

"The last time I raced short course was the worlds in Melbourne four years ago so I'm really looking forward to racing the big dogs," he said.

"Comm Games was a good taste test for me with Matt Richards [Wales] and obviously Kyle [Chalmers].

"I know David Popovici [Romania's Olympic 200m champion] isn't doing worlds but Jack Alexy [USA] is someone else on my list who I'm looking forward to racing.

"As for expectation — bring on the pressure. Sometimes it does make me nervous, but I love it, and I breathe it."

Olivia Wunsch claimed the 100m free by almost a second and a half in a dominant performance. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

In the women's 100m free, Olivia Wunsch needed a personal best of 51.72 to beat Lani Pallister into silver.

The 20-year-old led from the gun to power away from the field, beating distance specialist Pallister by a colossal 1.46 seconds.

"It was pretty special to go under 52 for the first time. Doing 52 at World Cups last year was nice, but I think I surprised myself a little bit off the sort of short prep I've had into short course," Wunsch said.

"I had about three weeks off in total … it's been nice to just get back in the water, swim a little bit less, and just focus on getting my speed and enjoying getting back into it."

Rowan Crothers claimed a second victory of the week following his world record on Tuesday. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

In the men's multiclass 50m freestyle, Rowan Crothers equalled his national record to beat S10 rival Alex Tuckwell into silver.

"I'm blessed to be Australian and to have the chance to race the best in the world over and over again at these meets … watch this space because we'll be sharing a podium in LA," Tuckfield said.

Two-time Paralympic champion Crothers simply said it was "bloody exciting" to see how fast his 21-year-old rival was going.

World.title: Man City could face fines, EPL expulsion, over financial rules scandal
World.content:
Manchester City faces an uncertain future after the decorated English soccer club was found guilty of systematically breaking the Premier League's financial rules for nearly a decade.

The verdict, delivered by an independent disciplinary commission, leaves open an array of sanctions, including a fine, points deduction or even expulsion from the Premier League.

City could also face possible compensation claims from rival teams, while its ownership — the Abu Dhabi-controlled City Football Group — is coming under increasing scrutiny.

The club has rejected the verdict in a case that dates to 2018 and mainly covers its financial dealings from 2009 to 2018, and promises a relentless campaign to clear its name.

Here's a look at what's next in one of the biggest scandals in English soccer history.

Loading...

City promises 'relentless' challenge to the verdict

City can appeal the verdict and has insisted it will.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions," City said in a statement.

"The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums."

To make its appeal, City would need to send an email to the chair of the independent commission's three-person panel, who would then appoint a new appeal board — also consisting of three people, one of whom "shall have held judicial office", according to the Premier League handbook.

The board will then schedule a hearing that should finish within 12 weeks after the appeal is filed and not exceed five consecutive days.

Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) and chief executive Ferran Soriano in 2024. (AP: Dave Thompson)

Sanctions will be decided later

City's punishment will be addressed in a separate, confidential hearing with the independent commission.

The Premier League statement didn't mention whether sanctions could be imposed before the decision of the appeal was reached, only that it was the league's intention that the process be concluded "as soon as possible".

According to the Premier League, the independent commission could issue a reprimand, fine, suspension, points deduction or, in the worst case, expel the club from the competition.

Clubs have been expelled from lower leagues in England but never from the Premier League.

A club that is expelled from the Premier League could apply for membership in the English Football League, which runs the three divisions below the Premier League: the Championship, League One and League Two. The EFL's regulations say it "could be asked to accommodate any former Premier League Club(s) in League Two".

The biggest points deduction handed to a Premier League team was 10 to Everton in 2023, for overspending in one three-year financial period. That deduction was later reduced to six after an appeal.

City's breaches are much more widespread and included a refusal to cooperate, unlike Everton.

Some have called for criminal charges

The Man City case is a disciplinary proceeding, not a criminal investigation. However, some have suggested that British authorities also should look at the matter.

"If accounts have been falsified and auditors have been misled, then it is potentially a criminal matter," Lord Cruddas, a Conservative peer, told the BBC.

"The auditors will call in the police, directors are personally liable for any fraud of a UK company even if it is foreign-owned."

According to the Fraud Act of 2006, individuals can face up to 10 years in prison if they are found to have dishonestly made a false representation with the intention of making a gain or avoiding a loss.

There have been no reports of any criminal investigation in the case.

City sponsor Etihad Airways considers legal action

Etihad Airways, City's main sponsor, was considering legal against the Premier League for the way the investigation findings were communicated, Sky News reported late on Wednesday.

Sky News quoted an Etihad statement saying "we stand with the club", adding that the Abu Dhabi-based airline said it would "seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests … at no time did the Premier League reach out to or engage with Etihad in the process associated with the commission's opinion".

Rival teams could make claims for compensation

No club has publicly announced its intention to make a compensation claim based on the impact of City's rule-breaking. However, the BBC has reported that a number of clubs had started seeking advice over whether they would have a case for financial compensation, before the verdict had been announced.

A precedent was set this year when Everton was ordered to pay more than 35 million pounds ($67 million) in compensation to Burnley, which successfully argued to a disciplinary commission that it would have survived relegation — at Everton's expense — in the 2021–22 campaign had its rival been given its six-point penalty for the financial breaches that season.

In City's case, top teams could argue they lost out on titles or Champions League qualification — worth tens of millions of dollars each season — because of City's conduct, and weaker teams could claim defeats to City's expensively assembled squads contributed to relegation or lower finishing positions in the league standings, and therefore reduced prize money.

AP

World.title: Five things to know ahead of the NRL and NRLW grand finals
World.content:
The final day of the NRL and NRLW season is almost here. The grand finals for the men and women will be held on Sunday.

In the women's decider, the Sydney Roosters and Brisbane Broncos face off in a rematch of last year's grand final.

In the men's grand final, the Sydney Roosters are facing the Newcastle Knights.

Here's everything you need to know about the NRL and NRLW grand finals day.

What time are the NRL and NRLW grand finals?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals will be held on Sunday, October 4, the first day of daylight saving time in many states and territories across the country.

Here is when each grand final begins in each state and territory.

NRL grand final

7:30pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

7pm ACDT: South Australia

6:30pm: Queensland

6pm: Northern Territory

4:30pm: Western Australia

NRLW grand final

4pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

3:30pm ACDT: South Australia

3pm: Queensland

2:30pm: Northern Territory

1pm: Western Australia

How can you watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 9 and 9Now, but be very aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire NRL season that is exclusive to Channel 9.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

Where are the NRL and NRLW grand finals being played?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals are being played at Stadium Australia in Sydney.

Stadium Australia has hosted every NRL grand final since 1999, with the exception of the 2021 decider which was played at Brisbane's Lang Park during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since the NRLW's inception in 2018, all grand finals have been played at Stadium Australia, again with 2021 being the exception. That decider was played at Dolphin Stadium in Redcliffe.

Who is playing in the NRL grand final?

The Sydney Roosters face the Newcastle Knights for the NRL premiership.

The Roosters finished the season fourth on the ladder, and lost their opening match of the finals before victories over Cronulla and the Dolphins.

The Newcastle Knights finished seventh on the ladder. After defeating Souths in the first week of the finals, the Knights went to Auckland and defeated the Warriors, then beat Penrith while being down to 12 players for all of the second half.
