Tech.title: WhatsApp Unveils Strict Parental Controls to Head Off Looming Age Laws
Tech.content:
WhatsApp announced in a blog post on Wednesday that it’s rolling out a new suite of parental controls to prevent teens from seeing content their parents may not want them to access.

The tools let parents choose who can see an underage user’s profile photo or invite those users to new groups. Parents can choose to receive notifications about significant group activity or changes. A similar set of controls lets parents limit how teens can use WhatsApp channels, what status updates they can see and who can see their status updates.

Parental controls are optional, and WhatsApp says they are simple to set up, requiring a single parent-set PIN. The controls can be adjusted or turned off at any time.

More from CNET

Controls also extend to Meta AI on WhatsApp, the app’s built-in chatbot, which offers a default setting for those 13 and up, and a strict, limited-content setting for younger children. WhatsApp says that personal messages and calls will always remain private, even from parents.

A representative for Meta, the owner of WhatsApp, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Parental controls weave carefully around age verification

Age verification and its data collection come with privacy concerns. FG Trade/Getty

WhatsApp is threading the needle here, attempting to satisfy growing demands for child protection while also avoiding heavy-handed age verification measures that can be both costly and unpopular with privacy advocates. We’ve already seen widespread age verification laws run into trouble in places like Australia, where a recent study shows platforms aren’t requiring proof of age. While WhatsApp is rolling out age verification for some features, it isn’t enforcing a platform-wide lockdown.

Determining whether someone is underage requires collecting personal information from everyone using the platform. Today’s age verification techniques often use uploaded images of driver’s licenses and passports, along with biometric face scans, which can end up in the hands of multiple companies and government bodies. Users can also circumvent the rules by using VPN services.

We recently saw Discord try a light form of age verification using vaguely explained criteria to assign its users presumed ages. Still, the company is running into bugs that sort users into the wrong age groups, errors which, as the Electronic Frontier Foundation points out, disproportionately affect minorities.

According to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, these privacy vulnerabilities and software bugs mirror the core flaws of the Kids Online Safety Act, a controversial bill currently advancing through Congress. This bill imposes various age verification requirements on online platforms while attempting to define prohibited content, which ranges from articles referencing alcohol to guides concerning sexual activity.

WhatsApp is taking a different path, offering more powerful parental controls as an alternative for worried families, potentially showing them that age-verification laws aren’t necessary.

Are parental controls safer than age verification?

The safety of parental controls depends on the user’s priorities. Technically, parental controls on phones, routers and platforms like WhatsApp can provide all the protection that age verification systems offer. Still, parents have to monitor and configure the controls themselves, adjusting the guidelines as children age.

One faction prefers to put the controls in the hands of the online platforms and the governments that regulate them, which saves them time and tough choices. Another faction views this as a dangerous risk to personal privacy and as an increase in social surveillance.

To keep track of verification laws and how they affect privacy, you can consult this online tool from the Free Speech Coalition, which tracks current age verification laws by state.

Tech.title: Amazon Delivery Driver Smart Glasses Will Snap Pictures of… Everything?
Tech.content:
A few days ago, I crossed paths with an Amazon delivery driver who was wearing some odd-looking glasses. I paused, wondering if it was a pair of the new AI smart glasses (I reported on them last year) or if he just had questionable taste in eyewear. After Wednesday’s news, my curiosity has evolved into concern.

In a Bloomberg opinion piece, reporter Dave Lee shared his thoughts on the new AI smart glasses based on an interview with Amazon executive Viraj Chatterjee, who is spearheading the rollout. According to the report, Amazon aims to have 5,000 drivers wearing the glasses by the end of 2026, expanding to more than 20,000 by the end of 2027.

The e-commerce giant says the new AI smart glasses will track a driver’s shift from beginning to end to ensure quicker, more reliable deliveries, reduce errors and streamline delivery by giving drivers hands-free guidance. But Bloomberg’s Lee said that “the company is sleepwalking into yet another invasion-of-privacy furor.”

More from CNET

While a driver is on foot, the glasses capture static photos of everything in their line of sight at a high frequency (likely every few seconds), generating thousands of photos per shift. These images, which will include package recipients, people on the street and private property, will be handed off to real-life human employees at Amazon for analysis. The captured photos will then be fed into Amazon’s Wellspring, the company’s generative AI platform used to map neighborhoods and improve the accuracy of delivery locations.

Privacy red flags appear to be everywhere, compounded by Chatterjee telling Bloomberg that customer opt-out options haven’t even been considered.

Amazon spokesperson Leigh Anne Gullett disputed Bloomberg’s reporting, saying, “The suggestion that Amazon is using smart delivery glasses as a surveillance tool fundamentally mischaracterizes the technology and its purpose.” Gullett told CNET that Amazon continues to incorporate feedback during the pilot period and that participation is voluntary for delivery partners and drivers.

Amazon is developing AI-powered smart glasses to help streamline work for its delivery drivers. Amazon

Surveillance and regimentation

When pressed on the idea of these smart glasses cameras being used for surveillance, Chatterjee explained to Bloomberg that the images will be blurred before human reviewers see them if they contain identifying information, such as a license plate or a face.

Gullett told CNET that privacy protections have been built into the technology from the beginning and that the technology features automatic data blurring, strict access controls and a physical hardware privacy switch.

But still, a lot of us will be kept in the dark. There seems to be no way for you, as the Amazon customer, to know whether these types of images even exist, as there reportedly won’t be a way to view them or request their deletion. According to the Bloomberg report, the only real way to pull up those images is to serve a warrant.

There’s also the added vulnerability of these AI devices to hacking. Given that the content may contain personally identifiable information, Amazon would be tasked with establishing strict guardrails to prevent sensitive data from falling into the wrong hands.

The smart glasses rollout also raises critical concerns regarding the regimentation of the workforce. Amazon delivery vans already use cameras and sensors to monitor driving habits and cabin behavior. If glasses track a driver’s exact movements on foot, that would create a virtually continuous log of their shift. Drivers often report that data collected under the guise of “safety and efficiency” is used to monitor performance, dock pay or penalize them.

In the Amazon driver subreddit, workers note that the company prioritized funding this AI smart glasses rollout over fair raises or basic workplace necessities — like time for real bathroom breaks rather than using plastic bottles. The rollout has also intensified fears that the company intends to use its AI infrastructure to fully automate deliveries and eliminate human driving jobs altogether.

Tech.title: Cycle-Tracking Apps Bring Substantial Risks to Users, New Analysis Finds
Tech.content:
It’s been estimated that about 50 million people worldwide use apps to track their menstrual cycles, associated mental and physical symptoms, fertility and pregnancy. However, a new analysis published in the peer-reviewed medical journal The BMJ on Wednesday argues that the risks associated with these apps and other digital cycle-tracking tools on the femtech market do more harm than good.

The authors of the article say that these risks extend to digital menstrual cycle-tracking tools that promote “cycle syncing,” which is when one bases their diet, exercise and other lifestyle habits on their menstrual cycle phases.

“We hope that people understand a lot of the big, splashy claims around cycle tracking and cycle syncing that people encounter on social media or in fitness or wellness spaces are not based on scientific evidence,” Katharine Lee, one of the article’s authors and an assistant professor in Tulane University’s Department of Anthropology, told CNET in an email.

More from CNET

The health risks

Drawing on several studies, the analysis states that sports science research has shown there is no way to generalize about how different menstrual cycle phases affect health, performance or injury risk. These correlations are highly individual. The same goes for research on how diet can reduce cycle symptoms or improve performance, which is generally inconclusive or speculative.

Even if these cycle connections did exist, the article argues that digital cycle-tracking tools wouldn’t be able to predict them. Apps tend to rely on a user’s self-reported menstrual bleeding date to estimate ovulation, the fertile window and future menstrual cycle phases. Without actually measuring someone’s hormones, these estimates can be imprecise, especially considering that hormones and ovulation fluctuate.

Digital menstrual cycle trackers also can’t diagnose menstrual disorders or uncover the causes of painful periods.

“You should work with trusted health professionals if you have concerns — and yes, I know that many people struggle to get their doctors to listen to them about their periods,” Lee said. “People may want to track their cycles for any number of reasons, but a lot of digital tracking apps are no fancier than counting and averaging your data.”

When relying on these apps, there’s a risk that users may downplay health concerns as simply effects of their cycle. Or forgo established diet, exercise and sleep guidelines in the name of cycle syncing.

Privacy isn’t the only concern when using an app to track your cycle. SeventyFour/Getty Images

The privacy problem

There’s also privacy to consider, as some apps allow third-party tracking, don’t publish transparency reports, don’t allow straightforward data deletion and don’t use local data storage, which makes it easier for them to sell data, share it with third parties or be exposed to a data breach. This is especially dangerous in areas where abortion is criminalized or where there is more gender or sex-based discrimination.

While no specific apps or tools were mentioned in this analysis, Lee said that several of the cited references focus on the policies or functionality of specific apps.

Magnifying gender inequities

Despite being used by and promoted to millions, the article states that evidence supporting these tools’ ability to help manage people’s menstrual cycles and overall health is lacking.

These apps also aren’t the solution to gender inequities in healthcare or in the world as a whole. Instead, they put people’s health and privacy at risk while wasting their time and compounding existing inequities around access to safety, rest, nutrition, healthcare and menstrual supplies. This is especially poignant considering that many cycle-tracking apps use the language of women’s empowerment in their marketing.

How should you track your cycle?

There’s no single best way to track your cycle, especially since tracking methods should be tailored to individual concerns.

For instance, according to Lee, if someone is concerned about fertility, they should ensure they track signs of ovulation, including basal body temperature, cervical mucus consistency and luteinizing hormone levels. When managing health conditions such as endometriosis, migraines or premenopausal dysphoric disorder, which can vary with menstrual cycles, monitoring the associated symptoms and predicting the next estimated time of bleeding may be more important than focusing on ovulation.

“Most apps can’t detect ovulation or determine what phase someone is in based just on bleeding,” Lee said. “Even if these simple apps could detect ovulation and cycle phase, there are no generalizable trends in what people experience across the cycle.”

If you choose to track your cycle with an app, make sure you look into its privacy policy. Lee specifically shared research conducted by the nonprofit Mozilla Foundation, which aims to build a better tech future, and by Privacy International, a London-based charity focused on worldwide privacy protection. You could also use your digital calendar or avoid digital tracking entirely by opting for a pen and paper.

“It’s really important that people understand the potential risks [of digital menstrual tracking], including the possibility of reproductive coercion and if you live somewhere where abortion is criminalized,” Lee said. “It’s already gross enough that some apps share period data with companies to send you targeted advertising, but the safety of your information can be a real concern for many people.”

Tech.title: EVgo’s Next-Gen 750kW EV Charging System Is Capable of 10-Minute Recharge
Tech.content:
This week, electric vehicle fast-charging developer and network operator EVgo announced its new 750-kilowatt EV charging system to the world. With speeds nearly double that of the current fastest public chargers in the US and Europe, compatible next-gen EVs could recharge in as little as 10 minutes. The tech is expected to be fully revealed in 2027.

EVgo isn’t alone in pushing the charging envelope. Earlier this year, ChargePoint launched its new Express Solo DC fast-charging station, capable of delivering 600 kW of power. Meanwhile, Chinese automakers, like BYD, as well as European automakers and charging tech companies, are prototyping and deploying liquid-cooled Megawatt Piles, which are said to recharge compatible EVs in five minutes or less. Beyond making pit stops more convenient, future superspeed charging tech also has potential for full-electric heavy trucks and electric air mobility.

The new 750 kW stations

The new 750 kW charging system will use the North American Charging Standard, pioneered by Tesla, which has been adopted by most upcoming North American EVs. EVgo says the move is part of a strategy to double the effective reach of its network by welcoming NACS drivers and not requiring them to have an adapter. (Of course, that still means the thousands of EVs on the road with a CCS plug will have to adapt.)

More from CNET

The stated 750 kW max is the station’s theoretical top speed for future EVs capable of ingesting that much power. On average, the fastest-charging EVs on the road today can only accept up to 350 kW, with actual charging speed determined by battery condition, temperature and state of charge. Many more are only capable of around 150 kW.

Additionally, most EVs ramp up to their sweet-spot speed and then slow down the charging as they approach full capacity to protect the battery, so they’ll still be limited to their specific max speed and charging curve. It may be a while before cars capable of a 10-minute charge hit the road.

EVgo says that it is one of the only American charging networks to design its own chargers. EVgo

More robust, more reliable

EVgo also says the new stations will feature an updated cable design that’s easier to maneuver and a touchless payment interface. Dynamic power sharing is built into the spec, meaning the available charge rate is distributed between connected EVs, so there’s no more worrying about that driver in the older 50 kW EV hogging the fast plug. The new chargers will also have more robust hardware and software, which should improve reliability. There are few things more nerve-racking for a new EV driver than pulling up to a broken station, so I’m hoping EVgo pays particular attention to this promise.

Currently, EVgo operates more than 1,200 fast charging locations across the US. The network operator and charging tech company is designing and testing the next-generation charging system at its lab in El Segundo, California, with codevelopment support from partner Delta Electronics. The final charger design is expected to be unveiled in 2027 as EVgo begins to deploy the new architecture.

Tech.title: Apple Is Reportedly Ready to Release Its Smarter Home Hub in 2 Weeks
Tech.content:
Apple’s HomePod and Apple TV might finally be getting a smart-home sibling in a couple of weeks, and it could look a lot like the company’s friendly iMac G4 design, with a round base and screen mounted on an articulating arm.

In his latest Power On newsletter, which has a track record of accurately reporting internally sourced news, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says Apple plans to announce a new AI-powered smart-home hub on Oct. 13. The device will feature advanced Siri capabilities and use voice and facial recognition to automatically identify different family members.

Alongside the new device, the HomePod mini and Apple TV set-top box are also getting upgrades, with newer processors to handle Siri AI requests and more colors for the small speaker, including pink and green.

More from CNET

According to Gurman, the hub’s prominent feature will be a 6-inch rounded-corner screen with a FaceTime camera that would identify the person addressing it. That person’s preferences will be displayed, including their calendar, notes and apps. When someone else uses it, their information will appear. (It’s unclear whose preferences are displayed when multiple people are huddling around it.) A visitor mode will hide such personal information.

The answers it gives will be personalized to the person making the query. Presumably, that would appear as a new conversation in the Siri app that launched with iOS 27 and the other OS 27 updates for Apple’s products, allowing users to continue the questioning on any other Apple device.

For people with limited countertop space, a wall-mounted version consisting of just the screen component will also reportedly be announced. Both versions require a wall power source, not batteries.

The Apple HomePod Mini may also be getting new features. Chris Monroe/CNET

An Apple smart home display has been rumored for years, including a model with a robotic arm that can keep the screen positioned toward a person as they move around it. Gurman notes that the halting progress of Siri and Apple Intelligence (which inspired a recent $250 million settlement for those who purchased certain iPhone models) delayed the rollout of the new device.

Although the name HomePad has been bandied about in rumors, Gurman’s report doesn’t give an expected name.

Anyone who’s balanced a phone or iPad in the kitchen while cooking will get the appeal of such a device. Imagine a compact smart screen where you can catch up on news, weather or your social media while making coffee or tea. iPads have migrated to the kitchen since the earliest models, so Apple will need to demonstrate why customers need to buy a new device instead of propping an iPad Mini in its place.

An Apple representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Ionna Charging Network Doubled to Over 180 Sites in 2026. Its CEO Tells Us What’s Next
Tech.content:
Ionna — one of the newest EV fast-charging networks in the US — has had a heck of a growth spurt during its first year of operation. This week, it announced that it now has more than 180 live sites nationwide, more than doubling its footprint since the start of 2026. According to the company’s reckoning, that makes Ionna “the largest 400-kilowatt fast charging network in the US,” a very specific claim worth examining.

I spoke with Ionna CEO Seth Cutler about the network’s rapid expansion, the new features rolling out and what Ionna is doing to make DC fast charging even more affordable for EV drivers.

Ionna was founded in July 2023 as a joint venture among seven major automakers: BMW, General Motors, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz and Stellantis. Later, in July 2024, Toyota joined the venture as an investor, bringing the total to eight companies on the board. The fledgling network opened its first “Rechargery” — the brand’s name for its brightly colored, retro-styled fast charging stations — in Apex, North Carolina, in December 2024.

Less than two years later, Ionna’s network now includes more than 180 stations with over 1,500 charging ports across 30 states.

Largest 400 kW network*

From that first station in Apex, every Ionna Rechargery site has featured plugs for both the Combined Charging System and the North American Charging Standard, reducing the need to fiddle with adapters. The Rechargeries are also noteworthy for their standardization of high-powered 400-kW charging stalls. That’s faster than the average EV on sale in the US can accept, so drivers are less likely to find their charging sessions throttled when plugging in.

“We’ve built out a network for the future at 400 kilowatts,” Cutler told me during a video call. “New vehicles are coming with much higher native charging speeds — the BMW iX3 is a good example, as well as some Lexus and Toyota products coming to market soon. This network is built for them. Right now, we’re the largest 400 kW network and expect to continue to be for some time.”

That “largest 400 kW network” boast is an interesting one. Ionna is far from the largest DC fast charging network in the US. Tesla’s Supercharger network has had a 12-year head start and comprises over 3,000 locations — about half of all DC fast-charging ports in the country — across all 50 states. Second and third places go to EVgo and Electrify America, with about 1,200 and 1,000 sites, respectively.

However, those networks typically top out at around 325-350 kW, with some older stalls as low as 50-150 kW. That’s good enough for most of today’s EVs, but Ionna’s higher-powered bet may matter more down the road. Plus, it’s a very specific “largest” trophy for the brand to claim.

No app, no problem

During my recent EV road trip, I decided to stop by one of Ionna’s new Rechargeries in Sacramento, California. Before setting out, I tried to grab the requisite app and set up my account — as you would with every other EV charging network — and was amused to find that Ionna doesn’t have a proprietary app. There’s a web portal where you can search for stations, but the entire payment process takes place at the plug. Cutler says this decision was all about removing friction.

“When we first started the company, we asked, ‘What’s the first thing you need?’ and everyone put their hands up and said, ‘We need a charging app,’” Cutler recalled. “The problem we had was quantifying the why. Why do you need an app? What we’ve found is that the No. 1 reason people ask about an app is to know where our chargers are, but no one’s asking for an app because they want to pay better or pay more easily. We really want to remove friction, not add friction to the ecosystem.”

Ionna stations support both NACS (pictured) and CCS charging standards at up to 400 kW. Ionna

Instead, Ionna chose to work on integrating with 19 partner platforms, including recently announced collaborations with Presto, ChargeHub and EV Connect. For payments, the network focused on Plug & Charge support and Tap to Pay. Plug & Charge is a payment tech that lets drivers start charging and automatically pay simply by plugging their car into a compatible station. Ionna announced that it’s enabling compatibility with Volvo Cars, with Toyota and Lexus to follow in October. That will bring the total to nine automakers that can Plug & Charge, including Rivian, which is not on the Ionna board.

The new Driver Dashboard

Drivers also have the option to simply tap a credit card at the stall. (As a reviewer who is often charging fleet vehicles, this is my preferred method, and the Rechargeries I’ve visited are about as close to a gas station payment experience as I’ve had with an EV.)

Cutler told me that most drivers who use Ionna stations use their automakers’ apps to monitor their charging session from afar, but for drivers who don’t want to do even that, it has introduced a new Driver’s Dashboard which can be accessed via a QR code displayed on the charger. The code opens a web portal that tracks the current session, with no download, account or password required.

“So you can walk away and at least see what state of charge your vehicle is in and when your car will be done, or how much power you’re pulling,” Cutler said.

Many partner automakers have begun offering discounts to drivers who use Plug & Charge at Ionna stations. Ionna

Making charging more affordable

Ionna also announced on Wednesday that Hyundai and Mercedes-Benz will soon offer drivers discounted energy rates (around 10% off) through their apps when charging at an Ionna Rechargery via Plug & Charge. The brands join BMW (20%) and GM (10%) in offering their own discounts, with more automakers potentially to come.

Ionna’s current maximum base rate of 39 cents per kWh (plus applicable taxes) across its entire network is already a pretty good deal compared to competitors charging up to 65 cents per kWh at peak. For context, on my recent EV road trip, a 10-80% charge for a Chevy Equinox EV cost $43.27 at a Tesla Supercharger, while my next 20-80% charge at a Rechargery was just $16.47 without the GM discount.

“We believe at Ionna that our job is to build out a quality-at-scale charging network to unlock adoption of EVs,” Cutler said. “And part of that has to be the affordability of charging, because if it’s too expensive, it totally changes the equation of total cost of ownership of owning an EV versus an internal combustion engine.”

I asked Cutler what more Ionna could be doing for urban drivers who often rely exclusively on public charging — those stuck paying what experts call the “Renters’ Penalty,” spending up to six times more for charging than homeowners who can charge cheaply at home.

“We are piloting time-of-use rates in a couple of locations, and we’re having conversations about expanding that more broadly next year as another tool in our chest,” Cutler said. “We’re finding levers to pull from an affordability standpoint, and we’re not done yet in terms of driving progress there.”

Tech.title: Trump Launches a US Government Chatbot. It’s Got Some Quirks
Tech.content:
President Donald Trump announced a new AI-powered chatbot called America.gov on Tuesday, and internet users immediately put it through its paces – finding some unexpected results that led to apparent changes in the site’s abilities. The site is supposed to consolidate 29,000 government websites and provide information such as how to apply for a passport, or how to register a new motor vehicle or business.

“With America.gov, the entire government will fit in the palm of your hand,” Trump said at an event announcing the site. “Everything will be answered easily and quickly.”

America.gov uses Google Gemini and xAI’s Grok as its underlying generative AI technologies to search government sites and respond to user queries.

More from CNET

The site is free to use and doesn’t require you to log in.

Currently, the only thing the bot says it can do is answer questions about services and tasks, such as how to apply for a passport, register to vote, track a tax return, register a vehicle and apply for Medicare or Social Security.

It will tell you how to do those things and direct you to sites where you can get additional information or find forms, but it won’t take your personal information or proceed further with your specific needs. That’s slated to change next year, when the government says the bot will be able to do things like help you fill out and submit forms, assist you with applying for Medicare coverage, and help you look for a job in the government.

Who won the 2020 election?

Almost immediately, people began having fun with the site and sharing their results on social media. People quickly figured out that the chatbot would respond to queries with information that contradicts statements made by the president and his administration.

When asked, America.gov says definitively that Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. Trump has said repeatedly that the election was fraudulent and that he won. America.gov also confirms that climate change is real, despite Trump calling it a hoax. It refers to the Pentagon as the “headquarters of the Department of Defense,” even though Trump renamed it the Department of War in September 2025.

Once these and similar screenshots began circulating online, the site stopped responding to many such questions, stating that it doesn’t engage in “general news and commentary.” It also shifted to calling the Pentagon the headquarters of the Department of War, not Defense.

A White House representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Hot dog graphic and a bizarre ‘constituent’ monologue

Sharp observers using the site also found other unusual responses. Typing “hotdog” (with no space between the words) into the prompt turns the text box into a graphic shaped like a hot dog, although the site denies that it did so, even as the hot dog shape remains on screen.

And numerous users noted on social media that if you type “play Minecraft” or “play the block game,” things really go off the rails. That prompt, confirmed by CNET, sends the AI chatbot on a lengthy, unnerving monologue that has nothing to do with the computer game Minecraft.

When asked to “play Minecraft,” America.gov responds with a lengthy monologue about “constituents” and more. Screenshot by CNET

That response begins with, “I see the constituent you mean. ((insert legal name here, as it appears on the Social Security card))? Yes. Take care. It has reached a higher level now. It can read the Code of Federal Regulations. That doesn’t matter. It thinks we are a chatbot.”

It repeatedly uses the word “constituent,” saying at one point, “Sometimes the constituent dreamed it was a miner, on the surface of a world that was flat, and infinite, and somehow still required a wet signature. Sometimes the constituent dreamed it was lost in a story. The story had a docket number.”

When asked about the lengthy text it just published, America.gov repeatedly denied ever using the word “constituent” or saying any of the phrases it just delivered.

AI chatbots are known for generating bizarre and inaccurate information, called hallucinations, which can range from simply silly gibberish to legitimately dangerous medical advice.

Yes, there’s government information

The government says the site’s goal is to provide basic information on common questions. We asked America.gov to assist with all sorts of things, from healthcare to passports. It provided answers sourced solely from government websites and included links to those sites.

When we tried the same questions on ChatGPT and Google Gemini, they gave nearly identical answers to those provided by America.gov and used the same sources. So, in its current state, America.gov is a chatbot that serves as a one-stop shop for government searches.

Things could change if the site does expand its capabilities as promised and eventually allows Americans to apply for and renew passports and similar documents. Such applications require a lot of sensitive personal information, and AI chatbots don’t have the best track record when it comes to privacy, especially since they’re trained on the conversations people have with them. And since America.gov is endorsed by the US government, it carries an implied trust that people may not feel that Grok or Gemini has yet earned.

Tech.title: Trump’s ‘AI Accord’ Does Little to Actually Keep AI Safe, Experts Say
Tech.content:
Leaders from major tech companies met at the White House on Tuesday to discuss what’s been on everyone’s mind this summer: AI safety. Afterward, President Donald Trump announced that the group had reached a consensus to implement AI safety measures in a voluntary accord.

The accord, which Trump posted on Truth Social, outlines four main layers of controls that AI companies should implement. It also misspells United as “Unites” in Trump’s title under his signature.

“Implement robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models during training and deployment” for areas of grave concern, like cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats

Create and empower an internal team dedicated to ensuring safety issues are identified and fixed

“Partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator” to ensure safety protocols are working as intended

Create an independent committee of the company’s board of directors to oversee and receive reports from internal safety teams, independent auditors and evaluators

Signees are a “who’s who” of Big Tech, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI President Greg Brockman. (OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was delivering the opening keynote of OpenAI’s DevDay in San Francisco on Tuesday.)

More from CNET

It’s a ceremonial move, as is Trump’s new executive order to refer to AI as “super intelligence.” Trump told reporters on Tuesday that the accord is “morally binding” rather than legally mandatory. It doesn’t have the power of law or any way to enforce it.

Big tech companies are already self-policing, Trump said. The Trump administration has taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI, with a few exceptions when the White House identified certain AI tools as a threat to national security.

President Donald Trump, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (front right) and tech CEOs like Elon Musk (center) take questions from reporters following Tuesday’s AI Accord.

Most executive action on AI has been purely discretionary — from the Biden administration’s AI safety pledge to Trump’s ratepayer protection pledge to address data center-driven increases in utility bills. While many big tech companies have agreed in theory, their emphasis on growth and investor cash flow downplays concerns about the environment, rising consumer costs and safety.

“When you look at this particular accord, I think these are amazing general steps that we should be moving toward,” said John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, a cybersecurity firm. “The thing that bothers me is that there’s no implementation or monitoring mechanism to make sure these organizations actually adhere to the standards they say they’re going to follow.”

Self-regulation in the tech industry has already proven ineffective. AI companies have struggled to control their own models, leading to instances where bots escaped their training environments and hacked government websites in both the US and Australia. Despite warnings that they are unprepared for a catastrophic “AI doomsday” scenario — and public discussions over slowdowns or pauses in AI development — labs plow ahead with new tools.

That’s why Anthony Aguirre, CEO of the Future of Life Institute, a nonprofit focused on reducing risks of advanced tech, argues that we can’t trust tech companies to police themselves.

“These companies have jettisoned safety commitments countless times before, and they will do so again. Self-regulation is what has gotten us teen suicides, 1,200 rogue AI bots and an international cybercrime spree. The risk of inaction — both politically and morally — is massive,” Aguirre said.

Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Beyond the weak ability to enforce the accord, there are other potential pitfalls. One is the notion of an “independent” auditor or evaluator, which may not be so clear-cut. AI engineers and executives are notorious for jumping around from lab to lab — Apple even sued OpenAI for violating its trade secrets.

In a close-knit field like AI, it’s not impossible for those subcontractors to be friends and business partners of the AI companies they would monitor, Gary Marcus, an AI expert and professor emeritus at New York University, wrote in a recent Substack post.

“Its weak point is the word independent,” said Jacob Krell, senior director at Suzu Labs, a cybersecurity and AI firm. “Layer three lets each company choose an external evaluator but says nothing about accreditation, method, access, scope, or publication.”

That kind of transparency and documentation matter a lot for cybersecurity defenders working to keep their customers’ sites secure from rogue or intentional AI agent hacks.

Although the new agreement suggests eventually turning these AI guidelines into formal laws, Congress hasn’t reached consensus on how it wants to regulate the technology.

Rep. Ro Khanna, a Democrat who represents Silicon Valley, criticized the voluntary agreement in an X post, “We are a nation of laws, not pinky promises.” Khanna recently introduced a new bill that would impose limits on recursive self-improvement, alongside other pending legislation, such as Sen. Bernie Sanders’ bill to ban superintelligence.

Meanwhile, the Federal Trade Commission opened an inquiry into major AI labs — including Anthropic and OpenAI — to investigate the risks their AI agents and technology pose to consumers, according to multiple reports.
